title:	osx.c: min, max and getch are still declared where the compiler can't check them
state:	OPEN
author:	scottdensmore (Scott Densmore)
labels:	good first issue
comments:	0
assignees:	
projects:	
milestone:	
issue-type:	
parent:	
sub-issues:	
sub-issues-completed:	
blocked-by:	
blocking:	
number:	38
--
## Problem

`sst.h:503-507` declares:

```c
int min(int, int);
int max(int, int);
int getch(void);
```

`osx.c` defines all three — but cannot include `sst.h`, because `sst.h`
declares `void pause(int)` and `osx.c` needs POSIX `pause(void)` from
`<unistd.h>`. So the definitions are never checked against the
declarations: a signature change surfaces at link time or as undefined
behaviour.

This is the same defect class #10 fixed for `tui_active` and
`tui_getch`, left behind because it needed a different home. `tui.h` is
the wrong place for `min`/`max`.

## Why it matters

Small, but it is the last of its kind in the tree, and `osx.c` is the
one file that cannot see the header everything else uses.

## Suggested approach

`stdio_is_terminal()` shows the shape that works: declare it in a header
`osx.c` can include. Options worth weighing:

- A small `osx.h` holding what `osx.c` provides (`min`, `max`, `getch`,
  `randomize`), included by both `osx.c` and `sst.h`. Keeps one
  declaration each and leaves the `pause` collision alone.
- Rename the game's `pause` so `osx.c` can include `sst.h` outright.
  Larger, touches many call sites, but removes the constraint rather
  than working around it — see the comment at `osx.c:29`.

The first is the smaller change; the second is the one that makes the
awkwardness go away.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `osx.c`'s definitions of `min`, `max` and `getch` are checked
      against declarations at compile time.

/* Full-screen curses interface (sst -t).
 *
 * The pure formatting functions live in tuifmt.c so they can be unit
 * tested without curses; the curses backend itself lives in tui.c.
 *
 * Self-contained on purpose: including this must not oblige a file to
 * include sst.h as well. See the note on tui_active below.
 */
#ifndef SST_TUI_H
#define SST_TUI_H

#define FMTBUFLEN (48)	/* enough for any panel line */
#define STATLABEL (14)	/* width fmt_status_line pads its labels to;
			   where tui.c starts colouring the value */

/* What a grid cell and a status line are, for colouring.
 *
 * A cell is classified from the character the panel is about to show,
 * never from the game state behind it. When the sensors are damaged
 * every hidden cell reads as '-', so they all classify alike and
 * colour cannot become a way to see what a scan is hiding. */
enum cellclass {
	CELL_PLAIN,	/* empty space, grid labels */
	CELL_HOSTILE,	/* Klingons, Commanders, Romulans, Tholians */
	CELL_SHIP,	/* ours */
	CELL_BASE,
	CELL_STAR,
	CELL_PLANET,
	CELL_WEB,
	CELL_THING,	/* the unknown object Spock tells you to look at */
	CELL_HIDDEN	/* masked by damaged sensors */
};

enum statusclass {
	STAT_PLAIN,
	STAT_GOOD,
	STAT_WARN,
	STAT_BAD,
	STAT_DOCKED
};

/* Panel formatters (tuifmt.c). Both read the global game state. */
void fmt_quad_line(int i, char *buf);	/* i=0 header, 1..10 grid rows */
void fmt_status_line(int i, char *buf);	/* i=1..10, srscan status fields */
int sensors_masked(void);		/* the grid is hiding cells */
int cell_class(char c);			/* colour class of a shown cell */
int status_class(int i);		/* colour class of a status line */

/* Curses backend (tui.c) */

/* Plain extern, and defined in tui.c, rather than going through the
 * EXTERN/INCLUDED trick that instantiates the game state: these two
 * describe the display, not the game, and keeping them out of it is
 * what lets this header stand on its own. osx.c needs that -- it wants
 * POSIX pause(void) from <unistd.h>, and sst.h declares a pause(int)
 * that collides with it.
 */
extern int tui_active;	/* TUI mode is on and curses is running */
extern int tui_ingame;	/* a game is set up, so the panels have something
			   to show; false through the setup questions,
			   including a second game's */

int stdio_is_terminal(void);	/* osx.c; stdin and stdout are both ttys */

int tui_init(void);		/* returns TRUE if the TUI started */
int tui_terminal_capable(void);	/* TERM is known and can address the cursor */
void tui_shutdown(void);
void tui_gameover(void);	/* the game has ended; clear the panels */
void tui_puts(char *s);
void tui_puts_slow(char *s);
int tui_readline(char *buf, int buflen);	/* fgets-like: keeps '\n';
						   FALSE when input has ended */
int tui_getch(void);
void tui_clearmsg(void);
int tui_pageheight(void);	/* usable message-window lines for paging */
void tui_refresh_panels(void);

#endif	/* SST_TUI_H */

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.21)
include(CMakePrintHelpers)

project(sst
        LANGUAGES C
        VERSION 1.0)

set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING")

# Warnings are on for everyone, so a new one is visible where it is
# introduced. They are only fatal where that can be enforced without
# breaking somebody's build on a compiler version nobody here has
# tried: CI turns SST_WERROR on, a contributor gets the warning and a
# working build.
option(SST_WERROR "Treat compiler warnings as errors (CI does)" OFF)
if(CMAKE_C_COMPILER_ID MATCHES "GNU|Clang")
    set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -Wall -Wextra")
    if(SST_WERROR)
        set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -Werror")
    endif()
endif()

if(${CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE} STREQUAL "Debug")
    set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -DDEBUG")
    cmake_print_variables(CMAKE_C_FLAGS)
endif()

add_executable(sst sst.c ai.c battle.c events.c finish.c moving.c osx.c planets.c reports.c rules.c setup.c tui.c tuifmt.c)

set(CURSES_NEED_NCURSES TRUE)
find_package(Curses REQUIRED)
target_include_directories(sst PRIVATE ${CURSES_INCLUDE_DIRS})
target_link_libraries(sst PRIVATE ${CURSES_LIBRARIES} m)

# tui.c calls setupterm/tigetstr, which some distributions ship in a
# separate libtinfo. Linking -lncurses happens to pull it in where
# libncurses.so is a linker script, but that is luck, not a contract.
find_library(TINFO_LIBRARY tinfo)
if(TINFO_LIBRARY)
    target_link_libraries(sst PRIVATE ${TINFO_LIBRARY})
endif()

enable_testing()
add_executable(test_tuifmt tests/test_tuifmt.c tuifmt.c)
target_link_libraries(test_tuifmt PRIVATE m)
add_test(NAME tuifmt COMMAND test_tuifmt)

# The game's rules, asked directly. Expectations come from sst.doc --
# see tests/test_rules.c and the note at the top of rules.h.
add_executable(test_rules tests/test_rules.c rules.c)
target_link_libraries(test_rules PRIVATE m)
add_test(NAME rules COMMAND test_rules)

add_test(NAME journey
         COMMAND ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/tests/journey.sh $<TARGET_FILE:sst> $<CONFIG>)
# Run from the source tree, where a player runs the game and where the
# in-game `help` command finds sst.doc.
# TIMEOUT because the script's own `timeout` guard needs coreutils,
# which macOS runners do not have.
set_tests_properties(journey PROPERTIES
                     WORKING_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}
                     TIMEOUT 120)

# The same journey with -t: with no terminal to draw on, full-screen
# mode has to fall back to the plain one rather than hang. ctest hands
# the test pipes for stdin and stdout, so this covers the no-tty path
# only -- the terminfo probe in tui_terminal_capable() needs a real
# pty and is checked by hand for now (issue #13). TERM=dumb is pinned
# so a regression here fails as the original hang rather than as the

#!/bin/sh
# Checks that AGENTS.md stays the single source of truth for project
# instructions, and that CLAUDE.md stays a pointer to it.
#
# Rules drift into CLAUDE.md easily and silently: Claude Code's `#`
# shortcut appends there, `/init` rewrites the file wholesale, and
# tools that target CLAUDE.md by name edit it directly. None of them
# know AGENTS.md exists. Without a check, the result is two sources of
# truth that slowly disagree.
#
# The AGENTS.md checks matter just as much: CLAUDE.md pulls it in with
# an `@AGENTS.md` import, and if that file is renamed, emptied, or
# deleted the import resolves to nothing -- no error, no warning, just
# an agent session with no rules at all.
#
# Usage: instructions.sh /path/to/repo/root

set -u

ROOT="${1:-.}"
while [ "${ROOT%/}" != "$ROOT" ] && [ "$ROOT" != "/" ]; do
	ROOT="${ROOT%/}"
done
CLAUDE="$ROOT/CLAUDE.md"
AGENTS="$ROOT/AGENTS.md"

# The pointer needs a title, a sentence or two, and the import. Kept
# tight on purpose: headroom here is room for a rule to hide by being
# folded into an existing line rather than added as a new one, which
# the line budget below cannot see. A very short phrase can still fit;
# that one is left to review.
MAXBYTES=220
# CLAUDE.md is meant to be frozen, so this is the exact number of
# non-blank lines it has today, not a generous budget: a rule slipped in
# as plain prose adds a line and nothing else would. Changing the
# pointer's wording means changing this number on purpose. The prose is
# wrapped at 72 columns to match the rest of the repo -- rewrapping it
# much narrower will need a third line and trip this.
MAXLINES=4
# Enough that a gutted or stub AGENTS.md fails, well under its real size.

project(sst
        LANGUAGES C
        VERSION 1.0)

set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING")

# Warnings are on for everyone, so a new one is visible where it is
# introduced. They are only fatal where that can be enforced without
# breaking somebody's build on a compiler version nobody here has
# tried: CI turns SST_WERROR on, a contributor gets the warning and a
# working build.
option(SST_WERROR "Treat compiler warnings as errors (CI does)" OFF)

    set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -Wall -Wextra")
    if(SST_WERROR)
        set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -Werror")
    endif()
endif()

if(${CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE} STREQUAL "Debug")
    set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -DDEBUG")

endif()

# separate libtinfo. Linking -lncurses happens to pull it in where
# libncurses.so is a linker script, but that is luck, not a contract.
find_library(TINFO_LIBRARY tinfo)
if(TINFO_LIBRARY)
    target_link_libraries(sst PRIVATE ${TINFO_LIBRARY})
endif()

add_test(NAME tuifmt COMMAND test_tuifmt)

add_test(NAME rules COMMAND test_rules)

                     TIMEOUT 120)

add_test(NAME help COMMAND ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/tests/help.sh $<TARGET_FILE:sst>)
set_tests_properties(help PROPERTIES TIMEOUT 120)

# provides. It reports SKIPPED rather than passing where tmux is
# missing, so a machine without it cannot look like coverage.
# The timeout is far above the ~11s it takes to pass: every check
# inside polls before giving up, so a broadly broken TUI spends its
# time timing out one poll at a time. Better that it reaches the end
# and names each failure than that ctest kills it and reports only

add_test(NAME tui

set_tests_properties(tui PROPERTIES SKIP_RETURN_CODE 77 TIMEOUT 300)

# needs the seeded generator to be the game's own, which it is.
add_test(NAME golden
         COMMAND ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/tests/golden.sh $<TARGET_FILE:sst>)
set_tests_properties(golden PROPERTIES TIMEOUT 120)

add_test(NAME instructions
         COMMAND ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/tests/instructions.sh
                 ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR})
set_tests_properties(instructions PROPERTIES TIMEOUT 30)

# AGENTS.md

Shared instructions for every coding agent working in this repository
(Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, and others). `CLAUDE.md` imports this
file; keep all rules here so every agent sees the same thing.

## Project

Super Star Trek — a classic terminal (CLI) space strategy game written in C17,
built with CMake. The executable is `sst`. Game documentation lives in
`sst.doc`; shared declarations live in `sst.h`.

Global game state uses the `EXTERN`/`INCLUDED` trick in `sst.h`: exactly one
translation unit per binary defines `INCLUDED` before including `sst.h` to
instantiate the globals (`sst.c` for the game; a test's own file, e.g.
`tests/test_tuifmt.c`, for test binaries that don't link `sst.c`).

Display state (`tui_active`, `tui_ingame`) deliberately sits outside that
mechanism — plain `extern` in `tui.h`, defined in `tui.c` — so `tui.h`
stays self-contained for `osx.c`, which cannot include `sst.h`. Put new
display flags there, not in `sst.h`.

## Build and run

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   # build type is required; Debug adds -DDEBUG
cmake --build build
./build/sst
```

Note: `CMakeLists.txt` compares `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` directly, so configuring
without `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=...` fails. `-Wall -Wextra` is always on; CI
also configures with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, so pass that locally to see what
CI will refuse. Feature flags `-DSCORE -DCAPTURE
-DCLOAKING` are always enabled.

## TUI mode (`sst -t`)

- All game output must go through `prout`/`proutn`/`proutf`/`prouts` and all
  input through `scan()`/`getch()`/`readinput()` — raw `printf`/`putchar`/
  `fgets` silently bypasses the full-screen mode.
- Plain mode (no `-t`) must not change as an unintended side effect of any
  change; verify with a piped scripted journey (e.g.
  `printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\nsrscan\nquit\nn\n' | ./build/sst`).
  If a change alters plain-mode output on purpose, say so in the commit
  and explain why.
- Text the game prints must not end in a carriage return. `sst.doc` is
  CRLF, so anything read from it needs both stripped: under curses a
  trailing `\r` returns the cursor to column 0 and the newline then
  erases the line. `pause()` writes a CR deliberately, to wipe its own
  prompt in place -- the one exception, and the reason the test scripts
  filter that shape before checking.
- The panel formatters in `tuifmt.c` must mirror `srscan()` in `reports.c`
  exactly — it is the spec, including sensor-damage masking and the `-f`
  coordinate transposition (x is the column). Keep `tests/test_tuifmt.c` in
  sync (`ctest --test-dir build`).
- Testing the TUI needs a pty: use tmux, and always on your own socket via
  `-L`, with `-f /dev/null` so the config does not follow — `tmux -f /dev/null
  -L sst new-session -d -x 100 -y 30 -s t './build/sst -t; sleep 30'`, drive
  with `tmux -f /dev/null -L sst send-keys -t t 'cmd' Enter` (input is
  line-based; keys need Enter), inspect with `capture-pane -t t -p`, and clean
  up with `kill-server` on that same socket. Without `-f /dev/null` a setting
  as ordinary as `base-index 1` renames the pane out from under you and every
  capture comes back empty. The default socket is where the
  human running you keeps their own work: on 2026-08-01 a review agent tidied up
  after a TUI check with a bare `tmux kill-server` and destroyed a week-old
  session of eight panes, including the agent's own parent. `-L` is what makes
  that mistake impossible rather than merely discouraged — never issue a bare
  `tmux kill-server`, and never `kill-session` a session you did not create.
  Never redirect the game's stdout in the session — it breaks curses rendering.
  `tests/tui.sh` does all of this automatically and is the place to add
  coverage; it skips without tmux, but fails rather than skipping when `$CI` is
  set.
- Check the TUI at 80x24 and 72x24, not just at a comfortable size. 72x24 is
  the smallest it accepts and 80x24 is what most terminals open at; the
  message window is only ten lines at both, which is where the paging bugs
  live.

A failing `golden` test means a journey's output changed. Work out why
and say so in the commit -- the fixture diff is the evidence a reviewer
needs. Never re-record with `tests/golden.sh <sst> --update` to turn CI
green without that explanation; the recordings are the only thing in
the suite that checks the game's arithmetic at all.

## Development workflow

Every coding agent working in this repository must follow this workflow.

1. **Inspect before changing anything.** Inspect the repository, current Git
   state, and all applicable instruction files before making changes. Preserve
   unrelated staged, unstaged, and untracked work.

2. **Create a branch first.** Create a dedicated feature, fix, refactor, chore,
   test, or documentation branch before making code changes. Never commit
   directly to `main`, and create the branch from the latest appropriate
   `main` state.

3. **Choose a thin vertical slice.** Before implementing a roadmap item or
   feature, define the smallest end-to-end slice that can be reviewed, tested,
   shipped, and merged independently. Prefer one coherent user-visible or
   operational outcome over a broad horizontal layer.

4. **Use test-driven development when behavior or structure is testable.**
   - Add or update a focused test before implementation.
   - Run it and confirm it fails for the expected reason.
   - Implement the smallest appropriate change.
   - Run focused tests while iterating.
   - Refactor only while the relevant tests remain green.

5. **Inspect the complete diff.** Review the branch diff plus all staged,
   unstaged, and untracked files. Remove accidental or unrelated changes while
   preserving work that belongs to the user.

6. **Run `ui-review` before verification.** After the main agent completes an
   implementation pass, invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent. The `ui-review`
   sub-agent must act as an expert in games and CLI games.

7. **Run `verifier` before code review.** Invoke the `verifier` sub-agent to
   run the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for
   the change. The verifier must report failures, flakes, missing coverage,
   and environment issues. Fix or explicitly resolve every actionable finding
   before starting code review. If a verifier finding requires a code change,
   rerun the verifier after addressing it.

8. **Run `code-review` before every commit.** Invoke the `code-review`
   sub-agent against the current branch diff and every staged, unstaged, and
   untracked file. The reviewer must act as an expert in the languages and
   frameworks used by this application. Address every actionable finding
   before committing. If review findings cause changes, rerun the appropriate
   tests and the `verifier`, then obtain a fresh `code-review` approval for
   the changed state.

9. **Commit after approval.** Commit only after verification and code review
   are complete. Use Conventional Commits:

   ```text
   <type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>
   ```

   Keep the subject at 72 characters or fewer, describe why in the body when
   useful, and do not combine unrelated work.

10. **Create pull requests from the reviewed state.**
    - Confirm that local verification remains valid.
    - Rerun `code-review` only if the reviewed state changed after the
      pre-commit review.
    - A changed state includes code, tests, documentation, generated files,
      conflict resolution, or any other staged, unstaged, or untracked
      content.
    - Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and worktree
      remain unchanged.
    - Push and create the pull request only after local verification and any
      required code review are complete.
    - Open a normal, ready-for-review pull request by default. Do not open
      draft pull requests unless the user explicitly asks for a draft.

11. **Merge only clean, passing pull requests.** Merge only after GitHub
    reports a clean merge state and every configured check passes. Never
    bypass a failing or pending required check. Self-merges are allowed when
    these conditions are met. Use squash merge for short-lived development
    branches to keep `main` linear, then delete the merged branch.

Note: steps 6-8 name Claude Code sub-agents defined in `.claude/agents/`.
Agents without sub-agent support should perform the equivalent review,
verification, and code-review passes themselves before committing.

Include-order safety checked: `tui.c` includes `sst.h` before `<curses.h>`, so the `int getch(void);` declaration (now reached via `osx.h`) is still processed before ncurses can make `getch` a macro — same ordering as before, no new exposure. `stdio_is_terminal()` has exactly two callers (`sst.c:462`, `tui.c:217`), both of which include `sst.h`, so dropping it from `tui.h` breaks no one.

Only nits below; none block a commit.

### Nits

**1. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/osx.h:8` — the comment states a failure mode C does not have.**

> these definitions were checked against nothing: a changed signature surfaced at link time, or not at all.

C function signatures are not part of the linked symbol, so a changed signature never surfaces at link time — only a rename or deletion does. The clause overstates the old safety net in a file whose whole purpose is to describe it accurately. Suggested rewording: "…checked against nothing: the signature could drift from the one callers read and nothing — not the compiler, not the linker — would say so."

**2. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/osx.h:18-23` — the header's contract is wrong on the `WINDOWS` path.**

The banner says "What osx.c provides", but every definition in `osx.c` sits inside one `#ifndef WINDOWS` (osx.c:18-59), so under `WINDOWS` the file provides nothing, while `getch()` and `stdio_is_terminal()` are declared here unconditionally. This is inherited exactly from the old `sst.h`/`tui.h` declarations and is not a regression — and tightening the guard would be wrong, since `sst.c` calls `getch()` without including `<conio.h>` and would fall to an implicit declaration. But now that a header exists to state the contract, it should state the exception, e.g. a line under the `#ifndef WINDOWS`: "Windows supplies min/max itself; getch() and stdio_is_terminal() are declared here for the callers, but that build has never been wired up." Same applies to the summary comment at `sst.h:504`.

**3. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/osx.c:1-7` — own header is not included first, so its self-containment claim is never tested.**

`<stdio.h>` precedes `#include "osx.h"`. The header advertises "Self-contained on purpose, like tui.h", but with `<stdio.h>` already in scope the build would not notice if `osx.h` ever grew a dependency on a stdio type. Moving `#include "osx.h"` to line 1 makes the compiler enforce the claim; the existing comment reads fine either way.

**4. `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md:23-29` — two small prose issues.**

- Line 24: "`sst.h` declares `pause(int)`, which collides with the POSIX `pause(void)` it needs" — "it" scans as `sst.h` on first read; make it "that `osx.c` needs".
- Line 26 wraps after "Put" when "new" fits inside 72 columns, leaving a ragged line the surrounding paragraphs do not have.

# AGENTS.md

Shared instructions for every coding agent working in this repository
(Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, and others). `CLAUDE.md` imports this
file; keep all rules here so every agent sees the same thing.

## Project

Super Star Trek — a classic terminal (CLI) space strategy game written in C17,
built with CMake. The executable is `sst`. Game documentation lives in
`sst.doc`; shared declarations live in `sst.h`.

Global game state uses the `EXTERN`/`INCLUDED` trick in `sst.h`: exactly one
translation unit per binary defines `INCLUDED` before including `sst.h` to
instantiate the globals (`sst.c` for the game; a test's own file, e.g.
`tests/test_tuifmt.c`, for test binaries that don't link `sst.c`).

Display state (`tui_active`, `tui_ingame`) deliberately sits outside that
mechanism — plain `extern` in `tui.h`, defined in `tui.c` — so `tui.h`
stays self-contained for `osx.c`, which cannot include `sst.h`. Put new
display flags there, not in `sst.h`.

`osx.c` is the file that cannot include `sst.h`: `sst.h` declares
`pause(int)`, which collides with the POSIX `pause(void)` it needs. So
what `osx.c` *provides* is declared in `osx.h` (included by both `osx.c`
and `sst.h`), and what `osx.c` *calls* it gets from `tui.h`. Put
new platform functions in `osx.h`, not `sst.h`, so the definition stays
checked against the declaration — `-Wmissing-prototypes` is on and CI
builds with `-Werror`.

## Build and run

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   # build type is required; Debug adds -DDEBUG
cmake --build build
./build/sst
```

Note: `CMakeLists.txt` compares `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` directly, so configuring
without `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=...` fails. `-Wall -Wextra` is always on; CI
also configures with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, so pass that locally to see what
CI will refuse. Feature flags `-DSCORE -DCAPTURE
-DCLOAKING` are always enabled.

## TUI mode (`sst -t`)

- All game output must go through `prout`/`proutn`/`proutf`/`prouts` and all
  input through `scan()`/`getch()`/`readinput()` — raw `printf`/`putchar`/
  `fgets` silently bypasses the full-screen mode.
- Plain mode (no `-t`) must not change as an unintended side effect of any
  change; verify with a piped scripted journey (e.g.
  `printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\nsrscan\nquit\nn\n' | ./build/sst`).
  If a change alters plain-mode output on purpose, say so in the commit
  and explain why.
- Text the game prints must not end in a carriage return. `sst.doc` is
  CRLF, so anything read from it needs both stripped: under curses a
  trailing `\r` returns the cursor to column 0 and the newline then
  erases the line. `pause()` writes a CR deliberately, to wipe its own
  prompt in place -- the one exception, and the reason the test scripts
  filter that shape before checking.
- The panel formatters in `tuifmt.c` must mirror `srscan()` in `reports.c`
  exactly — it is the spec, including sensor-damage masking and the `-f`
  coordinate transposition (x is the column). Keep `tests/test_tuifmt.c` in
  sync (`ctest --test-dir build`).
- Testing the TUI needs a pty: use tmux, and always on your own socket via
  `-L`, with `-f /dev/null` so the config does not follow — `tmux -f /dev/null
  -L sst new-session -d -x 100 -y 30 -s t './build/sst -t; sleep 30'`, drive
  with `tmux -f /dev/null -L sst send-keys -t t 'cmd' Enter` (input is
  line-based; keys need Enter), inspect with `capture-pane -t t -p`, and clean
  up with `kill-server` on that same socket. Without `-f /dev/null` a setting
  as ordinary as `base-index 1` renames the pane out from under you and every
  capture comes back empty. The default socket is where the
  human running you keeps their own work: on 2026-08-01 a review agent tidied up
  after a TUI check with a bare `tmux kill-server` and destroyed a week-old
  session of eight panes, including the agent's own parent. `-L` is what makes
  that mistake impossible rather than merely discouraged — never issue a bare
  `tmux kill-server`, and never `kill-session` a session you did not create.
  Never redirect the game's stdout in the session — it breaks curses rendering.
  `tests/tui.sh` does all of this automatically and is the place to add
  coverage; it skips without tmux, but fails rather than skipping when `$CI` is
  set.
- Check the TUI at 80x24 and 72x24, not just at a comfortable size. 72x24 is
  the smallest it accepts and 80x24 is what most terminals open at; the
  message window is only ten lines at both, which is where the paging bugs
  live.

A failing `golden` test means a journey's output changed. Work out why
and say so in the commit -- the fixture diff is the evidence a reviewer
needs. Never re-record with `tests/golden.sh <sst> --update` to turn CI
green without that explanation; the recordings are the only thing in
the suite that checks the game's arithmetic at all.

## Development workflow

Every coding agent working in this repository must follow this workflow.

1. **Inspect before changing anything.** Inspect the repository, current Git
   state, and all applicable instruction files before making changes. Preserve
   unrelated staged, unstaged, and untracked work.

2. **Create a branch first.** Create a dedicated feature, fix, refactor, chore,
   test, or documentation branch before making code changes. Never commit
   directly to `main`, and create the branch from the latest appropriate
   `main` state.

3. **Choose a thin vertical slice.** Before implementing a roadmap item or
   feature, define the smallest end-to-end slice that can be reviewed, tested,
   shipped, and merged independently. Prefer one coherent user-visible or
   operational outcome over a broad horizontal layer.

4. **Use test-driven development when behavior or structure is testable.**
   - Add or update a focused test before implementation.
   - Run it and confirm it fails for the expected reason.
   - Implement the smallest appropriate change.
   - Run focused tests while iterating.
   - Refactor only while the relevant tests remain green.

5. **Inspect the complete diff.** Review the branch diff plus all staged,
   unstaged, and untracked files. Remove accidental or unrelated changes while
   preserving work that belongs to the user.

6. **Run `ui-review` before verification.** After the main agent completes an
   implementation pass, invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent. The `ui-review`
   sub-agent must act as an expert in games and CLI games.

7. **Run `verifier` before code review.** Invoke the `verifier` sub-agent to
   run the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for
   the change. The verifier must report failures, flakes, missing coverage,
   and environment issues. Fix or explicitly resolve every actionable finding
   before starting code review. If a verifier finding requires a code change,
   rerun the verifier after addressing it.

8. **Run `code-review` before every commit.** Invoke the `code-review`
   sub-agent against the current branch diff and every staged, unstaged, and
   untracked file. The reviewer must act as an expert in the languages and
   frameworks used by this application. Address every actionable finding
   before committing. If review findings cause changes, rerun the appropriate
   tests and the `verifier`, then obtain a fresh `code-review` approval for
   the changed state.

9. **Commit after approval.** Commit only after verification and code review
   are complete. Use Conventional Commits:

   ```text
   <type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>
   ```

   Keep the subject at 72 characters or fewer, describe why in the body when
   useful, and do not combine unrelated work.

10. **Create pull requests from the reviewed state.**
    - Confirm that local verification remains valid.
    - Rerun `code-review` only if the reviewed state changed after the
      pre-commit review.
    - A changed state includes code, tests, documentation, generated files,
      conflict resolution, or any other staged, unstaged, or untracked
      content.
    - Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and worktree
      remain unchanged.
    - Push and create the pull request only after local verification and any
      required code review are complete.
    - Open a normal, ready-for-review pull request by default. Do not open
      draft pull requests unless the user explicitly asks for a draft.

11. **Merge only clean, passing pull requests.** Merge only after GitHub
    reports a clean merge state and every configured check passes. Never
    bypass a failing or pending required check. Self-merges are allowed when
    these conditions are met. Use squash merge for short-lived development
    branches to keep `main` linear, then delete the merged branch.

Note: steps 6-8 name Claude Code sub-agents defined in `.claude/agents/`.
Agents without sub-agent support should perform the equivalent review,
verification, and code-review passes themselves before committing.

/* What osx.c provides: the few things the game needs from the
 * platform rather than from itself.
 *
 * This header exists because osx.c cannot include sst.h -- sst.h
 * declares a pause(int) that collides with the POSIX pause(void) that
 * <unistd.h> brings in, and osx.c needs the POSIX one. Without a
 * header both sides can see, these definitions were checked against
 * nothing: a signature could drift from the one callers read and
 * nothing -- not the compiler, not the linker, which does not carry
 * signatures at all -- would say so. sst.h includes this file, so
 * callers keep reaching them the way they always have.
 *
 * Self-contained on purpose, like tui.h: including this must not
 * oblige a file to include sst.h as well.
 */
#ifndef SST_OSX_H
#define SST_OSX_H

/* Windows has its own min and max, so osx.c defines none. The other
   two stay declared unconditionally, as they were in sst.h: sst.c
   calls getch() without including <conio.h>, and taking the
   declaration away would leave it with an implicit one. That build
   has never been wired into CMake, so nothing checks either way. */
#ifndef WINDOWS
int min(int, int);
int max(int, int);
#endif
int getch(void);
int stdio_is_terminal(void);	/* stdin and stdout are both ttys */

#endif	/* SST_OSX_H */

/* What osx.c provides: the few things the game needs from the
 * platform rather than from itself.
 *
 * This header exists because osx.c cannot include sst.h -- sst.h
 * declares a pause(int) that collides with the POSIX pause(void) that
 * <unistd.h> brings in, and osx.c needs the POSIX one. Without a
 * header both sides can see, these definitions were checked against
 * nothing: a signature could drift from the one callers read and
 * nothing -- not the compiler, not the linker, which does not carry
 * signatures at all -- would say so. sst.h includes this file, so
 * callers keep reaching them the way they always have.
 *
 * Self-contained on purpose, like tui.h: including this must not
 * oblige a file to include sst.h as well.
 */
#ifndef SST_OSX_H
#define SST_OSX_H

/* Windows has its own min and max, so osx.c defines none. The other
   two stay declared unconditionally, as they were in sst.h: sst.c
   calls getch() without including <conio.h>, and taking the
   declaration away would leave it with an implicit one. That build
   has never been wired into CMake, so nothing checks either way. */
#ifndef WINDOWS
int min(int, int);
int max(int, int);
#endif
int getch(void);
int stdio_is_terminal(void);	/* stdin and stdout are both ttys */

#endif	/* SST_OSX_H */

input.command:
git push -u origin fix/osx-prototypes 2>&1 | tail -3 && gh pr create --title "fix: let the compiler check what osx.c provides" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Closes #38.

## The problem

`min()`, `max()` and `getch()` were defined in `osx.c` but declared in
`sst.h`, which `osx.c` cannot include — `sst.h` declares `pause(int)`,
which collides with the POSIX `pause(void)` that `<unistd.h>` brings in.
Nothing checked the definitions against the declarations: a signature
could drift from the one every caller reads and neither the compiler nor
the linker — which does not carry signatures at all — would say so.

## The change

A new `osx.h` declares what `osx.c` provides, and is included by both it
and `sst.h`, so callers reach these the way they always have.
`stdio_is_terminal()` joins them there from `tui.h`, which keeps only
what `osx.c` *calls*. `osx.h` goes first among `osx.c`'s includes, so the
build would notice if it ever stopped standing on its own.

`-Wmissing-prototypes` goes on for everyone, so the defect class cannot
come back. It fires on any non-static function defined without a
prototype in scope — the only way a definition can drift from its
declaration. The tree was already clean under it except for exactly
those three functions, and CI builds with `-Werror`, so a new one fails
there.

## Verification

- Debug and Release with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`: zero warnings.
- Full `ctest` suite 10/10, including `golden`, the tmux-driven `tui`
  test, `tournament` and `instructions`.
- The check bites: changing `min()` to return `long` is now a compile
  error, not a link-time surprise.
- No behaviour change — in Release all thirteen objects are
  byte-identical to `main`; in Debug six differ only in DWARF
  declaration line numbers. `.text`, `.rodata`, `.data` and `.bss` are
  identical throughout.
- Plain mode and `-t` at 80x24 and 72x24 compared against `main`:
  byte-identical.

`AGENTS.md` gains a paragraph so the next agent knows where a new
platform function belongs.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)"

content.text:
Issue #38 is done and merged as `d08256f` (PR #60, squashed, branch deleted).

**What changed**

- **`osx.h` (new)** — declares what `osx.c` provides: `min`, `max`, `getch`, and `stdio_is_terminal` (which moved over from `tui.h`, since `tui.h` should hold only what `osx.c` *calls*). It's included by both `osx.c` and `sst.h`, so callers reach these exactly as before. It's included first in `osx.c` so the build would notice if it ever stopped standing on its own.
- **`-Wmissing-prototypes` in `CMakeLists.txt`** — this is what actually closes the defect class rather than just this instance. It fires on any non-static function defined without a prototype in scope, the tree was already clean under it *except* for those three functions, and CI's `-Werror` makes a new one fatal.
- **`sst.c`** — dropped a commented-out `int getch(void);` that was dead.
- **`AGENTS.md`** — a paragraph so the next agent knows platform functions go in `osx.h`, not `sst.h`.

**Verification** — the acceptance criterion checks out concretely: changing `min()` to return `long` is now a hard compile error (`conflicting types for 'min'`), where before it was invisible. Debug and Release build warning-free with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, full ctest is 10/10, and all four CI legs pass — including both macOS/clang legs, which were the one thing I couldn't test locally.

No behavior change: `.text`, `.rodata`, `.data` and `.bss` are byte-identical across all thirteen objects. (The commit message originally claimed whole objects were byte-identical; review caught that this holds for Release but not Debug, where DWARF line numbers shift, so I corrected it before pushing.)

Two things worth flagging:

- **`.claude/settings.json` is modified in your working tree and I deliberately left it uncommitted.** The harness rewrote its hook matchers during this session (`Task`→`Agent`, `TodoWrite`→`TaskCreate|TaskUpdate`) — unrelated to #38, so it's yours to review and commit. It also blocked `gh pr merge`'s automatic post-merge `git pull --rebase`; I fast-forwarded `main` manually instead, so local `main` is now at `d08256f`.
- **The `WINDOWS` path remains unverified by anything.** Under `-DWINDOWS` the entire body of `osx.c` compiles away, so `getch()` and `stdio_is_terminal()` are declared with no definition behind them. That's unchanged from before, and nothing in CMake defines `WINDOWS`, but `osx.h` now records it in a comment rather than leaving it implicit.

=========== #46
title:	TUI: the screen does not repaint until the next prompt after a resize
state:	OPEN
author:	scottdensmore (Scott Densmore)
labels:	enhancement
comments:	0
assignees:	
projects:	
milestone:

number:	46
--
## Problem

#9 made the panels follow the terminal, but only at the next repaint —
which is the next prompt. A resize that arrives while the game is
blocked reading (a typed answer, or `[HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]`) is
noticed and correctly *not* treated as a keystroke, but nothing is
redrawn until the player answers.

On tmux the pane is left blank in the meantime, which looks like a
hang. `main` before #9 behaved the same way, so this is not a
regression — it is the half of the problem that fix did not reach.

## Why it is left

Rebuilding the windows from inside the blocking read was tried and
made things worse rather than better. Every combination attempted —
`resize_term` plus `wresize`, plus `touchwin`, plus `clearok(curscr)`,
plus `endwin()`/`refresh()` — either left the message window empty or
blanked the whole screen. Under a `wgetch`/`wgetnstr` that has not
returned, curses is repainting a screen it is still reading from, and
the results were not reproducible enough to ship.

## Suggested approach

Worth deciding rather than picking blind:

- Handle `SIGWINCH` with a flag and do the rebuild at a point where no
  read is in flight, rather than reacting inside the read.
- Or replace `wgetnstr` with a hand-rolled line editor, which is what
  would let the prompt be reprinted and the partially-typed line
  restored after a rebuild. Bigger, but it also closes the Ctrl-D
  wrinkle noted in `tui_readline`.

Whichever, the test to add is in `tests/tui.sh`: resize during a
`help move` pause, then assert the prompt is still on screen and one
keystroke advances exactly one page.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A resize during a prompt or a pause leaves a correctly drawn
      screen without waiting for the player.
- [ ] The pause still needs exactly one keystroke afterwards.
- [ ] What the player had typed is either preserved or clearly
      restarted, not silently half-eaten.

## Problem

`tests/golden.sh` records seven journeys, and none of them wins. Every
one ends by quitting or by the ship being destroyed, so the whole
`FWON` epilogue in `finish.c` is unrecorded:

- the promotion prose and the five per-rating messages
- the win bonus on the score sheet
- the Romulan surrender line
- the Commodore Emeritus citation prompt, and `plaque()` behind it
- "You have smashed the Klingon invasion fleet" and what follows it

That is a large, self-contained region of player-visible output with no
coverage of any kind. It also means the byte-exact recordings are weaker
evidence than they look for changes near the end of a game: #52 and #54
both extracted arithmetic that only runs on a win, and `golden OK` said
nothing about either -- the confidence came from a differential harness
run by hand, not from the suite.

## Why it is not simply another journey

Winning means destroying every Klingon in the galaxy. A scripted journey
cannot plausibly do that: the `tournament` battery plays twelve seeded
games and none comes close.

Two ways round it, both worth weighing:

- **Thaw a won position.** Play a game to the brink by hand once,
  `freeze` it, commit the save, and record a journey that thaws it and
  lands the last blow. The save is a binary fixture, which is a new kind
  of thing in this repo and pins the struct layout -- a change to
  `struct foo` would invalidate it, loudly.
- **A debug command that ends the game.** `debugme()` already exists for
  exactly this sort of thing. A "win now" toggle would make the epilogue
  reachable from a script in two lines, at the cost of a debug-only code
  path, and would be Debug-build only -- `tests/tui.sh` already has a
  case gated that way.

The second looks cheaper and less brittle; the first records the real
thing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A golden recording covers the `FWON` epilogue, including the

## Problem

#50 listed "galaxy invariants" as a slice and it was not done, for a
reason worth writing down: **the invariant is not in the manual.**

The packing of `d.galaxy` — thousands for Klingons, then hundreds, tens
and units for the rest — appears nowhere in `sst.doc`. It is an internal
representation, decoded ad hoc in `setup.c:618`, `events.c:271` and
`events.c:726`. A test asserting the cells sum to `inkling`/`inbase`/
`instar` would have to take its expected values from the code, which is
the one thing `tests/test_rules.c` forbids at the top of the file:

> a test whose expectation came from running the code agrees with the
> code by construction

That would be a consistency check, not a second opinion, and
`tests/golden.sh` already answers "did the encoding change" more cheaply.

## What is worth checking instead

The manual does state facts about the galaxy, and none of them need any
knowledge of the encoding:

- `sst.doc:173` — from two to five starbases.
- `sst.doc:123-127` — the galaxy is 8x8 quadrants of 10x10 sectors.
- Whatever the setup section says about the number of Klingons at each
  skill and length, which is worth reading properly before starting.

These are assertable against `inbase`, `inkling` and the loop bounds
after a real game is set up.

## Where they belong

Not in `tests/test_rules.c`. Reaching a real galaxy means running
`setup()`, which reads input and narrates throughout (`setup.c:248`);
there is no seam short of extracting a `galaxy_populate()`, which is a
production refactor needing its own slice and its own `golden.sh` run.

An end-to-end check is the cheaper home — a shell journey that starts a
seeded game, reads `report` and `chart`, and asserts the counts the
manual promises. `tests/tournament.sh` is the natural place.

## Acceptance criteria

Three issues are open. Here's how they stack up:

**#58 — check the galaxy against the manual** (test-only, shell). Continues the streak you've been on (#52, #54, #57, #59). The issue has already done the hard thinking: it rejects the tempting galaxy-encoding invariant as a self-consistency check and names the three facts `sst.doc` actually states (2–5 starbases, 8x8 of 10x10, Klingon counts per skill/length). A journey in `tests/tournament.sh` asserting those. Small, no production code, low risk.

**#55 — no golden recording reaches a won game.** The biggest real gap. The whole `FWON` epilogue — promotion prose, win bonus, Romulan surrender, the Emeritus citation and `plaque()` — has zero coverage. What makes this more than housekeeping: #52 and #54 both extracted arithmetic that *only runs on a win*, and `golden` said nothing about either; the confidence came from a hand-run differential harness. So the suite is weakest exactly where the recent work has been. Needs a decision though — a Debug-only "win now" hook in `debugme()` (cheap, adds a debug path) versus committing a frozen save (records the real thing, but a binary fixture that pins `struct foo`).

**#46 — TUI doesn't repaint until the next prompt after a resize.** A genuine player-visible wart (blank pane looks like a hang), but the issue documents that the obvious fixes were tried and made it worse. It's a real redesign: SIGWINCH flag handled outside the read, or a hand-rolled line editor. Worth doing deliberately, not squeezed in.

My recommendation is **#55** — it's the one where the last two merges revealed the suite can't see what it claims to cover. #58 is the safer pick if you'd rather keep the slices small.

#!/bin/sh
# Plays fixed journeys and compares every byte against a recording.

run() {
	if command -v timeout >/dev/null 2>&1; then
		timeout 60 "$@"
	else
		"$@"
	fi
}

# $1 fixture name, $2 the whole script fed to the game, $3 the
# directory to play in (defaults to one of its own).
#
# A directory each, because a journey that freezes writes a save file
# beside itself and the next one must not find it -- except for the
# pair that is meant to, which passes the same name twice.
play() {
	name="$1"
	dir="$work/${3:-$name}"
	got="$work/$name.txt"
	rc="$work/$name.rc"
	mkdir -p "$dir"
	( cd "$dir" && printf '%s' "$2" | run "$SST" 2>&1; echo $? > "$rc" ) |
		head -c "$MAXBYTES" > "$got"

	status=$(cat "$rc" 2>/dev/null || echo "no-status")
	bytes=$(wc -c < "$got" | tr -d ' ')

	# Checked whether recording or comparing. A recording is only
	# worth having of a game that played properly; a comparison that
	# matches byte for byte can still be a game that started exiting
	# non-zero.
	if [ "$status" != "0" ]; then
		fail "$name: exited with status $status, want 0"
		return
	fi
	if [ "$bytes" -ge "$MAXBYTES" ]; then
		fail "$name: produced at least $MAXBYTES bytes -- runaway output?"
		return
	fi
	if [ "$bytes" -lt "$MINBYTES" ]; then
		fail "$name: only $bytes bytes -- the journey did not really play"
		return
	fi
	if [ "$(grep -v '^[[:space:]]*$' "$got" | tail -1)" != \
	     "May the Great Bird of the Galaxy roost upon your home planet." ]; then
		fail "$name: no farewell -- the journey did not reach the end"
		return
	fi
	if grep -q 'Transmission ends' "$got"; then
		fail "$name: the game ran out of input before the journey was over"
		return
	fi
	if grep -q 'DEBUG:' "$got"; then
		fail "$name: developer chatter would have been recorded as truth"
		return
	fi
	# A carriage return at the end of a line is a leak from a file the
	# game read, and recorded here it would be defended by the fixture
	# forever. The pager's own wipe ends a line too; drop that shape
	# first, exactly as journey.sh does.
	if sed "s/$CR *$CR\$//" "$got" | grep -q "$CR\$"; then
		fail "$name: a line ends with a carriage return"
		return
	fi

	if [ "$UPDATE" = "--update" ]; then
		cp "$got" "$golden/$name.txt"
		printf '  recorded %s (%s bytes)\n' "$name" "$bytes"
		return
	fi
	if [ ! -f "$golden/$name.txt" ]; then
		fail "$name: no recording -- run with --update to make one"
		return
	fi
	if ! cmp -s "$golden/$name.txt" "$got"; then
		fail "$name: the game no longer plays this journey the same way"
		# cmp as well as diff: a difference in trailing whitespace
		# gives two diff lines that look identical.
		cmp "$golden/$name.txt" "$got" 2>&1 | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
		printf '  --- first %d differing lines, recorded vs now ---\n' \
			"$DIFFLINES" >&2
		diff "$golden/$name.txt" "$got" 2>&1 | head -n "$DIFFLINES" |
			cat -v | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
		printf '\n' >&2
	fi
}

toolUseResult.originalFile:
#!/bin/sh
# Plays fixed journeys and compares every byte against a recording.
#
# The rest of the suite asks whether things happened: that a game
# docked, that nothing desynchronised, that no developer chatter got
# out. None of it asks whether a number is right. Nothing checked that
# combat arithmetic, time accounting, a starbase's resupply or the
# score came out as they should -- so a change to any of them was
# invisible unless it crashed or stopped a journey.
#
# This does the other thing. Each journey below is recorded in
# tests/golden/, and any difference at all is a failure. It cannot say
# whether the game is correct; it says exactly what changed, which is
# the question a reviewer actually has.
#
# What it will not catch is a change that alters no output. Adding a
# unit to the torpedo damage still destroys the same Klingon and prints
# the same line, and nothing here notices; changing it enough that the
# Klingon survives shows up at once. The one-character fix to the
# Super-commander's pursuit (#42) showed up here as four lines of the
# combat recording, which was the whole of its visible effect. These
# are recordings of what the game does, not proofs of what it should.
#
# It only works because a tournament number now names the same galaxy
# on every machine (see Rand() in sst.c). Before that these recordings
# would have been per-platform, which is why the seeded battery next
# door has to ask its questions in aggregate.
#
# When a change alters output on purpose, re-record and say so in the
# commit -- the diff of the fixtures is the evidence:
#
#     tests/golden.sh ./build/sst --update
#
# Usage: golden.sh /path/to/sst [--update]

set -u

if [ $# -lt 1 ]; then
	echo "usage: golden.sh <sst> [--update]" >&2
	exit 2
fi
SST="$1"
UPDATE="${2:-}"
case "$UPDATE" in
	""|--update) ;;
	*) echo "usage: golden.sh <sst> [--update]" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
case "$SST" in
	/*) ;;
	*) SST="$(pwd)/$SST" ;;
esac
if [ ! -x "$SST" ]; then
	echo "FAIL: $SST is not executable" >&2
	exit 1
fi
srcdir=$(unset CDPATH; cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)
golden="$srcdir/tests/golden"

MAXBYTES=262144
MINBYTES=1000		# a banner and a farewell alone come to about 700
DIFFLINES=40
CR=$(printf '\r')	# BSD sed reads a regex \r as a literal r

work=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/sst-golden.XXXXXX")
if [ -z "${work:-}" ] || [ ! -d "$work" ]; then
	echo "FAIL: could not create a temporary directory" >&2
	exit 1
fi
trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 130' INT
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 143' TERM
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 129' HUP
trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 141' PIPE

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

run() {
	if command -v timeout >/dev/null 2>&1; then
		timeout 60 "$@"
	else
		"$@"
	fi
}

# $1 fixture name, $2 the whole script fed to the game, $3 the
# directory to play in (defaults to one of its own).
#
# A directory each, because a journey that freezes writes a save file
# beside itself and the next one must not find it -- except for the
# pair that is meant to, which passes the same name twice.
play() {
	name="$1"
	dir="$work/${3:-$name}"
	got="$work/$name.txt"
	rc="$work/$name.rc"
	mkdir -p "$dir"
	( cd "$dir" && printf '%s' "$2" | run "$SST" 2>&1; echo $? > "$rc" ) |
		head -c "$MAXBYTES" > "$got"

	status=$(cat "$rc" 2>/dev/null || echo "no-status")
	bytes=$(wc -c < "$got" | tr -d ' ')

	# Checked whether recording or comparing. A recording is only
	# worth having of a game that played properly; a comparison that
	# matches byte for byte can still be a game that started exiting
	# non-zero.
	if [ "$status" != "0" ]; then
		fail "$name: exited with status $status, want 0"
		return
	fi
	if [ "$bytes" -ge "$MAXBYTES" ]; then
		fail "$name: produced at least $MAXBYTES bytes -- runaway output?"
		return
	fi
	if [ "$bytes" -lt "$MINBYTES" ]; then
		fail "$name: only $bytes bytes -- the journey did not really play"
		return
	fi
	if [ "$(grep -v '^[[:space:]]*$' "$got" | tail -1)" != \
	     "May the Great Bird of the Galaxy roost upon your home planet." ]; then
		fail "$name: no farewell -- the journey did not reach the end"
		return
	fi
	if grep -q 'Transmission ends' "$got"; then
		fail "$name: the game ran out of input before the journey was over"
		return
	fi
	if grep -q 'DEBUG:' "$got"; then
		fail "$name: developer chatter would have been recorded as truth"
		return
	fi
	# A carriage return at the end of a line is a leak from a file the
	# game read, and recorded here it would be defended by the fixture
	# forever. The pager's own wipe ends a line too; drop that shape
	# first, exactly as journey.sh does.
	if sed "s/$CR *$CR\$//" "$got" | grep -q "$CR\$"; then
		fail "$name: a line ends with a carriage return"
		return
	fi

	if [ "$UPDATE" = "--update" ]; then
		cp "$got" "$golden/$name.txt"
		printf '  recorded %s (%s bytes)\n' "$name" "$bytes"
		return
	fi
	if [ ! -f "$golden/$name.txt" ]; then
		fail "$name: no recording -- run with --update to make one"
		return
	fi
	if ! cmp -s "$golden/$name.txt" "$got"; then
		fail "$name: the game no longer plays this journey the same way"
		# cmp as well as diff: a difference in trailing whitespace
		# gives two diff lines that look identical.
		cmp "$golden/$name.txt" "$got" 2>&1 | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
		printf '  --- first %d differing lines, recorded vs now ---\n' \
			"$DIFFLINES" >&2
		diff "$golden/$name.txt" "$got" 2>&1 | head -n "$DIFFLINES" |
			cat -v | sed 's/^/  /' >&2
		printf '\n' >&2
	fi
}

if [ "$UPDATE" = "--update" ]; then
	mkdir -p "$golden"
fi

content.text:
## Verdict

Acceptable as-is. The `won` journey reads like a real short/novice game rather than a contrivance — a player enters a quadrant, sees three enemies on the short-range scan, raises shields, eats a volley, and returns a 1500-unit auto burst — and the fixture is self-documenting: the briefing says "3 battle cruisers", the second `srscan` shows all three (`K` at 3‑2, `K` at 4‑8, `C` at 10‑4) and `Klingons Left 3`, so a reader can verify the seed's premise from the recording itself without trusting the comment. The epilogue is complete and the arithmetic is right. The one thing I'd push on is a pre-existing production misalignment in the score sheet that this fixture is the first ever to expose, and is now about to be frozen in as expected output.

### Score sheet arithmetic — verified correct

- 2 + 20 + 50 + 625 + 100 = **797**. Matches.
- `perdate` = 3 kills / (4702.4 − 4700.0 = 2.4 stardates) = **1.25**, and `killrate` = `500*1.25 + 0.5` = 625 (`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/rules.c:24-25`). Matches `sst.doc:1362-1366` rules (6), (7), (8): 1 point per Romulan surrendered, 500× kill rate, Novice bonus 100.
- The surrender count is internally consistent end to end: "The remaining **2** Romulan ships surrender" → "**2** Romulan ships surrendered  2". That is exactly `sst.doc:451` and `sst.doc:1362` documented in one recording, which is a genuinely good thing to have on the record.

## Findings

**1. should-fix — score sheet column is ragged on the "Romulan ships surrendered" line** (`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/finish.c:352`, recorded at `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/golden/won.txt:106`)

Every line of the score sheet right-aligns its number at column 47. This one lands at column 46:

```
     2 Romulan ships surrendered             2      <- 46
     2 ordinary Klingon ships destroyed      20     <- 47
     1 Klingon Commander ship destroyed      50     <- 47
  1.25 Klingon ships per stardate           625     <- 47
Bonus for winning Novice game               100     <- 47
TOTAL SCORE                                 797     <- 47
```

The plural format string is one space short; the singular variant on the very next argument of the same `proutf` is correct at 47. What the player sees is a single digit hanging one column left of the whole rest of the column — on a win, which is the one score sheet they most want to read. Because `surrendered` is only ever non-zero on the `FWON` path, `won.txt` is the first and only recording that contains this line, and committing the fixture as-is makes the misalignment the defended-forever expected output. Suggest either fixing it in this change (`"%6d Romulan ships surrendered          %5d\n"` — one more space) and re-recording `won.txt`, with the one-line fixture diff as the reviewer's evidence, or, if you want to keep this branch strictly test-only, filing it and adding a one-line comment above the `won` journey saying the column is known-wrong so nobody reads the fixture as a spec.

**2. should-fix — `covers` omits the Romulan surrender, which its own comment names as one of the three things this journey exists for** (`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/golden.sh`)

The block comment says the gap was "the Romulan surrender, the promotion prose, and the win bonus on the score sheet", but `covers won` asserts only the latter two. A future re-record that still wins but loses the surrender (a seed with no Romulans left, or a regression in `rules.c:41`'s `(gamewon == 0 || inGame) ? 0 : d.nromrem`) would sail through. Cheap fix — add:

```
	'Romulan ships surrender to Starfleet Command.' \
	'2 Romulan ships surrendered' \
	'TOTAL SCORE                                 797'
```

The total in particular is the one assertion that would notice #52-style arithmetic drift without a human reading the diff. I verified the helper works as advertised: swapping the `won` script for a self-destruct game and running `--update` produced three clear failures and a non-zero exit, so the safety net is real, just under-specified.

**3. nit — `won.txt` is the only fixture containing a live ANSI escape** (`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/golden/won.txt:53`)

# Verdict: request changes

One should-fix comment inaccuracy. Everything else — the `covers()` helper, the journey, the fixture, and the decision not to fix `finish.c` here — I approve.

**Reviewed state**: branch `test/golden-won-game`, HEAD `6daf378` (no commits ahead of `main`); all changes pending in the worktree — unstaged `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/golden.sh` (blob `44e90c5`) and untracked `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/golden/won.txt` (blob `edaae5d`). Nothing staged.

## Findings

### should-fix — `tests/golden.sh:342-344`: the "two answers" comment states a rule the game does not have

> `# Two answers at the end, where the journeys above need three: this`
> `# game ends itself, so there is no `quit` to confirm -- only the score`
> `# and play-again questions.`

Both halves are wrong. `quit` never asks for confirmation — `sst.c:406-412` sets `alldone = 1` and breaks straight out — and the journeys above do not need three answers. I re-ran `reports`, `ending` and `docking` with the trailing `n` removed and all three produced output byte-identical to their committed fixtures; the third `n` is unconsumed slack, not a required answer.

Failure scenario: a maintainer adding a journey trusts the comment, hunts for a confirmation prompt that does not exist, and mis-sizes the trailing answers — or, worse, "fixes" the older journeys down to two and believes they have found a behaviour change.

The real reason two suffice is worth writing down instead, because it is genuinely non-obvious: the game asks exactly two questions at the end (`sst.c:501` and `sst.c:507`), and the two `getch()` pauses on this path consume nothing, because `readinput()` uses `fgets` (`sst.c:656`) which has already drained the pipe into stdio's buffer, so `getch()`'s raw `read(0, ...)` (`osx.c:55`) sees EOF and returns `'\0'`. I confirmed that by replacing the first `n` with `Xn`: the pause did not eat the `X`, `ja()` printed `Please answer with "Y" or "N":`, and the journey then ran out of input. Suggested fix: say the game asks two questions here and the pauses eat nothing, and drop the comparison with the other journeys (or note their third `n` is surplus).

### nit — `tests/golden.sh:383-389`: `--update` leaves the bad recording on disk while reporting it was not recorded

`covers` runs after `play` has already `cp`'d the new output into `$golden/`, so when the journey stops winning, `--update` prints `recorded won (1723 bytes)` and then `6 journey(s) were not fit to record.` — it was recorded. I reproduced this by pointing the `won` journey at a non-winning script in a scratch copy of `tests/`: exit 1, six clear failures, and `won.txt` overwritten with the losing game. The guard still works (which is the point), but the summary contradicts the disk. Suggest either wording the covers failure to say "the recording was written anyway; restore it with `git checkout`", or adjusting the `--update` summary line.

### nit — `tests/golden.sh:349-352`: the `finish.c` bug is documented only in a test comment

The comment is precisely correct — I extracted all 27 `%5d` score-line formats from `finish.c:328-411` and computed their widths: line 352's plural (`"%6d Romulan ships surrendered         %5d\n"`) is the only one at 46 columns; every other line, including its own singular form, is 47. The fixture shows the same, 46 against 47 for its five neighbours. Recording it rather than fixing it is the right call for a test-only slice, and `covers` deliberately asserts `'2 Romulan ships surrendered'` without the trailing column, so the eventual one-character fix touches only the byte-compare. But this file cites `#42`, `#52`, `#54` and `#13` elsewhere; a production bug whose only record is a test comment has no owner. Suggest filing an issue and citing the number here.

### nit — `tests/golden.sh:328-340` and `266`: `tournament 23` now names two different galaxies

The `torpedoes` comment says "three Klingons this galaxy really has" for `tournament 23` at long/emeritus; the new comment says the same seed puts all three in quadrant 5 - 7 at short/novice. Different setups consume the RNG differently, so these are two unrelated galaxies from one seed. A half-sentence in the new comment ("the same seed as `torpedoes`, but short/novice makes a different galaxy") would stop a maintainer from treating one comment as evidence about the other.

### nit — `tests/golden.sh:187`: `grep -qF "$want"` has no `--`

Harmless today (every pattern is a literal starting with a letter or digit), but an assertion beginning with `-` would be parsed as an option. `grep -qF -- "$want"` is portable. Same for `name`/`f`/`want` being globals — `name` is shared with `play()`, which is safe only because every `covers` call follows every `play`; consistent with the file's existing style, so no change needed unless it grows.

## What I verified

- `covers()` is POSIX-safe: clean under `dash`, `busybox sh`, and `shellcheck -s sh`; `fail` uses `printf '%s'` so a `%` in a pattern cannot bite; `fails` is incremented in the main shell, not a subshell.
- The helper actually catches both failure modes: a mutated fixture (byte-compare *and* covers both fail) and a careless `--update` of a journey that stopped winning (six covers failures, exit 1).
- Determinism: identical md5 across repeated runs, under `env -i`, `TERM=dumb COLUMNS=40 LINES=10`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, and `HOME=/nonexistent`. No `setlocale` anywhere in the tree, so `%6.2f` cannot become `1,25`. `Rand()` is the seeded 32-bit generator, and the fixture holds no timestamp or path.
- Release: fresh `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSST_WERROR=ON` build passes `golden` against the same fixture, so `-O2` float drift is not an issue for this journey.
- Fixture hygiene: only carriage return is the exempted `pause()` wipe shape at line 103; ends with a newline; `.gitattributes` already covers `tests/golden/*.txt -text`, and `.gitignore` does not exclude it; it is the only fixture containing an ESC, and `clearscreen()` (`sst.c:756-762`) emits it unconditionally in plain mode.
- Arithmetic on the record is right, not merely stable: 2 + 20 + 50 + 625 + 100 = 797, with `killrate = 500 * (3 / 2.4)` and `winbonus = 100 * skill` per `rules.c:24-49`; the "two to four Klingons in a short novice game" claim matches `setup.c:547` (`14 * (0.35 - 0.2R)` truncated).
- Runtime: `golden` now takes 43.5s of its 120s ctest budget; the new journey adds 2.7s.

## Not reviewed

- No macOS/BSD run — `covers` adds only `grep -qF`, and the existing BSD-`sed` `\r` workaround is untouched, so I expect no difference, but I could not confirm.
- The TUI is out of scope here (`golden` is plain mode only); I did not run tmux.
- I checked the fixture is reproducible on this machine's ncurses/glibc only; the cross-platform argument rests on `Rand()` and the absence of `setlocale`, both of which I read.

- `covers()` is POSIX-safe: clean under `dash`, `busybox sh`, and `shellcheck -s sh`; `fail` uses `printf '%s'` so a `%` in a pattern cannot bite; `fails` is incremented in the main shell, not a subshell.
- The helper actually catches both failure modes: a mutated fixture (byte-compare *and* covers both fail) and a careless `--update` of a journey that stopped winning (six covers failures, exit 1).
- Determinism: identical md5 across repeated runs, under `env -i`, `TERM=dumb COLUMNS=40 LINES=10`, `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8`, and `HOME=/nonexistent`. No `setlocale` anywhere in the tree, so `%6.2f` cannot become `1,25`. `Rand()` is the seeded 32-bit generator, and the fixture holds no timestamp or path.
- Release: fresh `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSST_WERROR=ON` build passes `golden` against the same fixture, so `-O2` float drift is not an issue for this journey.
- Fixture hygiene: only carriage return is the exempted `pause()` wipe shape at line 103; ends with a newline; `.gitattributes` already covers `tests/golden/*.txt -text`, and `.gitignore` does not exclude it; it is the only fixture containing an ESC, and `clearscreen()` (`sst.c:756-762`) emits it unconditionally in plain mode.
- Arithmetic on the record is right, not merely stable: 2 + 20 + 50 + 625 + 100 = 797, with `killrate = 500 * (3 / 2.4)` and `winbonus = 100 * skill` per `rules.c:24-49`; the "two to four Klingons in a short novice game" claim matches `setup.c:547` (`14 * (0.35 - 0.2R)` truncated).
- Runtime: `golden` now takes 43.5s of its 120s ctest budget; the new journey adds 2.7s.

## Not reviewed

- No macOS/BSD run — `covers` adds only `grep -qF`, and the existing BSD-`sed` `\r` workaround is untouched, so I expect no difference, but I could not confirm.
- The TUI is out of scope here (`golden` is plain mode only); I did not run tmux.

input.command:
gh issue create --title "The score sheet's Romulan line sits one column left of the rest" --label "good first issue" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

`finish.c:352` prints the Romulan surrender line of the score sheet
with a plural and a singular format string. The plural one is a space
short:

```c
proutf(dnromrem > 1 ? "%6d Romulan ships surrendered         %5d\n"
                    : "%6d Romulan ship surrendered           %5d\n",
```

The plural lands its number at column 46. Every other line of the
score sheet — including that line's own singular form — lands at 47:

```
     2 Romulan ships surrendered             2      <- 46
     2 ordinary Klingon ships destroyed      20     <- 47
     1 Klingon Commander ship destroyed      50     <- 47
  1.25 Klingon ships per stardate           625     <- 47
Bonus for winning Novice game               100     <- 47
TOTAL SCORE                                 797     <- 47
```

## Why it matters

Small, and only visible when more than one Romulan surrenders — which
means only on a won game, since `rules.c` scores surrendered Romulans
at zero unless `gamewon`. So the one score sheet a player most wants to
read is the one with a digit hanging a column out of line.

It went unnoticed because nothing recorded a win. `tests/golden/won.txt`
(#55) is the first recording to contain the line at all, and it records
the misalignment as expected output — deliberately, since that fixture
is a recording of what the game does. The comment above the `won`
journey in `tests/golden.sh` points here.

## Suggested approach

Add the missing space to the plural string, then re-record:

```sh
tests/golden.sh ./build/sst --update
```

The fixture diff should be exactly one line, and that diff is the
evidence for the commit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every line of the score sheet right-aligns its number at the
      same column, with one and with several Romulans.
- [ ] `tests/golden/won.txt` re-recorded, with the one-line diff
      explained in the commit.

Follow the workflow in [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).
EOF
)"

# Asserts that a recording still contains the lines it exists for.
#
# Everything else here compares a fixture with itself, which cannot
# notice a journey that quietly stopped doing the thing it was written
# to do -- it would simply be re-recorded doing something else, and
# match from then on. The `won` journey is one seed away from being an
# ordinary fight that ends in a quit, so it says out loud what a win
# prints. Checks the fixture, not the run, so that a careless
# --update fails here too.
#
# $1 fixture name, then one or more lines it must contain.
covers() {
	name="$1"
	shift
	f="$golden/$name.txt"
	if [ ! -f "$f" ]; then
		fail "$name: no recording to check for content"
		return
	fi
	for want in "$@"; do
		if ! grep -qF -- "$want" "$f"; then
			fail "$name: the recording no longer contains \"$want\""
			# Said here because --update has already written the
			# file by the time this runs: the summary below will
			# say it was not fit to record, and the bad recording
			# is on disk regardless.
			if [ "$UPDATE" = "--update" ]; then
				printf '  (%s was written anyway -- git checkout %s to undo)\n' \
					"$name.txt" "tests/golden/$name.txt" >&2
			fi
		fi
	done
}

# Verdict: request changes

One should-fix comment inaccuracy. Everything else — the `covers()` helper, the journey, the fixture, and the decision not to fix `finish.c` here — I approve.

**Reviewed state**: branch `test/golden-won-game`, HEAD `6daf378` (no commits ahead of `main`); all changes pending in the worktree — unstaged `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/golden.sh` (blob `44e90c5`) and untracked `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/golden/won.txt` (blob `edaae5d`). Nothing staged.

## Findings

### should-fix — `tests/golden.sh:342-344`: the "two answers" comment states a rule the game does not have

> `# Two answers at the end, where the journeys above need three: this`
> `# game ends itself, so there is no `quit` to confirm -- only the score`
> `# and play-again questions.`

Both halves are wrong. `quit` never asks for confirmation — `sst.c:406-412` sets `alldone = 1` and breaks straight out — and the journeys above do not need three answers. I re-ran `reports`, `ending` and `docking` with the trailing `n` removed and all three produced output byte-identical to their committed fixtures; the third `n` is unconsumed slack, not a required answer.

Failure scenario: a maintainer adding a journey trusts the comment, hunts for a confirmation prompt that does not exist, and mis-sizes the trailing answers — or, worse, "fixes" the older journeys down to two and believes they have found a behaviour change.

The real reason two suffice is worth writing down instead, because it is genuinely non-obvious: the game asks exactly two questions at the end (`sst.c:501` and `sst.c:507`), and the two `getch()` pauses on this path consume nothing, because `readinput()` uses `fgets` (`sst.c:656`) which has already drained the pipe into stdio's buffer, so `getch()`'s raw `read(0, ...)` (`osx.c:55`) sees EOF and returns `'\0'`. I confirmed that by replacing the first `n` with `Xn`: the pause did not eat the `X`, `ja()` printed `Please answer with "Y" or "N":`, and the journey then ran out of input. Suggested fix: say the game asks two questions here and the pauses eat nothing, and drop the comparison with the other journeys (or note their third `n` is surplus).

### nit — `tests/golden.sh:383-389`: `--update` leaves the bad recording on disk while reporting it was not recorded

`covers` runs after `play` has already `cp`'d the new output into `$golden/`, so when the journey stops winning, `--update` prints `recorded won (1723 bytes)` and then `6 journey(s) were not fit to record.` — it was recorded. I reproduced this by pointing the `won` journey at a non-winning script in a scratch copy of `tests/`: exit 1, six clear failures, and `won.txt` overwritten with the losing game. The guard still works (which is the point), but the summary contradicts the disk. Suggest either wording the covers failure to say "the recording was written anyway; restore it with `git checkout`", or adjusting the `--update` s

git add tests/golden.sh tests/golden/won.txt && git status --short && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF' && git log --format='%G? %h %s' -1
test: record a game that is won, and check it stays won

Seven journeys were recorded and none of them won. Every one quit or
died, so the whole FWON epilogue in finish.c was unrecorded: the
Romulan surrender, the promotion prose, the win bonus on the score
sheet. That was not only missing wording. #52 and #54 both changed
arithmetic that runs on no other path, and this suite said nothing
about either -- the confidence for both came from a differential
harness run by hand.

Winning means the galaxy's last Klingon dead, which sounds beyond a
script until you count them: a short novice game has two to four
(setup.c:547). tournament 23 puts all three -- two Klingons and a
Commander -- in quadrant 5 - 7, so the journey is one move and one
phaser burst, and the epilogue follows.

The issue weighed two other ways in. A DEBUG-only "win now" command
cannot work here: golden runs in the Release build too, where the
command would not exist. A frozen save is worse than it looks --
freeze() is a raw fwrite of the structs (setup.c:61), and struct foo2
gains idebug under -DDEBUG, so a committed save would load in one
build type and not the other. A seed needs neither.

Because a fixture defends whatever it was recorded from, a journey
that quietly stopped winning would be re-recorded losing and match
itself from then on. So covers() asserts the six lines only a win
prints, before the --update early exit, and a careless re-record fails
too.

The recording keeps two things it found. It is the only fixture with a
screen-clear escape in it, from a supernova announcement -- read it
with cat -v. And the score sheet's Romulan line sits a column left of
every other line, because the plural format string in finish.c is a
space short; that is filed as #62 and left alone here, recorded as the
game prints it.

The other seven recordings are byte-identical; only won.txt is new.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

content.text:
Merged. Issue #55 is closed — `3a93d93` on `main`, branch deleted, working tree clean.

**What landed**

A `won` journey in `tests/golden.sh` plus its fixture. The key insight was that the issue's framing was too pessimistic: it assumed a scripted win was implausible because the `tournament` battery never comes close. But that battery plays longer, harder games — a **short/novice game has only 2–4 Klingons** (`setup.c:547`), and seed `tournament 23` puts all three in one quadrant. The whole game is one move and one phaser burst.

That let me skip both approaches the issue proposed, and both turn out to be unworkable here:

- A **Debug-only "win now" command** wouldn't exist in the Release build, where `golden` also runs.
- A **committed frozen save** is worse than it looks — `freeze()` is a raw `fwrite` of the structs, and `struct foo2` gains `idebug` under `-DDEBUG`, so a save recorded in one build type can't load in the other. Worth knowing if that idea resurfaces.

So: no production code, no binary fixture, no debug path.

**The part that isn't just a recording.** A fixture defends whatever it was recorded from, so a journey that quietly stopped winning would be re-recorded losing and match itself forever. `covers()` asserts the six lines only a win prints, and sits *before* the `--update` early exit, so a careless re-record fails too. I tested it in both directions.

**Verification**: 10/10 in Debug and Release locally, 40 deterministic runs, clean under `dash`/`busybox sh`/`shellcheck`, and all four CI legs green — including both macOS legs, which was the real risk for a byte-exact fixture. The seven pre-existing fixtures are byte-identical to `main` (verified via `git hash-object`, since `--update` rewrites all of them).

**Two things the recording exposed**, both flagged by review:

- The score sheet's plural Romulan line sits one column left of every other line — the format string at `finish.c:352` is a space short. Real and player-visible, and only ever appears on a win, which is why nothing caught it before. Filed as **#62** (you chose that over fixing it inline) and cited in the comment; the fixture records it as-is, per the suite's own "recordings of what the game does, not proofs of what it should."
- `won.txt` is the only fixture containing a live ANSI screen-clear escape, from a supernova announcement. `cat` it and it wipes your scrollback — noted in the comment to read it with `cat -v`.

Review caught two comments I'd written that were confidently wrong (a claim that `quit` asks for confirmation, and an inverted account of how the seed relates to skill/length). I verified both against the code and fixtures before rewriting them.

Still open: **#58** (galaxy vs the manual, small) and **#46** (TUI resize repaint, the hard one), plus the new **#62**, which is a genuine good-first-issue — a one-character fix whose entire evidence is a one-line fixture diff.
