tests/instructions.sh . && git add AGENTS.md && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF' && git log --format='%G? %h %s' -1
docs: have every agent get its review from a reader, not itself

The workflow's three review passes ran on Claude Code sub-agents, and the
only thing said to any other agent was a line at the end telling it to
perform the equivalent passes itself. That is the weakest possible
reading of a review: the author and the reader share a memory of what was
intended, which is the one thing a reviewer is for.

An agent that is not Claude Code now gets the same three passes. The
mechanism is stated in a way any harness can act on -- a reviewer is a
fresh session holding the reviewer's instructions, the change, and
nothing else, which is a sub-agent where the harness has them and a
second non-interactive invocation of its own CLI where it does not. A new
session reading the change cold satisfies it; the same session a turn
later does not.

The per-tool definition points at `.claude/agents/` rather than restating
it. Three copies of a specification are three specifications, which is
what this file exists to prevent -- and the first draft proved the point
by describing code-review as a C17 and CMake expert while its definition
also asks for terminal game expertise and an explicit verdict.

It lands as its own change, before the work it will review, because a
reviewer committed beside a feature is the unrelated work step 10
forbids, and because step 8 cannot be satisfied by the commit that
creates the reviewer -- the one place self-review is unavoidable, and it
has to say so.

Self-review survives only as a last resort, and taking it means naming
the mechanism looked for and why it was not there.

Nothing here claims a path into `.codex/` or `.cursor/`. Those hold hook
configuration and nothing either tool reads agent definitions from, so
the rule asks the author to confirm the harness loads what they wrote: a
definition somewhere the tool never reads is inert, and from the outside
looks exactly like a step that was carried out.

The new section quotes step numbers and its own title, both of which
break silently when either moves; that is added to #65 rather than filed
again.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

Merged as `b0caaba`. All four CI legs green, branch deleted, tree clean.

**What the rule now says.** A new `### The review sub-agents` section replaces the old one-line fallback. The key move is that it defines the mechanism instead of naming vendors: *a reviewer is a fresh session holding the reviewer's instructions, the change, and nothing else* — a sub-agent where the harness has them, a second non-interactive CLI invocation where it doesn't. With a falsifiable test attached: a new session reading the change cold satisfies it; the same session a turn later does not.

Around that:

- **Point at `.claude/agents/`, don't restate it.** The per-tool definition says "read the matching file and follow it" and carries only harness wiring.
- **Land it as its own change**, before the work it reviews — a reviewer committed beside a feature is the unrelated work step 10 forbids. That commit is the one place self-review is unavoidable (step 8 can't be satisfied by the commit creating the reviewer), and it has to say so.
- **Confirm the harness actually loads it** — an inert definition looks from the outside exactly like a completed step.
- **Self-review is last resort**, and taking it means naming what you looked for and why it wasn't there.

**Two review findings changed the substance, not just the wording.** My first draft said "Codex, Cursor and others have an equivalent; use it" — an assertion with no instruction behind it, and wrong for Codex, which has no project-scoped sub-agent definition. An agent would have found no such feature and fallen straight through to self-review, defeating the change. My draft also restated each reviewer's role and got two of them wrong in the process, demonstrating the exact drift it warned about — which is why it's a pointer now.

I also had it claiming definitions belong "beside the configuration `.codex/`/`.cursor/` already keep". Verification showed those hold only Entire hook wiring, nothing either harness reads agents from. No path is claimed now.

**Worth flagging:** the section quotes step numbers *and* its own heading, both of which break silently if either moves. I added that to **#65** as a comment rather than opening a duplicate — the first time the new step 9's "search first" clause got exercised.

One thing I could not verify from here, and the section is written to admit it: whether a Codex or Cursor agent actually loads a definition from a project directory. Neither harness is available in this environment. That's why the rule puts the check on the agent that writes the file rather than asserting a path — but the first non-Claude agent to follow it will be the real test.

message.content:
<bash-stdout># AGENTS.md

Shared instructions for every coding agent working in this repository
(Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, and others). `CLAUDE.md` imports this
file; keep all rules here so every agent sees the same thing.

## Project

Super Star Trek — a classic terminal (CLI) space strategy game written in C17,
built with CMake. The executable is `sst`. Game documentation lives in
`sst.doc`; shared declarations live in `sst.h`.

Global game state uses the `EXTERN`/`INCLUDED` trick in `sst.h`: exactly one
translation unit per binary defines `INCLUDED` before including `sst.h` to
instantiate the globals (`sst.c` for the game; a test's own file, e.g.
`tests/test_tuifmt.c`, for test binaries that don't link `sst.c`).

Display state (`tui_active`, `tui_ingame`) deliberately sits outside that
mechanism — plain `extern` in `tui.h`, defined in `tui.c` — so `tui.h`
stays self-contained for `osx.c`, which cannot include `sst.h`. Put new
display flags there, not in `sst.h`.

`osx.c` is the file that cannot include `sst.h`: `sst.h` declares
`pause(int)`, which collides with the POSIX `pause(void)` that `osx.c`
needs. So what `osx.c` *provides* is declared in `osx.h` (included by
both `osx.c` and `sst.h`), and what `osx.c` *calls* it gets from
`tui.h`. Put new platform functions in `osx.h`, not `sst.h`, so the
definition stays checked against the declaration — `-Wmissing-prototypes`
is on and CI builds with `-Werror`.

## Build and run

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   # build type is required; Debug adds -DDEBUG
cmake --build build
./build/sst
```

Note: `CMakeLists.txt` compares `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` directly, so configuring
without `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=...` fails. `-Wall -Wextra` is always on; CI
also configures with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, so pass that locally to see what
CI will refuse. Feature flags `-DSCORE -DCAPTURE
-DCLOAKING` are always enabled.

## TUI mode (`sst -t`)

- All game output must go through `prout`/`proutn`/`proutf`/`prouts` and all
  input through `scan()`/`getch()`/`readinput()` — raw `printf`/`putchar`/
  `fgets` silently bypasses the full-screen mode.
- Plain mode (no `-t`) must not change as an unintended side effect of any
  change; verify with a piped scripted journey (e.g.
  `printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\nsrscan\nquit\nn\n' | ./build/sst`).
  If a change alters plain-mode output on purpose, say so in the commit
  and explain why.
- Text the game prints must not end in a carriage return. `sst.doc` is
  CRLF, so anything read from it needs both stripped: under curses a
  trailing `\r` returns the cursor to column 0 and the newline then
  erases the line. `pause()` writes a CR deliberately, to wipe its own
  prompt in place -- the one exception, and the reason the test scripts
  filter that shape before checking.
- The panel formatters in `tuifmt.c` must mirror `srscan()` in `reports.c`
  exactly — it is the spec, including sensor-damage masking and the `-f`
  coordinate transposition (x is the column). Keep `tests/test_tuifmt.c` in
  sync (`ctest --test-dir build`).
- Testing the TUI needs a pty: use tmux, and always on your own socket via
  `-L`, with `-f /dev/null` so the config does not follow — `tmux -f /dev/null
  -L sst new-session -d -x 100 -y 30 -s t './build/sst -t; sleep 30'`, drive
  with `tmux -f /dev/null -L sst send-keys -t t 'cmd' Enter` (input is
  line-based; keys need Enter), inspect with `capture-pane -t t -p`, and clean
  up with `kill-server` on that same socket. Without `-f /dev/null` a setting
  as ordinary as `base-index 1` renames the pane out from under you and every
  capture comes back empty. The default socket is where the
  human running you keeps their own work: on 2026-08-01 a review agent tidied up
  after a TUI check with a bare `tmux kill-server` and destroyed a week-old
  session of eight panes, including the agent's own parent. `-L` is what makes
  that mistake impossible rather than merely discouraged — never issue a bare
  `tmux kill-server`, and never `kill-session` a session you did not create.
  Never redirect the game's stdout in the session — it breaks curses rendering.
  `tests/tui.sh` does all of this automatically and is the place to add
  coverage; it skips without tmux, but fails rather than skipping when `$CI` is
  set.
- Check the TUI at 80x24 and 72x24, not just at a comfortable size. 72x24 is
  the smallest it accepts and 80x24 is what most terminals open at; the
  message window is only ten lines at both, which is where the paging bugs
  live.

A failing `golden` test means a journey's output changed. Work out why
and say so in the commit -- the fixture diff is the evidence a reviewer
needs. Never re-record with `tests/golden.sh <sst> --update` to turn CI
green without that explanation; the recordings are the only thing in
the suite that checks the game's arithmetic at all.

## Development workflow

Every coding agent working in this repository must follow this workflow.

1. **Inspect before changing anything.** Inspect the repository, current Git
   state, and all applicable instruction files before making changes. Preserve
   unrelated staged, unstaged, and untracked work.

2. **Create a branch first.** Create a dedicated feature, fix, refactor, chore,
   test, or documentation branch before making code changes. Never commit
   directly to `main`, and create the branch from the latest appropriate
   `main` state.

3. **Choose a thin vertical slice.** Before implementing a roadmap item or
   feature, define the smallest end-to-end slice that can be reviewed, tested,
   shipped, and merged independently. Prefer one coherent user-visible or
   operational outcome over a broad horizontal layer.

4. **Use test-driven development when behavior or structure is testable.**
   - Add or update a focused test before implementation.
   - Run it and confirm it fails for the expected reason.
   - Implement the smallest appropriate change.
   - Run focused tests while iterating.
   - Refactor only while the relevant tests remain green.

5. **Inspect the complete diff.** Review the branch diff plus all staged,
   unstaged, and untracked files. Remove accidental or unrelated changes while
   preserving work that belongs to the user. What you drop because it was
   unrelated is often worth filing; see step 9.

6. **Run `ui-review` before verification.** After the main agent completes an
   implementation pass, invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent. The `ui-review`
   sub-agent must act as an expert in games and CLI games. Address every
   actionable finding before moving on, as with the two steps below. If you
   are not Claude Code, read "The review sub-agents" after this list before
   running this step or the two that follow.

7. **Run `verifier` before code review.** Invoke the `verifier` sub-agent to
   run the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for
   the change. The verifier must report failures, flakes, missing coverage,
   and environment issues. Fix or explicitly resolve every actionable finding
   before starting code review. If a verifier finding requires a code change,
   rerun the verifier after addressing it.

8. **Run `code-review` before every commit.** Invoke the `code-review`
   sub-agent against the current branch diff and every staged, unstaged, and
   untracked file. The reviewer must act as an expert in the languages and
   frameworks used by this application. Address every actionable finding
   before committing. If review findings cause changes, rerun the appropriate
   tests and the `verifier`, then obtain a fresh `code-review` approval for
   the changed state.

9. **File what you found outside the slice.** Work turns up problems that
   belong to no slice in particular: a defect the change did not cause, a
   test that cannot fail, a comment that is no longer true. Open a GitHub
   issue for each as you find it, without waiting to be asked — a finding
   that lives only in a session summary is a finding nobody will act on.
   Standing here at step 9 makes this the last check that nothing was left
   unfiled, not the moment to begin. The main agent files them; the review
   sub-agents only report.

   - Search the open issues first. If it is already filed, add what you
     learned to that issue instead of opening a second one.
   - File a real defect — anything that would mislead a player or a
     maintainer — and a coverage gap, meaning a test that cannot fail or
     that asserts less than it appears to. Leave style preferences and
     speculative ideas out; they belong in the pull request body. When it
     is genuinely unclear, file it: a wrong issue costs one close.
   - **Do not fix it in this slice.** An unrelated fix buried in an
     unrelated diff is how both the fix and the finding go unreviewed. Fix
     it here only if it belongs to the slice.
   - That is not license to file what steps 6-8 require you to fix. A
     `ui-review`, `verifier` or `code-review` finding about *this* change is
     resolved here; filing it is not resolving it. What gets filed is what
     those reviews turn up about code the change did not touch, and
     whatever you meet while reading for some other purpose.
   - Give the issue what the next person needs: what is wrong, why it
     matters, where it was found, and how to see it, citing `sst.doc` or a
     file and line where one applies.
   - Where the work depends on the unfixed behavior, name the issue in a
     comment beside it. Write that comment as part of the implementation,
     so it reaches the reviewer rather than arriving after approval.
   - Say which issues were filed, in the pull request body and in the
     summary of the work — in the summary alone when there is no pull
     request. An agent that cannot open issues says so plainly and lists
     the findings in the same places, marked as unfiled, so a human can
     file them. Silence is the one outcome this step exists to prevent.

10. **Commit after approval.** Commit only after verification and code review
    are complete. Use Conventional Commits:

    ```text
    <type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>
    ```

    Keep the subject at 72 characters or fewer, describe why in the body when
    useful, and do not combine unrelated work.

11. **Create pull requests from the reviewed state.**
    - Confirm that local verification remains valid.
    - Rerun `code-review` only if the reviewed state changed after the
      pre-commit review.
    - A changed state includes code, tests, documentation, generated files,
      conflict resolution, or any other staged, unstaged, or untracked
      content.
    - Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and worktree
      remain unchanged.
    - Push and create the pull request only after local verification and any
      required code review are complete.
    - Open a normal, ready-for-review pull request by default. Do not open
      draft pull requests unless the user explicitly asks for a draft.

12. **Merge only clean, passing pull requests.** Merge only after GitHub
    reports a clean merge state and every configured check passes. Never
    bypass a failing or pending required check. Self-merges are allowed when
    these conditions are met. Use squash merge for short-lived development
    branches to keep `main` linear, then delete the merged branch.

### The review sub-agents

Steps 6-8 invoke Claude Code sub-agents defined in `.claude/agents/`:
`ui-review`, `verifier` and `code-review`. What matters is not the tool. It
is that the work is judged by a reader who did not write it, and who
reaches its conclusions from the diff rather than from a memory of having
intended something.

An agent that is not Claude Code gets the same three passes, and does not
skip them.

- **A reviewer is a fresh session holding the reviewer's instructions, the
  change, and nothing else.** A sub-agent where the harness has them; a
  second non-interactive invocation of your own CLI — `codex exec` and its
  equivalents — where it does not. A new session reading the change cold
  satisfies this. The same session in a later turn does not.
- **Point at the definitions here rather than restating them.**
  `.claude/agents/ui-review.md`, `verifier.md` and `code-review.md` are the
  specifications. A per-tool definition should say to read the matching
  file and follow it, and carry only the wiring its own harness needs: the
  name, and that the reviewer reports findings and never edits. Copying the
  text is how three tools come to review three different things, which is
  the whole reason this file exists.
- **Keep the three names.** The workflow above, the commit history and the
  issue tracker all refer to them by name.
- **Land the definition as its own change,** on its own branch and commit,
  before the work it will review — not beside a feature, which step 10
  forbids and step 3 argues against. It belongs in the repository rather
  than in someone's local configuration for the same reason this file
  does: the next session in that tool then inherits a reviewer instead of
  improvising one, and an improvised reviewer drifts. That commit is also
  the one place self-review cannot be avoided, since step 8 cannot be
  satisfied by the commit that creates the reviewer. Say so in the commit,
  and disclose it as below.
- **Confirm the harness actually loads what you wrote.** A definition in a
  directory the tool never reads is inert, and from the outside it looks
  exactly like a step that was carried out.
- **Self-review is the last resort, not the default.** Taking it means
  saying which mechanism you looked for and why it was not there — or, for
  the commit that creates the reviewer, that it did not yet exist. Say it
  in the pull request body and in the summary of the work — in the summary
  alone when there is no pull request. A reviewer who shares the author's memory
  of what was intended is the one thing this section exists to prevent.</bash-stdout><bash-stderr></bash-stderr>

content.text:
The rewrap is in CI. Now your second question — here's what I'd actually change, from having run this workflow maybe a dozen times today.

**1. Nothing tells you to prove a test can fail. This is the big one.**

Step 4 covers TDD: write the test, watch it fail, implement. But a large share of the tests in this repo are written *against behavior that already exists* — the golden recordings, the manual checks in `tournament.sh`. For those, step 4's "confirm it fails for the expected reason" has no meaning, and the workflow goes quiet exactly where it's needed most.

Today three of my assertions passed against builds that broke them. The row count was counting rows from later scans; the novice Super-commander check looked for a line that skill level never prints; the starbases term was multiplied by a count that was zero in all twelve galaxies. All three looked completely reasonable in review. Only deliberately breaking the game found them. That's a rule the file should carry, and it's the same defect class step 9 already calls a "coverage gap" — the workflow names the disease but not the diagnostic.

**2. The three review passes are all-or-nothing, and nobody can actually follow that.**

Step 6-8 apply to every change, and the sub-agents section says "does not skip them". I've now skipped `ui-review` four times today on changes with no player-facing surface, and disclosed it each time. The reviewer's take was that step 7 already has proportionality baked in ("appropriate for the change") and step 6's trigger is an *implementation pass*, so the letter isn't quite as strict as it reads — but that's a lawyerly reading of a rule that plainly says "does not skip them". Either the rule should say which passes bind for which kinds of change, or every agent will keep improvising, which defeats a shared instruction file.

**3. Nothing says what to do when the issue itself is wrong.**

#58 asserted the galaxy check was impossible because the packing "appears nowhere in `sst.doc`". It's at `sst.doc:436-439`. I noted the correction in the PR, but only because I chose to — an agent following the workflow literally would either implement the issue's mistaken plan or silently do something else. Both are bad. A rule here is cheap: say so, correct the issue, and don't just quietly work around it.

**4. A misfiled paragraph.** The `golden`/`--update` rule sits at the end of `## TUI mode`, but it has nothing to do with the TUI — it's the most important rule in the file about test fixtures, hiding under an unrelated heading. Pure relocation.

I'd rank these **1 > 3 > 2 > 4**. The first prevents a class of silently-worthless test that this repo is actively accumulating; the fourth is tidying.

Two I considered and would *not* do: a rule about when to escalate to you (judgment, doesn't codify well), and one about capturing session learnings into AGENTS.md (that's what you and I just did twice, and a rule would invite churn).

4. **Use test-driven development when behavior or structure is testable.**
   - Add or update a focused test before implementation.
   - Run it and confirm it fails for the expected reason.
   - Implement the smallest appropriate change.
   - Run focused tests while iterating.
   - Refactor only while the relevant tests remain green.

   A test written against behavior that already exists — a recording, a
   check of something the game has always done — never has that failing
   first run to show for itself, and that is where tests which assert
   nothing come from. Prove it can fail some other way:

   - Break what it checks, in a scratch copy of the tree rather than in
     the repository, and watch the test report it. Say in the commit what
     was broken and what the test said. Break the game, not the test: if
     the game breaks and the test stays green, the test is what needs
     fixing.
   - Choose a break the test could see. Changing how something is stored
     can be undone by the code that reads it back — the store and the load
     agree with each other again, the output never moves, and a green run
     proves nothing. Break what the player or the file actually shows.

## Verdict: request changes

Reviewed state: branch `test/prove-a-test-can-fail` at `c3b3705` (identical to `main`); the entire pending change is unstaged edits to `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md` lines 118-141 — a prose paragraph plus three bullets appended to workflow step 4, and a five-line dated example. Nothing staged, nothing untracked, no code touched. `tests/instructions.sh` only checks AGENTS.md's size and that it has a `## Development workflow` heading, so no test needs updating.

The rule is well-aimed and the war story is factually accurate — I corroborated all three cases in the tree (`tests/tournament.sh:457-459` the nine-row srscan, `tests/tournament.sh:676-680` the line the game does not print at novice skill, `tests/tournament.sh:73-77` the starbase term multiplied by nothing). Two findings need fixing before commit.

### Blocker

**`AGENTS.md:123-124` — "in a scratch copy of the tree" names no mechanism, and the obvious mechanisms silently do the wrong thing.**

The file's house style is to name the mechanism that makes the mistake impossible (`-L` for tmux, the exact `cmake` line, the exact `printf` journey). Here it states a prohibition and leaves the method to the agent, and every method an agent will reach for first fails:

- `cp -a` the tree brings `build/` along, and `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/build/Makefile:60` bakes in `CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR = /home/scottdensmore/.../super-star-trek`. Running `cmake --build build` inside the copy compiles the **original, unbroken** sources into the **original** build dir. The agent breaks the game in the copy, gets a green test, and per bullet 1 ("if the game breaks and the test stays green, the test is what needs fixing") concludes a sound test is broken and rewrites it. It has also just overwritten the real `./build/sst`.
- `git worktree add` gives a tree from `HEAD`, which does **not** contain the uncommitted test being proved. The agent proves nothing about the test it wrote.
- The remaining path is editing in place and reverting with `git checkout --`, which destroys the unrelated unstaged work step 1 requires preserving.

Fix: name the recipe. Every shell test takes the binary as an argument (`tests/tournament.sh <sst> [build-type]`, `tests/golden.sh <sst>`, and the same in `CMakeLists.txt:61-123`), so the safe form is one line and never touches the repository:

> Copy the working tree — the current one, uncommitted test included — to a directory outside the repository, leaving `build/` behind; configure a fresh build there (`cmake -S <copy> -B <copy>/build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug`) — a copied `build/` still points its Makefiles at the original sources and would rebuild the tree you are trying not to touch. Then run the repository's own test against the broken binary: `tests/tournament.sh <copy>/build/sst Debug`. For the compiled tests (`test_rules`, `test_tuifmt`) run `ctest --test-dir <copy>/build`.

### Should-fix

**`AGENTS.md:128-131` — the storage-versus-display rule is wrong for the very case it is drawn from, and the repository's own comment says so.**

"Break what the player or the file actually shows" does not save you here: `lrscan()` prints the raw `d.galaxy` word, so the packing *is* displayed output, and a break in it still cancels. `tests/tournament.sh:490-498` states the real boundary precisely:

```
	# How much the two halves are worth differs... newqad() fills the
	# quadrant by decoding the same galaxy word that the long-range scan
	# prints, so for Klingons, starbases and stars this weighs an encoding
	# against its own decoding... The exclusions are the independent
	# half: Romulans and planets come from d.newstuf, by a path the
	# galaxy word knows nothing about... a genuine second opinion.
```

The general claim as put to me does not hold. What makes a mutation invisible is not that it lands in storage; it is that **both sides of the test's comparison descend from the same representation**. Displayed output is equally self-cancelling when the expected value is derived from the same word (galaxy packing), and equally invisible when the value is clamped, rounded (`%.2f`), or masked (sensor-damage masking in `srscan`) before it reaches the assertion. Conversely a storage break *is* visible whenever the expectation comes from elsewhere — the manual, a literal, a second subsystem.

Suggested reframing: *choose a break on a path where the test's expected value comes from somewhere independent — `sst.doc`, a literal, a subsystem that does not share the representation. A break upstream of a word the test only ever observes through code that decodes it the same way cancels out: setup writes it wrong, the quadrant is filled wrong to match, both scans agree, and nothing moves.* Two further conditions belong here: the break must make **the test you are proving** fail, not merely some test — a break so broad that the game will not start proves nothing about the new assertion.

Related ordering problem: bullet 1's conclusion "if the game breaks and the test stays green, the test is what needs fixing" is asserted before bullet 2 explains that a green run can also mean the break was invisible. As written it invites damaging a sound test. Either move that sentence after bullet 2 or qualify it ("green means one of two things — the test is blind, or the break was; rule out the second first").

### Nits

- **`AGENTS.md:123-125` vs `AGENTS.md:189-193`** — step 9's carve-out ("not license to file what steps 6-8 require you to fix") names only steps 6-8, while step 9's coverage-gap definition at line 183-184 is *"a test that cannot fail"* — exactly what this new rule produces about your own slice. A literal reader files an issue instead of fixing it. Widen the carve-out to "steps 4 and 6-8", or say in the new block that a test of yours that cannot fail is fixed here, not filed.
- **`AGENTS.md:123-125` — record the proof where the next reader will see it.** The rule asks only for a commit message, but the established practice in this tree is a comment beside the assertion: `tests/tournament.sh:458-459` reads *"an assertion that reads like this one and cannot fail. A build whose srscan drew nine rows is what showed it up."* A commit message is invisible to whoever next edits the test. Ask for both, or prefer the comment.
- **`AGENTS.md:118-121` — scope.** As written this applies to every characterisation test, including adding one literal-comparison case to `tests/test_tuifmt.c`, where the proof is changing the literal and the tree-copy ceremony is disproportionate. One sentence fixes it: *where the test compares against a literal in its own file, changing the literal proves it in a second; the copy is for tests that run the whole game and search its output.*
- **`AGENTS.md:137` — "on one day in August 2026" is less findable than its precedent.** The tmux story gives a date to the day, which is what lets a reader check it. Give the date or the PR numbers (#52, #54, #57, #59, #64 are the candidates). I would keep the story — it is the evidence for the rule and each case maps to a bullet — but it is five lines against fourteen of rule, and "multiplied a term that was zero in every galaxy in the battery" reads as a riddle to anyone who has not read `tests/tournament.sh:73-77`. Three lines would carry it.

### Not reviewed

- No build, test, or TUI run: the change is documentation only and touches no code path.
- I could not confirm the three war-story assertions against their originating commits by number (the text cites none); I verified them instead against the surviving explanatory comments in `tests/tournament.sh`, which corroborate all three.

   check of something the game has always done — never has that failing
   first run to show for itself, and that is where tests which assert
   nothing come from. Prove it can fail some other way.

   - Break what it checks, watch the test report it, and write down what
     was broken both in the commit and in a comment beside the assertion.
     The commit is invisible to whoever next edits the test.
   - Break it outside the repository. Copy the working tree — the current
     one, uncommitted test and all — somewhere else, leave `build/`
     behind, and configure a fresh one there: a copied `build/` still
     names the original source directory in its makefiles, so building in
     the copy rebuilds, and overwrites, the tree you were trying not to
     touch. Every test here takes the binary as an argument, so the run is
     `tests/tournament.sh <copy>/build/sst Debug`, or `ctest --test-dir
     <copy>/build` for the compiled ones. A `git worktree` will not do: it
     holds `HEAD`, not the test you have just written.
   - Break the game, not the test — and break it somewhere the test's
     expectation does not come from. A break that both sides of the
     comparison descend from cancels out: setup writes the galaxy word
     wrong, the code that reads it back fills the quadrant to match, both
     scans agree, and nothing moves. Rounding, clamping and sensor masking
     swallow a break the same way. Prefer a path where the expected value
     comes from somewhere independent — `sst.doc`, a literal, a subsystem
     that does not share the representation.
   - A green run means one of two things: the test is blind, or the break
     was. Rule out the second before touching the test.

     over — one seed, one galaxy, one game that happened to dock — assert

   - Where the test compares against a literal in its own file, changing
     the literal proves it in a second. The copied tree is for tests that
     run the whole game and read what it printed.

docs: make a test earn its green run

Step 4 covered writing a test before the code, watching it fail, then
implementing. Most of this suite is the other kind: recordings and
checks written against behaviour the game already had, which never have
that failing first run to show for themselves. The workflow said nothing
about them, and that silence is where tests that assert nothing come
from.

Three assertions in #64 passed against builds that broke them. One
counted rows from scans it was not looking at. One searched for a line
the game does not print at the skill it ran at. One multiplied a term
that was zero in every galaxy the battery then played, so any weight at
all passed. All three read convincingly in review; only a broken build
found them.

So: break what the test checks and watch it report. The rule names the
recipe, because the obvious ways to get a broken build are all wrong. A
copied build/ still names the original source directory in its cache, so
building in the copy compiles the original's sources -- the break never
reaches the binary and the test goes green for the wrong reason, which
is the very failure this is meant to catch. A git worktree holds HEAD,
not the test just written. Editing in place and reverting destroys the
unrelated work step 1 preserves.

It also says which breaks are worth making. One that both sides of the
comparison descend from cancels out: setup writes the galaxy word wrong,
the code reading it back fills the quadrant to match, and nothing moves.
A mutant that changed the starbase encoding from += 10 to += 20 passed
on every seed, which is why the rule asks for a break on a path whose
expectation comes from somewhere else -- sst.doc, a literal, a subsystem
that does not share the representation.

Step 9's carve-out widens to steps 4 and 6-8, so a test of your own that
cannot fail is fixed rather than filed as a coverage gap against
yourself.

content.text:
## Verdict: request changes

Reviewed state: branch `docs/which-reviews-bind` at `0a075a5`, with one unstaged modification to `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md` (nothing staged, no untracked files). The change replaces the two-line "An agent that is not Claude Code gets the same three passes, and does not skip them" with three paragraphs in the "The review sub-agents" section stating which of the three passes bind, a disclosure rule for skipping `ui-review`, and a softened non-Claude-agent sentence.

The direction is right: a rule that gets improvised around is worse than a narrower rule that gets followed, and tightening `verifier` to "always, at step 7's scope" while naming the doc-change case explicitly is a genuine net increase in discipline, not a decrease. Two findings block, both because the text as written can be used to justify exactly the skip it means to forbid.

### Findings

**1. should-fix (blocker for this change's purpose) — `AGENTS.md:270-272`: the exemption list is factually wrong about the build system, in this repo, today.**

> "This file, a test's plumbing, the build system and CI configuration give it nothing to read"

`CMakeLists.txt:9` is `set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING")`. Those three flags gate player-visible commands and output across `finish.c`, `events.c`, `battle.c` and `tuifmt.c` (`#ifdef CLOAKING` at `battle.c:4`, `tuifmt.c:134`, and so on). A one-line build-system change can therefore delete a player command and the score lines that follow it, and this sentence says a build-system change gives `ui-review` nothing to read. Failure scenario: an agent changes the flag line, cites this sentence verbatim, skips `ui-review`, and the pass that exists to notice a missing command is the one that was skipped. The list and the governing test one sentence earlier ("can alter what the game shows a player") flatly contradict each other, and an author looking for a cheap answer will reach for the list, because it is a lookup and the test is a judgement.

Fix: subordinate the list to the test rather than setting it beside it — e.g. "This file, a test's plumbing and CI configuration usually give it nothing to read; the build system does when it moves a feature flag, since `-DSCORE`, `-DCAPTURE` and `-DCLOAKING` decide which commands exist." Naming the one build-system case that binds also makes the list read as illustration rather than as an enumeration of safe categories.

**2. should-fix — `AGENTS.md:168-173`: a Claude Code agent following the numbered steps never learns this exemption exists.**

Step 6 is still an unconditional imperative ("invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent"), and its only pointer to the section that now qualifies it is `AGENTS.md:172` — "**If you are not Claude Code**, read 'The review sub-agents'". Grep confirms that is the sole cross-reference to the section in the file. So the agent the rule was written for (Claude Code, the one that skipped five times) reads step 6, sees no condition, and is back to a rule it cannot follow; the non-Claude agent is the only one routed to the escape hatch. That inverts the intent.

Fix, and this is also my answer to the placement question: keep the prose where it is — the section is the right home, it is already the "who these passes bind and on what terms" section, and #65 is correct that inserting a numbered item is the fragile move. But make the existing pointer in step 6 unconditional and name the condition inline, which is a sentence edit inside step 6 with no renumbering: "…invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent when the change can alter what the game shows a player or asks of them. See 'The review sub-agents' after this list for when this pass binds and what to say when it does not." No conflict with step 7's "appropriate for the change" (the new paragraph restates it accurately), none with step 8, none with step 4, and none with step 9's "not license to file what steps 4 and 6-8 require you to fix" — a skipped pass produces no findings to file.

**3. should-fix — `AGENTS.md:275-276`: the disclosure is written where no reviewer reads it.**

"say in the commit that it was skipped and why" is the only accountability the skip has, and step 8 runs `code-review` *before* the commit exists — I am reviewing a worktree, not a commit message, and neither `.claude/agents/code-review.md` nor `verifier.md` gives any reviewer a mandate to check a skip disclosure. Combined with squash merge (step 12), the sentence can end up in a body a human never reads. The section's own precedent for disclosing a review decision is `AGENTS.md:311-313`: "Say it in the pull request body and in the summary of the work — in the summary alone when there is no pull request", and step 9 uses the same formula. Fix: use that formula here too ("in the commit, and in the pull request body and the summary of the work, as below"), so the disclosure reaches a reader with standing to dispute it.

**4. should-fix — `AGENTS.md:269-270`: no tie-breaker for the unclear case, which is where the line gets stretched.**

To your question about brightness: "can alter" is a capability test, which is the strict reading and the right one — but nothing in the paragraph stops an author from reading it as an intent test ("I changed no strings, so it cannot alter output"), and a behaviour-preserving refactor of `srscan()` or `tuifmt.c` is precisely where output regressions hide. The file already knows how to close this kind of gap; `AGENTS.md:204-205` does it for issues: "When it is genuinely unclear, file it: a wrong issue costs one close." Add the parallel: "When it is unclear whether the change reaches the player, run it — a `ui-review` with nothing to say costs one pass. Code that runs while the game is running reaches the player, whether or not the change was meant to." That converts the ambiguity from a discretion into a default.

**5. nit — `AGENTS.md:280-281`: "does not stand in for them" is ambiguous and now redundant.**

"Stand in for" naturally takes a person as its object, so the reader has to work out that "them" is the passes and that the prohibition is on self-review. The bullet immediately below (`AGENTS.md:283-287`, "A reviewer is a fresh session… The same session in a later turn does not") says it precisely, and `AGENTS.md:309` says it again. Suggest: "An agent that is not Claude Code is bound on the same terms, and cannot satisfy a pass by reviewing its own work" — or drop the clause and keep only the scoping sentence.

**6. nit — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.claude/agents/ui-review.md:3`: the sub-agent's own description now disagrees about when it is invoked.**

Its front matter still reads "Invoke after the main agent completes an implementation pass and before running the verifier", unconditionally, and that description is what drives auto-delegation. Its Scope also covers "player-visible **and operator-visible**" surface, which is broader than AGENTS.md's new "what the game shows a player or asks of them". Not worth expanding this change's scope, but the two sources should be reconciled — either here or in a follow-up issue.

### Checked and clear

- Step references: "step 7" and "step 8" in the new text match the current numbering (6 `ui-review`, 7 `verifier`, 8 `code-review`).

## Verdict: request changes

Reviewed state: branch `docs/which-reviews-bind` at `0a075a5`, with one unstaged modification to `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md` (nothing staged, no untracked files). The change replaces the two-line "An agent that is not Claude Code gets the same three passes, and does not skip them" with three paragraphs in the "The review sub-agents" section stating which of the three passes bind, a disclosure rule for skipping `ui-review`, and a softened non-Claude-agent sentence.

The direction is right: a rule that gets improvised around is worse than a narrower rule that gets followed, and tightening `verifier` to "always, at step 7's scope" while naming the doc-change case explicitly is a genuine net increase in discipline, not a decrease. Two findings block, both because the text as written can be used to justify exactly the skip it means to forbid.

### Findings

**1. should-fix (blocker for this change's purpose) — `AGENTS.md:270-272`: the exemption list is factually wrong about the build system, in this repo, today.**

> "This file, a test's plumbing, the build system and CI configuration give it nothing to read"

`CMakeLists.txt:9` is `set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING")`. Those three flags gate player-visible commands and output across `finish.c`, `events.c`, `battle.c` and `tuifmt.c` (`#ifdef CLOAKING` at `battle.c:4`, `tuifmt.c:134`, and so on). A one-line build-system change can therefore delete a player command and the score lines that follow it, and this sentence says a build-system change gives `ui-review` nothing to read. Failure scenario: an agent changes the flag line, cites this sentence verbatim, skips `ui-review`, and the pass that exists to notice a missing command is the one that was skipped. The list and the governing test one sentence earlier ("can alter what the game shows a player") flatly contradict each other, and an author looking for a cheap answer will reach for the list, because it is a lookup and the test is a judgement.

Fix: subordinate the list to the test rather than setting it beside it — e.g. "This file, a test's plumbing and CI configuration usually give it nothing to read; the build system does when it moves a feature flag, since `-DSCORE`, `-DCAPTURE` and `-DCLOAKING` decide which commands exist." Naming the one build-system case that binds also makes the list read as illustration rather than as an enumeration of safe categories.

**2. should-fix — `AGENTS.md:168-173`: a Claude Code agent following the numbered steps never learns this exemption exists.**

Step 6 is still an unconditional imperative ("invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent"), and its only pointer to the section that now qualifies it is `AGENTS.md:172` — "**If you are not Claude Code**, read 'The review sub-agents'". Grep confirms that is the sole cross-reference to the section in the file. So the agent the rule was written for (Claude Code, the one that skipped five times) reads step 6, sees no condition, and is back to a rule it cannot follow; the non-Claude agent is the only one routed to the escape hatch. That inverts the intent.

Fix, and this is also my answer to the placement question: keep the prose where it is — the section is the right home, it is already the "who these passes bind and on what terms" section, and #65 is correct that inserting a numbered item is the fragile move. But make the existing pointer in step 6 unconditional and name the condition inline, which is a sentence edit inside step 6 with no renumbering: "…invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent when the change can alter what the game shows a player or asks of them. See 'The review sub-agents' after this list for when this pass binds and what to say when it does not." No conflict with step 7's "appropriate for the change" (the new paragraph restates it accurately), none with step 8, none with step 4, and none with step 9's "not license to file what steps 4 and 6-8 require you to fix" — a skipped pass produces no findings to file.

**3. should-fix — `AGENTS.md:275-276`: the disclosure is written where no reviewer reads it.**

"say in the commit that it was skipped and why" is the only accountability the skip has, and step 8 runs `code-review` *before* the commit exists — I am reviewing a worktree, not a commit message, and neither `.claude/agents/code-review.md` nor `verifier.md` gives any reviewer a mandate to check a skip disclosure. Combined with squash merge (step 12), the sentence can end up in a body a human never reads. The section's own precedent for disclosing a review decision is `AGENTS.md:311-313`: "Say it in the pull request body and in the summary of the work — in the summary alone when there is no pull request", and step 9 uses the same formula. Fix: use that formula here too ("in the commit, and in the pull request body and the summary of the work, as below"), so the disclosure reaches a reader with standing to dispute it.

**4. should-fix — `AGENTS.md:269-270`: no tie-breaker for the unclear case, which is where the line gets stretched.**

To your question about brightness: "can alter" is a capability test, which is the strict reading and the right one — but nothing in the paragraph stops an author from reading it as an intent test ("I changed no strings, so it cannot alter output"), and a behaviour-preserving refactor of `srscan()` or `tuifmt.c` is precisely where output regressions hide. The file already knows how to close this kind of gap; `AGENTS.md:204-205` does it for issues: "When it is genuinely unclear, file it: a wrong issue costs one close." Add the parallel: "When it is unclear whether the change reaches the player, run it — a `ui-review` with nothing to say costs one pass. Code that runs while the game is running reaches the player, whether or not the change was meant to." That converts the ambiguity from a discretion into a default.

**5. nit — `AGENTS.md:280-281`: "does not stand in for them" is ambiguous and now redundant.**

"Stand in for" naturally takes a person as its object, so the reader has to work out that "them" is the passes and that the prohibition is on self-review. The bullet immediately below (`AGENTS.md:283-287`, "A reviewer is a fresh session… The same session in a later turn does not") says it precisely, and `AGENTS.md:309` says it again. Suggest: "An agent that is not Claude Code is bound on the same terms, and cannot satisfy a pass by reviewing its own work" — or drop the clause and keep only the scoping sentence.

**6. nit — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.claude/agents/ui-review.md:3`: the sub-agent's own description now disagrees about when it is invoked.**

Its front matter still reads "Invoke after the main agent completes an implementation pass and before running the verifier", unconditionally, and that description is what drives auto-delegation. Its Scope also covers "player-visible **and operator-visible**" surface, which is broader than AGENTS.md's new "what the game shows a player or asks of them". Not worth expanding this change's scope, but the two sources should be reconciled — either here or in a follow-up issue.

- Step references: "step 7" and "step 8" in the new text match the current numbering (6 `ui-review`, 7 `verifier`, 8 `code-review`).

Two sources of truth about when a review runs is the same defect

## Problem

`AGENTS.md` now scopes the three review passes: `code-review` binds on
every commit, `verifier` always, and `ui-review` "when the change can
alter what the game shows a player or asks of them". A skip has to be
disclosed in the commit, the pull request body and the summary of the
work.

Nobody reads that disclosure in time to act on it.

- `code-review` runs at step 8, **before** the commit exists and before
  step 11 writes the pull request body. It never sees the sentence.
- Neither `.claude/agents/code-review.md` nor `verifier.md` gives any
  reviewer a mandate to ask whether `ui-review` was owed.
- The pull request body does reach a human, but at step 11 — after the
  work is shaped, reviewed and committed. That is a disclosure, not a
  gate.

## Why it matters

The old rule was absolute ("does not skip them"), and an absolute rule
needs no auditor. Scoping it to a judgement call put the author in sole
charge of the one pass the author has a standing incentive to skip, and
recorded the decision where the only always-binding reviewer cannot
object to it.

That is not hypothetical: `ui-review` was skipped five times in one
session before the rule existed, each time by the author's own judgement,
each time disclosed only in the commit.

## Suggested approach

`code-review` reads the whole diff, so it is the pass positioned to
notice. Roughly:

- A clause in `.claude/agents/code-review.md` telling the reviewer to
  check whether the diff touches player-visible surface and, if it does,
  whether `ui-review` ran — and to say so when it did not.
- A clause in `AGENTS.md` saying the skip and its reason are stated to
  `code-review` when it is invoked, so the reviewer has the claim in
  front of it rather than having to infer it.

Worth deciding at the same time whether the same treatment is owed for a
`verifier` whose scope was narrowed, which has the same shape.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A change that touches player-visible surface with no `ui-review`
      is something `code-review` is required to raise.
- [ ] The skip and its reason reach that reviewer while it can still
      object.

content.text:
## Verdict: pass

No failures, no flakes. One accuracy problem — not in the text, but in the evidence you were handed for claim (b).

## 1. Regression checks

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `tests/instructions.sh <root>` | pass — `instructions OK (CLAUDE.md 174 bytes, AGENTS.md 18579 bytes)` |
| `ctest` Debug, full suite | **10/10 pass** (tuifmt, rules, journey, journey-tui, eof, help, tui, tournament, golden, instructions), 161.75s |
| Release configure + build | clean, no warnings |
| `ctest -R instructions` Release | pass |

Nothing failed, so nothing needed a rerun.

## 2a. `-DSCORE` / `-DCAPTURE` / `-DCLOAKING` gate player-visible commands and output — **confirmed**

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/CMakeLists.txt:9` sets all three. The player-facing sites:

- `sst.c:114,117,120` — inside `listCommands()`, these are the `SCORE`/`CLOAK`/`CAPTURE` entries in the COMMANDS listing.
- `sst.c:229-236` — `#ifndef CLOAKING && i != 26` etc., which is what makes the command *recognized* at all.
- `sst.c:361,372,378` — dispatch to `cloak()`, `capture()`, `score()`.
- `reports.c:79` — `"%d Klingon%s in brig."` and `"%d captured Klingon%s turned in to Star Fleet."` in the status report.
- `reports.c:355` — `", CLOAKED"` on the Condition line.

Empirically, `commands` in a Debug build prints:
```
   COMPUTER  EMEXIT    PROBE     COMMANDS
   SCORE     CLOAK     CAPTURE   HELP
```

Context worth knowing: these three are hard-coded on at `CMakeLists.txt:9` with no `option()` to disable them, so no build in this repo turns them off. That does not make the sentence wrong — it is exactly the "the moment it changes what gets compiled in" trigger the text names — but the flags are latent, not live.

## 2b. `-DDEBUG` gates player-visible output — **text accurate, but your cited evidence is the weakest available and does not stand alone**

`setup.c:325` and `setup.c:331` are `proutf("DEBUG: ...")` calls, as you were told. But **both are inside `if (idebug)`** (`setup.c:324`, `setup.c:330`), and `idebug` is zeroed at the start of every new game (`setup.c:255-256`). The only two ways to turn it on are the secret password `debug` (`setup.c:534-535`) and the `Toggle idebug?` prompt inside `debugme()` (`sst.c:900-903`).

Measured, three journeys:
- Debug build, password `xyz`: **0** `DEBUG:` lines.
- Debug build, password `debug`: `DEBUG: Abandoning base #2 at 6-4`, `DEBUG: saving base #3, close to #1`, …
- Release build, password `debug`: **0**.

So a player running a Debug build cannot see those two lines. Worse for the citation: the comment immediately above `setup.c:325` records that this is deliberate —

> `/* Only for someone who asked, via the "debug" password. It used to print for every debug build, which was merely noisy until the newlines inside it started counting towards paging -- at which point it cost the player a whole screen of the briefing. */`

Citing those lines as proof that `-DDEBUG` reaches the player argues against a decision this repo made on purpose and wrote down.

**The claim is still true**, on evidence with no `idebug` gate at all:

- `sst.c:238` — `#ifndef DEBUG && i != 33 // ignore the DEBUG command`. The `DEBUG` command exists as a command only in Debug builds.
- `sst.c:884-888` → `debugme()` (`sst.c:885`+), which asks the player six questions: `Reset levels?`, `Reset damage?`, `Toggle idebug?`, `Cause selective damage?`, `Examine/change events?`, `Make universe visible?`. That is literally "what the game asks of them".
- `setup.c:630` — the password `tholianx` forces a Tholian into the quadrant, Debug only.
- `finish.c:134-135` — `thawed && !idebug` decides whether `"You cannot get a citation, so..."` prints at the end of a game.

Confirmed end-to-end — same input, the two builds:
```
Debug:   COMMAND> Reset levels? Reset damage? Toggle idebug? Cause selective damage? ...
Release: COMMAND> UNRECOGNIZED COMMAND. LEGAL COMMANDS ARE:
```

Recommendation: the AGENTS.md sentence needs no change. If anything ever cites a line for it, cite `sst.c:238` and `debugme()`, not `setup.c:325/331`.

## 3. Cross-references and numbering — **all resolve, nothing renumbered**

List runs 1-12 with no gaps; both diff hunks (`@@ -166,11 +166,13 @@`, `@@ -262,8 +264,31 @@`) land inside step 6's body and the section prose, and touch no numbered line.

- step 5 → "see step 9" → *File what you found outside the slice* ✓
- step 6 → "the two steps below" → steps 7, 8 ✓
- step 6 → "The review sub-agents" → `### The review sub-agents`, AGENTS.md:259 ✓ (the pointer is unconditional as intended, while the invocation carries the condition)
- section → "the gate step 8 describes" → `code-review` ✓
- section → "the scope step 7 already gives it" → `verifier` ✓
- section → "Steps 6-8 invoke Claude Code sub-agents" ✓
- section → "which step 10 forbids and step 3 argues against" → *Commit after approval* ("do not combine unrelated work") and *Choose a thin vertical slice* ✓
- section → "step 8 cannot be satisfied by the commit that creates the reviewer" ✓
- step 9 → "steps 4 and 6-8 require you to fix" ✓

No line in the added text exceeds 72 columns; the five over-79 lines in the file (9, 34, 66, 73, 78) are all pre-existing and untouched.

## One consistency gap outside the diff

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.claude/agents/verifier.md:3` still describes itself as `Invoke after ui-review and before code-review`, and `.claude/agents/ui-review.md:3` as `Invoke after the main agent completes an implementation pass and before running the verifier` — neither carries the new condition. After this edit, `ui-review` may legitimately not run, so the verifier description asserts an ordering that will not always hold, and the ui-review description states an unconditional trigger that AGENTS.md no longer does. Those `description` fields are what the harness reads to decide auto-invocation, so this is not purely cosmetic. Not a failure of this change; reporting it as a follow-up for you to decide on.

## Missing coverage

`tests/instructions.sh` checks only that CLAUDE.md stays a pointer and AGENTS.md stays non-trivial. Nothing in the suite can catch a false statement in AGENTS.md prose or a `step N` reference that stopped resolving — which is precisely the failure mode this diff risks. I verified both by hand above. Automating the cross-reference half would be feasible (grep `step \d+` against the numbered list); the fact-checking half is not, and I would not file it as a gap worth closing.

- `cppcheck`, `clang-tidy`, `scan-build`: **none installed**. Reporting as a gap per my instructions, though no C changed, so no static analysis was applicable.
- No markdown linter configured or installed.
- `tmux` present — the `tui` and `journey-tui` tests ran rather than skipping.

(Your session's git snapshot showed `main` at `be17114` — it is stale.)

## Verdict: pass

No failures, no flakes. One accuracy problem — not in the text, but in the evidence you were handed for claim (b).

## 1. Regression checks

| Check | Result |
|---|---|

## 2a. `-DSCORE` / `-DCAPTURE` / `-DCLOAKING` gate player-visible commands and output — **confirmed**

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/CMakeLists.txt:9` sets all three. The player-facing sites:

- `sst.c:114,117,120` — inside `listCommands()`, these are the `SCORE`/`CLOAK`/`CAPTURE` entries in the COMMANDS listing.
- `sst.c:229-236` — `#ifndef CLOAKING && i != 26` etc., which is what makes the command *recognized* at all.
- `sst.c:361,372,378` — dispatch to `cloak()`, `capture()`, `score()`.
- `reports.c:79` — `"%d Klingon%s in brig."` and `"%d captured Klingon%s turned in to Star Fleet."` in the status report.
- `reports.c:355` — `", CLOAKED"` on the Condition line.

Empirically, `commands` in a Debug build prints:
```
   COMPUTER  EMEXIT    PROBE     COMMANDS
   SCORE     CLOAK     CAPTURE   HELP
```

Context worth knowing: these three are hard-coded on at `CMakeLists.txt:9` with no `option()` to disable them, so no build in this repo turns them off. That does not make the sentence wrong — it is exactly the "the moment it changes what gets compiled in" trigger the text names — but the flags are latent, not live.

## 2b. `-DDEBUG` gates player-visible output — **text accurate, but your cited evidence is the weakest available and does not stand alone**

`setup.c:325` and `setup.c:331` are `proutf("DEBUG: ...")` calls, as you were told. But **both are inside `if (idebug)`** (`setup.c:324`, `setup.c:330`), and `idebug` is zeroed at the start of every new game (`setup.c:255-256`). The only two ways to turn it on are the secret password `debug` (`setup.c:534-535`) and the `Toggle idebug?` prompt inside `debugme()` (`sst.c:900-903`).

Measured, three journeys:
- Debug build, password `xyz`: **0** `DEBUG:` lines.
- Debug build, password `debug`: `DEBUG: Abandoning base #2 at 6-4`, `DEBUG: saving base #3, close to #1`, …
- Release build, password `debug`: **0**.

So a player running a Debug build cannot see those two lines. Worse for the citation: the comment immediately above `setup.c:325` records that this is deliberate —

> `/* Only for someone who asked, via the "debug" password. It used to print for every debug build, which was merely noisy until the newlines inside it started counting towards paging -- at which point it cost the player a whole screen of the briefing. */`

Citing those lines as proof that `-DDEBUG` reaches the player argues against a decision this repo made on purpose and wrote down.

- `sst.c:238` — `#ifndef DEBUG && i != 33 // ignore the DEBUG command`. The `DEBUG` command exists as a command only in Debug builds.
- `sst.c:884-888` → `debugme()` (`sst.c:885`+), which asks the player six questions: `Reset levels?`, `Reset damage?`, `Toggle idebug?`, `Cause selective damage?`, `Examine/change events?`, `Make universe visible?`. That is literally "what the game asks of them".
- `setup.c:630` — the password `tholianx` forces a Tholian into the quadrant, Debug only.
- `finish.c:134-135` — `thawed && !idebug` decides whether `"You cannot get a citation, so..."` prints at the end of a game.

```
Debug:   COMMAND> Reset levels? Reset damage? Toggle idebug? Cause selective damage? ...
Release: COMMAND> UNRECOGNIZED COMMAND. LEGAL COMMANDS ARE:
```

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.claude/agents/verifier.md:3` still describes itself as `Invoke after ui-review and before code-review`, and `.claude/agents/ui-review.md:3` as `Invoke after the main agent completes an implementation pass and before running the verifier` — neither carries the new condition. ## Verdict: request changes

Reviewed state: branch `docs/correct-a-wrong-premise` at `5aea596` (identical to `main`), with one unstaged, unstaged-only change: an 11-line paragraph added to workflow step 3 of `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/AGENTS.md` (lines 111-121). Nothing staged, no untracked files, no other worktree changes. `.entire/` and the `build-*/` directories are pre-existing tracked/ignored content, not part of this change.

Facts check out: `sst.doc:436-439` is exactly the four digit-meaning lines, `lrscan()` at `reports.c:144`/`160` prints `d.galaxy[x][y]` verbatim, and the internal packing (`setup.c:340`, `379`, `events.c:325`, `791`) matches the manual digit for digit. The quoted phrase is verbatim from #58. Line widths (max 75) and the three-space continuation indent match the file. No mirror copies of this text exist elsewhere (`.codex/`, `.cursor/`, `.claude/agents/` carry none of it), so this file is the only place to change.

The paragraph is worth having. The problems are that it is the least specific instruction in a file that is otherwise exacting, and that it does not close the door the author already identified.

## Findings

### 1. should-fix — `AGENTS.md:117`: "correct the issue" does not name a mechanism, in a file that always names one

Every comparable directive here specifies the act: step 9 says "Open a GitHub issue for each", "add what you learned to that issue instead of opening a second one", and even covers "An agent that cannot open issues says so plainly."

"Correct the issue" reads at least three ways — edit the body, post a comment, or merely fix your own plan. Failure scenario: agent A rewrites the human's issue body, so the record of what was actually asked disappears and the author's name sits above words they did not write; agent B changes nothing anywhere and considers itself compliant, having "corrected" the premise in its own head. Both can claim to have followed the rule. Worse, the exemplar behaved a third way: #58 was never touched (no comments, closed), and the correction went only into PR #64's body — the very placement the new sentence implies is not enough on its own. A literal reader also has no path for a closed issue, which #58 now is.

On the question you asked directly: **comment, do not edit.** An edit silently replaces the author's stated reasoning, buries the change behind an edit-history affordance nobody opens, and converts a disagreement into a fait accompli under the human's own byline. A comment is additive, attributable and timestamped, and it is the same mechanism step 9 already blesses. Suggested replacement for the sentence:

> When a premise does not hold, say so on the issue in a comment — what it claimed, what is actually the case, and the file and line that settles it. Do not rewrite the issue body; a comment keeps straight who said what. Where the issue is closed, or you cannot comment, say it in the pull request body and the summary of the work instead, marked as unposted.

### 2. should-fix — `AGENTS.md:118`: the disclosure channel breaks the file's own established pattern

"say in the pull request" is narrower than every other disclosure rule here. Step 9's last bullet and the self-review bullet both read "in the pull request body and in the summary of the work — in the summary alone when there is no pull request."

Failure scenario: a session that commits on a branch without opening a PR has nowhere the rule requires the correction to go, so the exact outcome the paragraph exists to prevent — the correction reaching nobody — is reachable while fully compliant. Use the file's standard phrasing verbatim.

### 3. should-fix — `AGENTS.md:117-118`: nothing separates correcting a fact from substituting your own judgment

This is the abuse you asked about, and as written the paragraph licenses it: silently building something else is forbidden, so loudly building something else is permitted, with a paragraph in the PR body as the entire price. Two guardrails are missing.

- The correction is not required to be *evidenced*. The example cites a line; the rule asks only that a premise "does not hold."
- There is no line between a **checkable claim** (what the code does, what `sst.doc` says at a given line — an agent can settle these and should) and a **judgment** (what is worth building — the author's call, and disagreeing with it is a conversation, not a unilateral re-plan).

Failure scenario: an agent that would rather do a refactor than the assigned test finds one inaccurate sentence anywhere in the issue, declares the premise broken, ships the refactor, and writes "the issue was wrong about X, so I did Y instead." Every word of the current rule is satisfied.

The phrase "what you did instead" is the specific invitation; it presumes the slice gets replaced. Suggested addition and swap:

> A claim you can check — what the code does, what `sst.doc` says at a given line — you check, and correct with the line that settles it. What is worth building is the author's judgment: if the facts change what the issue should ask for, say so and ask, rather than replacing the slice with one of your own. A wrong premise voids the claim it supports, not the issue; the acceptance criteria it did not touch still bind.

…and "say in the pull request what was wrong and what the correction changed about the slice."

### 4. should-fix — `AGENTS.md:112-116`: the #58 example overstates the damage and understates the issue's reasoning

Three separate inaccuracies, and the file's other examples (step 4: "one counted rows from scans it was not looking at") are exact about theirs.

- **"the wrong slice"** is not what happened. PR #64 delivered all four of #58's acceptance criteria; the wrong premise cost one *additional* check, not the slice. "A narrower slice than the facts allowed" is both true and a better warning, because "the wrong slice" primes an agent to conclude the whole issue is void — feeding finding 3.
- **"on the grounds that"** presents the doc-absence as the sole ground. #58 gave a second, independent one: "`tests/golden.sh` already answers 'did the encoding change' more cheaply." The doc claim was load-bearing, but "the check it ruled out was available all along" answers availability without touching the cost argument the issue also made. "On its main ground, that…" fixes it in three words.
- The issue's **method was right and this file now endorses it** — step 4 says "Prefer a path where the expected value comes from somewhere independent — `sst.doc`, a literal, a subsystem that does not share the representation," which is precisely #58's instinct. PR #64's own body then concedes that half the resulting check "weighs an encoding against its own decoding." As written, the takeaway is "#58 reasoned badly"; the record says "#58 reasoned well from one wrong fact." Since the paragraph's job is to teach fact-checking, not distrust of the author's method, saying so is both fairer to your own issue and aims the lesson where you want it.

### 5. nit — `AGENTS.md:222` (step 9): step 3 is now a step whose findings must be fixed here, and it is not in the list that says so

Step 9's bullet reads "That is not license to file what steps 4 and 6-8 require you to fix." A wrong premise in the issue driving *this* slice is inside the slice, so step 9's categories genuinely do not cover it — no conflict there — but an agent can still reach for step 9 ("a comment that is no longer true"), file the bad premise as a fresh issue, and defer it, while step 3 says act on it now. Fix: "steps 3, 4 and 6-8". Related: if finding 1 is resolved as "comment on the issue", that is the same mechanism as step 9's first bullet, and this file explicitly prefers pointing over restating ("Point at the definitions here rather than restating them") — one cross-reference beats a second description.

### 6. nit — step 3 is the right home for the consequence, but the check belongs earlier, and the entry condition is unstated

Step 3's opening sentence is scoped to "implementing a roadmap item or feature", and the word "issue" appears nowhere in steps 1-8 before line 111 — the new paragraph introduces "the issue" as though it were already established. Also, the *checking* is inspection and wants to happen before step 2 creates a branch, while the *response* is genuinely a slice decision. Keep the paragraph in step 3, and make two cheap adjustments: add "the issue or roadmap item you are working from" to step 1's inspection list (`AGENTS.md:97-99`), and lead the paragraph with the slice tie rather than the bare imperative — e.g. "The slice you choose inherits whatever the issue assumes, so check what it claims before building on it. Where the work comes from no issue, this is the user's own description of it."

### 7. nit — `AGENTS.md:118-119`: "Both silent alternatives are worse" has no referent

Worse than what? The comparison is to speaking up, which the preceding sentence states but the phrase does not point at. "Both silent alternatives are worse than saying so" closes it. (The first alternative is also only silent about the mistake, not about the work — the sentence survives that, but the added words make it read cleanly.)

## No conflict found

- **With step 4's prove-a-test-can-fail rule.** They reinforce each other: step 4 tells you to source expectations independently, step 3 tells you to verify a claim about where that independent source is silent. No overlap in mechanism or in what either requires you to do.
- **With step 9 in category.** Step 9 is for findings *outside* the slice; a wrong premise in the issue you are implementing is inside it. Only the cross-reference in finding 5 is missing.

## Not reviewed

- Whether any downstream tooling parses AGENTS.md structurally — I checked `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `.codex/`, `.cursor/` and `.claude/agents/`, and nothing lints or duplicates this file, so prose-only changes carry no build risk.
- Whether you want #58 itself commented on retroactively; the review covers the rule text, not the historical record it describes.

content.text:
All three merged, clean tree, all CI green.

**`5aea596` — which reviews a change owes.** `code-review` on every commit; `verifier` always, and *the sub-agent runs even when it has one test to run*; `ui-review` when the change can alter what the game shows a player. Review made this stricter than my draft in two places. My exemption list said the build system gives `ui-review` nothing to read — but `CMakeLists.txt:9` sets `-DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING`, so a one-line change there can delete a player command. And my pointer to the exemption was conditional on *not* being Claude Code, meaning the agent that had skipped five times would never find it.

I asked the reviewer to be adversarial about a rule that benefits me, and the answer was worth the asking: the skip is **unaudited**. `code-review` runs before the commit exists and has no mandate to ask whether `ui-review` was owed, so scoping an absolute rule into a judgement call put the author in sole charge of the one pass the author is tempted to skip. Filed as **#72** rather than hand-waved.

**`2855cf2` — check what the issue claims.** Settle checkable claims; comment on the issue rather than rewriting someone else's words; a wrong premise voids the claim, not the issue. That last clause is the guardrail review insisted on — without it, any agent that dislikes its task could find one wrong sentence and ship what it preferred.

Two things I got wrong here and had corrected. I'd written that #58 reasoned its way to "the wrong slice" — false: PR #64 delivered all four of its acceptance criteria, the wrong fact cost one *additional* check. And I'd presented the doc claim as its only ground when it gave a second, independent one that still stands. It reasoned *well* from one wrong fact, and its instinct is what step 4 now endorses. I also had a "closed issue" carve-out that would have forbidden the very comment I'd just posted on the closed #58.

**`6dbf728` — the golden recordings** got their own heading. Review confirmed the misfiling rather than taking my word: `golden.sh` never runs with `-t`, and its only TUI mention says the recordings deliberately don't cover it.

**Two issues filed** along the way, per the rule from earlier today: **#72** above, and **#71** (the sub-agents' own descriptions still assert an unconditional trigger and an ordering that may no longer hold — both fields drive auto-invocation). I also posted the #58 correction on the issue itself, which is what the new rule would have required at the time.

One nit I declined: pointing step 4's "a recording, a check of something the game has always done" at the new golden section by name. Review flagged it as better on its own than folded in, and it's a wording preference, not a defect — so by the step 9 bar it doesn't get filed either.

The tracker now has six open, and its shape has shifted: **#65, #66, #71, #72** are all workflow-integrity issues this session generated, while **#62** (one space) and **#46** (TUI resize) are the game itself. Worth knowing before picking next — four of six are about the process rather than the product.

#!/bin/sh
# Checks that the score sheet's columns line up.
#
# score() in finish.c prints one line per thing the player did, each a
# format string ending in %5d, and every one of them is meant to put its
# number in the same column. Nothing enforced that. The plural Romulan
# line spent years a space short, so a winning player's surrendered-ship
# count sat one column left of everything under it (#62) -- on the score
# sheet a player is most likely to read, since surrendered Romulans only
# count on a win.
#
# It went unnoticed because no test could see it. The recordings in
# tests/golden are the only place a score sheet is written down, and
# until a game was won there was none with a Romulan line in it at all.
#
# So this reads the format strings themselves rather than any output. It
# is the only way to reach the singular forms: "1 Romulan ship
# surrendered" needs exactly one Romulan left alive at the end, and a
# novice game starts with two or three, so no journey can produce one
# without hunting Romulans first. Both forms of all thirteen lines are
# checked here, which is what #62 asked for.
#
# What this cannot see, and golden does: the two lines assembled from
# pieces rather than printed from one format -- the winning bonus, built
# from proutn fragments and a skill name, and the killed penalty, a bare
# literal. tests/golden/won.txt records both at the same column as the
# rest.
#
# Usage: score.sh /path/to/repo/root

set -u

ROOT="${1:-.}"
FINISH="$ROOT/finish.c"

# Where the number ends on every line of the sheet. Not a number the
# code declares anywhere -- it is the shape all but one of the lines
# already had, and the one that the recordings show.
WIDTH=47

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

if [ ! -f "$FINISH" ]; then
	echo "FAIL: $FINISH not found" >&2
	exit 1
fi

# Every string literal that ends in a %5d field, with the conversions
# replaced by the width they print: %6d and %6.2f are six columns, %5d
# is five. A ternary puts two literals on one line, so the line is split
# on quotes and every other field taken.
report=$(awk -v want="$WIDTH" '
	/%5d\\n/ {
		n = split($0, part, "\"")
		for (i = 2; i <= n; i += 2) {
			lit = part[i]
			if (lit !~ /%5d\\n/) continue

			gsub(/\\n/, "", s)
			gsub(/%6\.2f/, "XXXXXX", s)
			gsub(/%6d/, "XXXXXX", s)
			gsub(/%5d/, "YYYYY", s)

				printf "%d:%d:%s\n", FNR, length(s), lit
			seen++
		}
	}
	END { printf "count:%d\n", seen+0 }
' "$FINISH")

count=$(echo "$report" | sed -n 's/^count:\([0-9]*\)$/\1/p')
echo "$report" | grep -v '^count:' | while IFS=: read -r line width lit; do
	[ -n "${line:-}" ] || continue
	printf 'FAIL: finish.c:%s puts its number at column %s, not %s -- "%s"\n' \
		"$line" "$width" "$WIDTH" "$lit" >&2
done
# The loop above runs in a subshell, so its failures are counted here.
bad=$(echo "$report" | grep -vc '^count:' || true)
[ "$bad" = 0 ] || fails=$((fails + bad))

# A count guards the guard. If the shape of these lines ever changes so
# that the pattern stops matching, every line would "align" by not being
# looked at, and this test would pass while checking nothing.
MINLINES=24
if [ -z "${count:-}" ] || [ "$count" -lt "$MINLINES" ]; then
	fail "only ${count:-0} score lines matched, expected at least $MINLINES -- has score() changed shape?"
fi

if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	printf '\n%d score-sheet column problem(s).\n' "$fails" >&2
	exit 1
fi

printf 'score OK (%s lines, column %s)\n' "$count" "$WIDTH"
