cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.21)
include(CMakePrintHelpers)

project(sst
        LANGUAGES C
        VERSION 1.0)

set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING")

# Warnings are on for everyone, so a new one is visible where it is
# introduced. They are only fatal where that can be enforced without
# breaking somebody's build on a compiler version nobody here has
# tried: CI turns SST_WERROR on, a contributor gets the warning and a
# working build.
option(SST_WERROR "Treat compiler warnings as errors (CI does)" OFF)
if(CMAKE_C_COMPILER_ID MATCHES "GNU|Clang")
    # -Wmissing-prototypes is what keeps a definition and its
    # declaration in agreement: it fires on any non-static function
    # defined without a prototype in scope, which is the only way a
    # signature can drift apart from the header the callers read. It
    # is the standing check for osx.c, the one file that cannot
    # include sst.h.
    set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes")
    if(SST_WERROR)
        set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -Werror")
    endif()
endif()

if(${CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE} STREQUAL "Debug")
    set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -DDEBUG")
    cmake_print_variables(CMAKE_C_FLAGS)
endif()

add_executable(sst sst.c ai.c battle.c events.c finish.c moving.c osx.c planets.c reports.c rules.c setup.c tui.c tuifmt.c)

set(CURSES_NEED_NCURSES TRUE)

target_include_directories(sst PRIVATE ${CURSES_INCLUDE_DIRS})
target_link_libraries(sst PRIVATE ${CURSES_LIBRARIES} m)

# separate libtinfo. Linking -lncurses happens to pull it in where
# libncurses.so is a linker script, but that is luck, not a contract.
find_library(TINFO_LIBRARY tinfo)
if(TINFO_LIBRARY)
    target_link_libraries(sst PRIVATE ${TINFO_LIBRARY})
endif()

enable_testing()
add_executable(test_tuifmt tests/test_tuifmt.c tuifmt.c)
target_link_libraries(test_tuifmt PRIVATE m)
add_test(NAME tuifmt COMMAND test_tuifmt)

target_link_libraries(test_rules PRIVATE m)
add_test(NAME rules COMMAND test_rules)

Suggest replacing that sentence with a note that the line used to be a column short (#62), was fixed, and that `tests/score.sh` now holds all the formats to column 47.

**nit — the new test's own comment overstates golden's coverage of the composed bonus line.**
`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/score.sh` says the winning bonus is "golden's to watch". Golden only ever records the *Novice* form: `covers won` asserts `'Bonus for winning Novice game'`, and no journey wins at Fair/Good/Expert/Emeritus. The bonus line's alignment is `"Bonus for winning "` (18) + a skill label padded to 13 + `"           %5d"` (16) = 47, and four of those five labels are checked by nothing at all. A player who wins at Emeritus is exactly the player most likely to care about the sheet. Concrete suggestion: have `score.sh` also sum the fragment literals — the awk pass already sees `Bonus for winning `, the five `... game  ` labels and the trailing `           %5d\n` — and assert 18 + 13 + 16 == 47, or at minimum assert all five skill labels are the same length.

#!/bin/sh
# Checks that the score sheet's columns line up.
#
# score() in finish.c prints one line per thing the player did, each a
# format string ending in %5d, and every one of them is meant to put its
# number in the same column. Nothing enforced that. The plural Romulan
# line spent years a space short, so a winning player's surrendered-ship
# count sat one column left of everything under it (#62) -- on the score
# sheet a player is most likely to read, since surrendered Romulans only
# count on a win.
#
# It went unnoticed because no test could see it. The recordings in
# tests/golden are the only place a score sheet is written down, and
# until a game was won there was none with a Romulan line in it at all.
#
# So this reads the format strings themselves rather than any output. It
# is the only way to reach the singular forms: "1 Romulan ship
# surrendered" needs exactly one Romulan left alive at the end, and a
# novice game starts with two or three, so no journey can produce one
# without hunting Romulans first. Both forms of all thirteen lines are
# checked here, which is what #62 asked for.
#
# What this cannot see, and golden does: the two lines assembled from
# pieces rather than printed from one format -- the winning bonus, built
# from proutn fragments and a skill name, and the killed penalty, a bare
# literal. tests/golden/won.txt records both at the same column as the
# rest.
#
# Usage: score.sh /path/to/repo/root

set -u

ROOT="${1:-.}"
FINISH="$ROOT/finish.c"

# Where the number ends on every line of the sheet. Not a number the
# code declares anywhere -- it is the shape all but one of the lines
# already had, and the one that the recordings show.
WIDTH=47

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

if [ ! -f "$FINISH" ]; then
	echo "FAIL: $FINISH not found" >&2
	exit 1
fi

# Every string literal that ends in a %5d field, with the conversions
# replaced by the width they print: %6d and %6.2f are six columns, %5d
# is five. A ternary puts two literals on one line, so the line is split
# on quotes and every other field taken.
# A literal with no letter in it is a fragment of a line built from
# several proutn calls -- the winning bonus ends in one -- and has no
# column of its own to check. Those are golden's to watch, not this
# script's.
report=$(awk -v want="$WIDTH" '
	/%5d\\n/ {
		n = split($0, part, "\"")
		for (i = 2; i <= n; i += 2) {
			lit = part[i]
			if (lit !~ /%5d\\n/) continue
			s = lit
			gsub(/\\n/, "", s)
			gsub(/%6\.2f/, "######", s)
			gsub(/%6d/, "######", s)
			gsub(/%5d/, "#####", s)
			# Asked once nothing is left but the label and its
			# padding. Before the substitutions, the n of \n and
			# the d of %5d both read as a label.
			if (s !~ /[A-Za-z]/) continue
			if (length(s) != want)
				printf "bad:%d:%d:%s\n", FNR, length(s), lit
			seen++
		}
	}
	END { printf "count:%d\n", seen+0 }
' "$FINISH")

count=$(printf '%s\n' "$report" | sed -n 's/^count:\([0-9]*\)$/\1/p')
printf '%s\n' "$report" | sed -n 's/^bad://p' | while IFS=: read -r line width lit; do
	printf 'FAIL: finish.c:%s puts its number at column %s, not %s -- "%s"\n' \
		"$line" "$width" "$WIDTH" "$lit" >&2
done
# That loop is a subshell and cannot raise the count, so it is counted
# here instead.
bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$report" | grep -c '^bad:' || true)
fails=$((fails + bad))

# A count guards the guard. If the shape of these lines ever changes so
# that the pattern stops matching, every line would "align" by not being
# looked at, and this test would pass while checking nothing.
MINLINES=24
if [ -z "${count:-}" ] || [ "$count" -lt "$MINLINES" ]; then
	fail "only ${count:-0} score lines matched, expected at least $MINLINES -- has score() changed shape?"
fi

if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	printf '\n%d score-sheet column problem(s).\n' "$fails" >&2
	exit 1
fi

printf 'score OK (%s lines, column %s)\n' "$count" "$WIDTH"

lines: bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$report" | grep -c '^bad:' || true)
fails=$((fails + bad))
+# The winning bonus is the one line built rather than printed: a prefix,
+# one of five skill labels, and a tail carrying the number. It lands in
+# the same column only if the three add up, and only the Novice label is
+# ever recorded -- no journey wins at Fair or above -- so the other four
+# are checked here or nowhere. A player who wins at Emeritus is the one
+# most likely to study the sheet.
+bonus=$(awk -v want="$WIDTH" '
+  /proutn\("Bonus for winning /  { n = split($0, p, "\""); prefix = length(p[2]) }
+  /proutn\("[A-Z][a-z]* game *"\)/ {
+      if (p[i] ~ /game/) { labels[++nl] = p[i] }
+    tail = length(s)
+  END {
+    printf "parts:%d:%d:%d\n", prefix+0, nl+0, tail+0
+    for (i = 1; i <= nl; i++)
+      if (prefix + length(labels[i]) + tail != want)
+        printf "bonus:%s:%d\n", labels[i], \
+          prefix + length(labels[i]) + tail
+' "$FINISH")
+parts=$(printf '%s\n' "$bonus" | sed -n 's/^parts://p')
+prefixlen=$(printf '%s' "$parts" | cut -d: -f1)
+nlabels=$(printf '%s' "$parts" | cut -d: -f2)
+taillen=$(printf '%s' "$parts" | cut -d: -f3)
+if [ "$prefixlen" = 0 ] || [ "$taillen" = 0 ] || [ "$nlabels" != 5 ]; then
+  fail "the winning bonus line did not parse (prefix $prefixlen, $nlabels labels, tail $taillen) -- has it changed shape?"
+fi
+printf '%s\n' "$bonus" | sed -n 's/^bonus://p' | while IFS=: read -r label got; do
+  printf 'FAIL: the winning bonus reads "%s" at column %s, not %s\n' \
+    "$label" "$got" "$WIDTH" >&2
+done
+badbonus=$(printf '%s\n' "$bonus" | grep -c '^bonus:' || true)
+fails=$((fails + badbonus))

# that the pattern stops matching, every line would "align" by not being
# looked at, and this test would pass while checking nothing.

#!/bin/sh
# Checks that the score sheet's columns line up.
#
# score() in finish.c prints one line per thing the player did, each a
# format string ending in %5d, and every one of them is meant to put its
# number in the same column. Nothing enforced that. The plural Romulan
# line spent years a space short, so a winning player's surrendered-ship
# count sat one column left of everything under it (#62) -- on the score
# sheet a player is most likely to read, since surrendered Romulans only
# count on a win.
#
# It went unnoticed because no test could see it. The recordings in
# tests/golden are the only place a score sheet is written down, and
# until a game was won there was none with a Romulan line in it at all.
#
# So this reads the format strings themselves rather than any output. It
# is the only way to reach the singular forms: "1 Romulan ship
# surrendered" needs exactly one Romulan left alive at the end, and a
# novice game starts with two or three, so no journey can produce one
# without hunting Romulans first. Both forms of all thirteen lines are
# checked here, which is what #62 asked for.
#
# What this cannot see, and golden does: the two lines assembled from
# pieces rather than printed from one format -- the winning bonus, built
# from proutn fragments and a skill name, and the killed penalty, a bare
# literal. tests/golden/won.txt records both at the same column as the
# rest.
#
# Usage: score.sh /path/to/repo/root

set -u

ROOT="${1:-.}"
FINISH="$ROOT/finish.c"

# Where the number ends on every line of the sheet. Not a number the
# code declares anywhere -- it is the shape all but one of the lines
# already had, and the one that the recordings show.
WIDTH=47

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

if [ ! -f "$FINISH" ]; then
	echo "FAIL: $FINISH not found" >&2
	exit 1
fi

# Every string literal that ends in a %5d field, with the conversions
# replaced by the width they print: %6d and %6.2f are six columns, %5d
# is five. A ternary puts two literals on one line, so the line is split
# on quotes and every other field taken.
# A literal with no letter in it is a fragment of a line built from
# several proutn calls -- the winning bonus ends in one -- and has no
# column of its own to check. Those are golden's to watch, not this
# script's.
report=$(awk -v want="$WIDTH" '
	/%5d\\n/ {
		n = split($0, part, "\"")
		for (i = 2; i <= n; i += 2) {
			lit = part[i]
			if (lit !~ /%5d\\n/) continue
			s = lit
			gsub(/\\n/, "", s)
			gsub(/%6\.2f/, "######", s)
			gsub(/%6d/, "######", s)
			gsub(/%5d/, "#####", s)
			# Asked once nothing is left but the label and its
			# padding. Before the substitutions, the n of \n and
			# the d of %5d both read as a label.
			if (s !~ /[A-Za-z]/) continue
			if (length(s) != want)
				printf "bad:%d:%d:%s\n", FNR, length(s), lit
			seen++
		}
	}
	END { printf "count:%d\n", seen+0 }
' "$FINISH")

count=$(printf '%s\n' "$report" | sed -n 's/^count:\([0-9]*\)$/\1/p')
printf '%s\n' "$report" | sed -n 's/^bad://p' | while IFS=: read -r line width lit; do
	printf 'FAIL: finish.c:%s puts its number at column %s, not %s -- "%s"\n' \
		"$line" "$width" "$WIDTH" "$lit" >&2
done
# That loop is a subshell and cannot raise the count, so it is counted
# here instead.
bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$report" | grep -c '^bad:' || true)
fails=$((fails + bad))

# The winning bonus is the one line built rather than printed: a prefix,
# one of five skill labels, and a tail carrying the number. It lands in
# the same column only if the three add up, and only the Novice label is
# ever recorded -- no journey wins at Fair or above -- so the other four
# are checked here or nowhere. A player who wins at Emeritus is the one
# most likely to study the sheet.
bonus=$(awk -v want="$WIDTH" '
	/proutn\("Bonus for winning /  { n = split($0, p, "\""); prefix = length(p[2]) }
	/proutn\("[A-Z][a-z]* game *"\)/ {
		n = split($0, p, "\"")
		for (i = 2; i <= n; i += 2)
			if (p[i] ~ /game/) { labels[++nl] = p[i] }
	}
	/proutf\(" *%5d\\n"/ {
		n = split($0, p, "\"")
		s = p[2]
		gsub(/\\n/, "", s)
		gsub(/%5d/, "#####", s)
		tail = length(s)
	}
	END {
		printf "parts:%d:%d:%d\n", prefix+0, nl+0, tail+0
		for (i = 1; i <= nl; i++)
			if (prefix + length(labels[i]) + tail != want)
				printf "bonus:%s:%d\n", labels[i], \
					prefix + length(labels[i]) + tail
	}
' "$FINISH")

parts=$(printf '%s\n' "$bonus" | sed -n 's/^parts://p')
prefixlen=$(printf '%s' "$parts" | cut -d: -f1)
nlabels=$(printf '%s' "$parts" | cut -d: -f2)
taillen=$(printf '%s' "$parts" | cut -d: -f3)
if [ "$prefixlen" = 0 ] || [ "$taillen" = 0 ] || [ "$nlabels" != 5 ]; then
	fail "the winning bonus line did not parse (prefix $prefixlen, $nlabels labels, tail $taillen) -- has it changed shape?"
fi
printf '%s\n' "$bonus" | sed -n 's/^bonus://p' | while IFS=: read -r label got; do
	printf 'FAIL: the winning bonus reads "%s" at column %s, not %s\n' \
		"$label" "$got" "$WIDTH" >&2
done
badbonus=$(printf '%s\n' "$bonus" | grep -c '^bonus:' || true)
fails=$((fails + badbonus))

# A count guards the guard. If the shape of these lines ever changes so
# that the pattern stops matching, every line would "align" by not being
# looked at, and this test would pass while checking nothing.
MINLINES=24
if [ -z "${count:-}" ] || [ "$count" -lt "$MINLINES" ]; then
	fail "only ${count:-0} score lines matched, expected at least $MINLINES -- has score() changed shape?"
fi

if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	printf '\n%d score-sheet column problem(s).\n' "$fails" >&2
	exit 1
fi

printf 'score OK (%s lines, column %s)\n' "$count" "$WIDTH"

## Verdict: request changes

One should-fix in `tests/score.sh`; the C fix, the fixture, and the CMake registration are correct as they stand.

**Reviewed state**: worktree on branch `fix/score-sheet-column` at base commit `6dbf728` (no commits on the branch yet). Covers unstaged edits to `CMakeLists.txt`, `finish.c`, `tests/golden.sh`, `tests/golden/won.txt`, and untracked `tests/score.sh`. Nothing staged.

**What I verified**: built with `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, full `ctest` suite 11/11 green (including `golden`, so the re-recorded fixture is byte-for-byte what the game now emits). Independently recomputed all 27 rendered widths — every one is 47 after the fix, and `Penalty for getting yourself killed        -200` is 47 too, so 47 is the right target and the one-space widen is the minimal correct change, not a case for widening something else. `shellcheck -s sh` clean; script passes under `dash`, `bash`, `mawk`, and busybox `awk`.

---

### 1. should-fix — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/score.sh:145` — `MINLINES=24` leaves three lines of silent slack, and I got a real false pass through it

The count is deterministic: the awk scans source text, so `CAPTURE`/`CLOAKING` don't change it, and it is exactly 27 today. `24` therefore isn't headroom for anything — it just lets three formats drop out of the check while the script still prints `score OK`.

Concrete failure, reproduced: wrap one of the ternary literals across two source lines (plain C string concatenation) with a **wrong** total width, and the script reports success.

```
FALSE-PASS: MISALIGNED format wrapped over 2 source lines   exit=0 | score OK (26 lines, column 47)
```

This is not hypothetical. All twelve dual-form `proutf` lines in `score()` are 118–122 columns (`finish.c:349,352,355,358,368,372,375,378,381,384,387,391`). A future "wrap the over-long lines" chore is exactly the change that splits them, and it would disable up to three of these checks invisibly — precisely the vacuous-pass the guard at line 142 says it exists to prevent. Deleting three whole score lines *is* caught (count drops to 21), so the guard works at the coarse end only.

Fix: make it exact.

```sh
EXPECTLINES=27
if [ "${count:-0}" -ne "$EXPECTLINES" ]; then
	fail "matched ${count:-0} score lines, expected exactly $EXPECTLINES -- has score() changed shape?"
fi
```

Adding a legitimate new score line then costs one number bump, which is the right amount of friction.

**The bonus guards, by contrast, are not theatre.** I mutated all five ways and every one bites: label one space wide, prefix one space wide, tail one space short, a label renamed out of the regex (`prefix 18, 4 labels, tail 16`), and the prefix reworded (`prefix 0`). The `nlabels != 5` and zero-length checks are load-bearing. Leave them.

### 2. nit — `tests/score.sh:17` and `CMakeLists.txt:128` — "the only way to reach the singular forms" is factually wrong

Two singular forms are already recorded by `golden`: `tests/golden/ending.txt:82` has `1 ship lost or destroyed` and `tests/golden/won.txt:109` has `1 Klingon Commander ship destroyed`. The defensible claim is narrower — 10 of the 12 singular forms and 4 of the 5 skill labels are unreachable by any journey, including the Romulan-surrender singular that #62 is about. Since this sentence is the whole justification for an unusual test shape, it should be accurate; a maintainer who checks it and finds it false will discount the rest.

### 3. nit — `tests/score.sh:20` — "Both forms of all thirteen lines" miscounts

There are 12 dual-form lines, plus 3 single-form formats (Super-Commander, Klingon-ships-per-stardate, TOTAL SCORE): 12×2+3 = 27, which is what the script reports.

### 4. nit — `tests/score.sh:59-84` — the awk scans all of `finish.c`, not `score()`

Today no other function in the file has a `%5d\n` format, so it's correct now. But a future `%5d\n` in `plaque()` or `finish()` would be conscripted into a 47-column layout it has nothing to do with, producing a confusing false failure. Either bracket the scan with a range pattern (`/^void score\(/,/^}/`) or say in the comment that the whole file is in scope by design.

---

### On the big question: is scraping format strings out of C source right here?

Your core argument holds and I'd keep the test. A rendered-output check would **not** have been enough — no journey produces a one-Romulan win or a win above Novice, so 10 singular forms and 4 skill labels are unreachable through the game, and #62 asked for exactly those. Golden can only ever pin the handful of lines a journey happens to print.

My objection is to the mechanism, not the goal, and it's the same objection as finding 1 generalized: **this test is coupled to source formatting rather than to source meaning.** Three consequences worth writing down somewhere:

- It degrades silently under reformatting, as demonstrated. A rendered check cannot.
- It re-implements printf width semantics in awk (`%6d`→6, `%6.2f`→6), and that model is only approximately true: `%6.2f` is six columns only while `perdate < 1000`, `%6d` only while the count is under a million. Both are unreachable in practice, but the model-vs-printf gap is a false-pass surface that a real render doesn't have.
- It cannot see the compiled game at all, which the header honestly admits.

The shape this should converge to, when someone next touches `score()`: hoist the 27 literals into a `static const char *const` table that `score()` indexes, and have a C test `snprintf` each entry with representative arguments and assert the result is 47 columns. That reaches every singular form and every skill label, uses printf's actual semantics instead of a model of them, is immune to wrapping, and deletes the awk. Too large for this fix — I'm not asking for it here — but it's the answer to "is this the right thing to have" in the long run. For now, tighten the count and it's a sound stopgap.

### Other checks

- **awk details**: `/%5d\\n/` and `gsub(/\\n/, ...)` correctly match a literal backslash-`n` under both mawk and busybox awk. The letter test is correctly ordered *after* the substitutions (before them, the `n` of `\n` and `d` of `%5d` would both read as label text — the comment at line 76 is right). `split` on `"` taking even fields is safe for the current source; I probed an escaped quote inside a label and it fails loudly rather than passing, which is the safe direction. The subshell/`grep -c` counting workaround at lines 96-98 and 137-139 is correct and the comment explains why.
- **Fixture re-record**: `won.txt:107` now measures 47 like every other line in both fixtures; `golden` passes without `--update`, so it is genuinely the game's output.
- **CMake**: matches the surrounding `add_test`/`set_tests_properties` style and the source-dir-argument convention used by `instructions`; 30s timeout is right for a 0.04s test.
- **golden.sh comment**: correctly retires the "recorded as a bug" note.
- **Commit-message obligation**: this deliberately changes plain-mode output, so per `AGENTS.md` the commit must say so and why. There's no commit yet — flagging so it isn't missed.

### Not reviewed

macOS's one-true-awk. CI runs `macos-latest` and `nawk` on this box is a symlink to mawk, so I could only cross-check mawk against busybox awk. `\\` in an ERE literal is portable and both agreed on all 27 lines, so I expect it's fine, but the macOS leg of CI is the first real test of it.

#!/bin/sh
# Checks that the score sheet's columns line up.
#
# score() in finish.c prints one line per thing the player did, each a
# format string ending in %5d, and every one of them is meant to put its
# number in the same column. Nothing enforced that. The plural Romulan
# line spent years a space short, so a winning player's surrendered-ship
# count sat one column left of everything under it (#62) -- on the score
# sheet a player is most likely to read, since surrendered Romulans only
# count on a win.
#
# It went unnoticed because no test could see it. The recordings in
# tests/golden are the only place a score sheet is written down, and
# until a game was won there was none with a Romulan line in it at all.
#
# So this reads the format strings themselves rather than any output. It
# is the only way to reach the singular forms: "1 Romulan ship
# surrendered" needs exactly one Romulan left alive at the end, and a
# novice game starts with two or three, so no journey can produce one
# without hunting Romulans first. Both forms of all thirteen lines are
# checked here, which is what #62 asked for.
#
# What this cannot see, and golden does: the killed penalty, a bare
# literal with no conversion in it to measure. tests/golden/ending.txt
# records it -- and only that fixture can, since the line prints when the
# ship is destroyed and the won journey ends alive.
#
# The winning bonus is checked below, because golden reaches only one
# fifth of it: no journey wins above Novice, so four of the five skill
# labels appear in no recording at all.
#
# And none of this sees the compiled game. If proutf ever stopped
# honouring these widths the recordings would notice and this would not.
#
# Usage: score.sh /path/to/repo/root

set -u

ROOT="${1:-.}"
FINISH="$ROOT/finish.c"

# Where the number ends on every line of the sheet. Not a number the
# code declares anywhere -- it is the shape all but one of the lines
# already had, and the one that the recordings show.
WIDTH=47

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

if [ ! -f "$FINISH" ]; then
	echo "FAIL: $FINISH not found" >&2
	exit 1
fi

# Every string literal that ends in a %5d field, with the conversions
# replaced by the width they print: %6d and %6.2f are six columns, %5d
# is five. A ternary puts two literals on one line, so the line is split
# on quotes and every other field taken.
# A literal with no letter in it is a fragment of a line built from
# several proutn calls -- the winning bonus ends in one -- and has no
# column of its own to check. Those are golden's to watch, not this
# script's.
report=$(awk -v want="$WIDTH" '
	/%5d\\n/ {
		n = split($0, part, "\"")
		for (i = 2; i <= n; i += 2) {
			lit = part[i]
			if (lit !~ /%5d\\n/) continue
			s = lit
			gsub(/\\n/, "", s)
			gsub(/%6\.2f/, "######", s)
			gsub(/%6d/, "######", s)
			gsub(/%5d/, "#####", s)
			# Asked once nothing is left but the label and its
			# padding. Before the substitutions, the n of \n and
			# the d of %5d both read as a label.
			if (s !~ /[A-Za-z]/) continue
			if (length(s) != want)
				printf "bad:%d:%d:%s\n", FNR, length(s), lit
			seen++
		}
	}
	END { printf "count:%d\n", seen+0 }
' "$FINISH")

count=$(printf '%s\n' "$report" | sed -n 's/^count:\([0-9]*\)$/\1/p')
printf '%s\n' "$report" | sed -n 's/^bad://p' | while IFS=: read -r line width lit; do
	printf 'FAIL: finish.c:%s puts its number at column %s, not %s -- "%s"\n' \
		"$line" "$width" "$WIDTH" "$lit" >&2
done
# That loop is a subshell and cannot raise the count, so it is counted
# here instead.
bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$report" | grep -c '^bad:' || true)
fails=$((fails + bad))

# The winning bonus is the one line built rather than printed: a prefix,
# one of five skill labels, and a tail carrying the number. It lands in
# the same column only if the three add up, and only the Novice label is
# ever recorded -- no journey wins at Fair or above -- so the other four
# are checked here or nowhere. A player who wins at Emeritus is the one
# most likely to study the sheet.
bonus=$(awk -v want="$WIDTH" '
	/proutn\("Bonus for winning /  { n = split($0, p, "\""); prefix = length(p[2]) }
	/proutn\("[A-Z][a-z]* game *"\)/ {
		n = split($0, p, "\"")
		for (i = 2; i <= n; i += 2)
			if (p[i] ~ /game/) { labels[++nl] = p[i] }
	}
	/proutf\(" *%5d\\n"/ {
		n = split($0, p, "\"")
		s = p[2]
		gsub(/\\n/, "", s)
		gsub(/%5d/, "#####", s)
		tail = length(s)
	}
	END {
		printf "parts:%d:%d:%d\n", prefix+0, nl+0, tail+0
		for (i = 1; i <= nl; i++)
			if (prefix + length(labels[i]) + tail != want)
				printf "bonus:%s:%d\n", labels[i], \
					prefix + length(labels[i]) + tail
	}
' "$FINISH")

parts=$(printf '%s\n' "$bonus" | sed -n 's/^parts://p')
prefixlen=$(printf '%s' "$parts" | cut -d: -f1)
nlabels=$(printf '%s' "$parts" | cut -d: -f2)
taillen=$(printf '%s' "$parts" | cut -d: -f3)
if [ "$prefixlen" = 0 ] || [ "$taillen" = 0 ] || [ "$nlabels" != 5 ]; then
	fail "the winning bonus line did not parse (prefix $prefixlen, $nlabels labels, tail $taillen) -- has it changed shape?"
fi
printf '%s\n' "$bonus" | sed -n 's/^bonus://p' | while IFS=: read -r label got; do
	printf 'FAIL: the winning bonus reads "%s" at column %s, not %s\n' \
		"$label" "$got" "$WIDTH" >&2
done
badbonus=$(printf '%s\n' "$bonus" | grep -c '^bonus:' || true)
fails=$((fails + badbonus))

# A count guards the guard. If the shape of these lines ever changes so
# that the pattern stops matching, every line would "align" by not being
# looked at, and this test would pass while checking nothing.
MINLINES=24
if [ -z "${count:-}" ] || [ "$count" -lt "$MINLINES" ]; then
	fail "only ${count:-0} score lines matched, expected at least $MINLINES -- has score() changed shape?"
fi

if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	printf '\n%d score-sheet column problem(s).\n' "$fails" >&2
	exit 1
fi

printf 'score OK (%s lines, column %s)\n' "$count" "$WIDTH"

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.21)
include(CMakePrintHelpers)

project(sst
        LANGUAGES C
        VERSION 1.0)

set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING")

# Warnings are on for everyone, so a new one is visible where it is
# introduced. They are only fatal where that can be enforced without
# breaking somebody's build on a compiler version nobody here has
# tried: CI turns SST_WERROR on, a contributor gets the warning and a
# working build.
option(SST_WERROR "Treat compiler warnings as errors (CI does)" OFF)
if(CMAKE_C_COMPILER_ID MATCHES "GNU|Clang")
    # -Wmissing-prototypes is what keeps a definition and its
    # declaration in agreement: it fires on any non-static function
    # defined without a prototype in scope, which is the only way a
    # signature can drift apart from the header the callers read. It
    # is the standing check for osx.c, the one file that cannot
    # include sst.h.
    set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes")
    if(SST_WERROR)
        set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -Werror")
    endif()
endif()

if(${CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE} STREQUAL "Debug")
    set(CMAKE_C_FLAGS "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS} -DDEBUG")
    cmake_print_variables(CMAKE_C_FLAGS)
endif()

add_executable(sst sst.c ai.c battle.c events.c finish.c moving.c osx.c planets.c reports.c rules.c setup.c tui.c tuifmt.c)

set(CURSES_NEED_NCURSES TRUE)

find_library(TINFO_LIBRARY tinfo)
if(TINFO_LIBRARY)
    target_link_libraries(sst PRIVATE ${TINFO_LIBRARY})
endif()

add_executable(test_tuifmt tests/test_tuifmt.c tuifmt.c)
target_link_libraries(test_tuifmt PRIVATE m)

gh issue create --title "Assert the score sheet's columns from the compiled game, not from its source text" --label "good first issue" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

`tests/score.sh` (added with #62) holds every score-sheet format string
in `finish.c` to column 47. It works, and it reaches what no journey can
— ten of the twelve singular forms and four of the five skill labels
appear in no recording — but it does so by scraping C source text, and
its own header admits the two costs:

- **It never sees the compiled game.** It re-implements printf width
  semantics in awk (`%6d` → 6, `%6.2f` → 6). If `proutf` ever stopped
  honouring those widths, only `golden` would notice.
- **It degrades under reformatting.** A literal split by C string
  concatenation drops out of the scan. That was a live false pass during
  review — a floor of 24 let it through silently — and it is now guarded
  by an exact count of 27, which is a tripwire rather than a fix. The
  twelve dual-form `proutf` lines are 118-122 columns, so "wrap the long
  lines" is a plausible future chore that trips it.

## Suggested approach

Hoist the literals into a table `score()` indexes:

```c
static const char *const score_lines[] = { ... };
```

Then assert in C — `tests/test_rules.c` is the existing home for a C
test, or a new one — by `snprintf`-ing each entry with representative
arguments and checking the result is 47 columns.

That reaches every singular form and every skill label, uses printf's
real semantics instead of a model of them, is immune to how the source
is wrapped, and deletes the awk.

Worth deciding while there what to do about the two lines the table
cannot hold as single formats: the winning bonus, assembled from a
prefix, a skill label and a tail, and the `Penalty for getting yourself
killed` literal, which carries no conversion at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The column invariant is asserted against what the compiled game
      prints, not against the text of `finish.c`.
- [ ] Every singular and plural form is still covered, and the skill
      labels with them.
- [ ] `tests/score.sh` is deleted, or reduced to whatever the C test
      cannot reach, and `CMakeLists.txt` updated to match.

Raised by the `code-review` sub-agent while reviewing #62, which is where
the scraping test came from. Follow the workflow in
[AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).
EOF
)"

**Two rounds of review earned their keep, and I'd flag this as the session's lesson.** As I first wrote it, the test counted rows in a window that ran past the block it meant to read; claimed `golden` covered a bonus line it records one fifth of; named the wrong fixture for the killed penalty (`won.txt` *can't* contain it — the ship survives); and its floor of 24 matched lines let the reviewer walk a genuine false pass through it. Splitting one literal across two source lines dropped a format out of the scan and it still printed `OK`. That's the fourth vacuous assertion this session — the rule added in `0a075a5` is earning its place faster than I'd like.

I reproduced both the false pass and its fix rather than accepting the report, and the count is now exact.

**Two things I'd want you to know:**

- **#76 is filed**, and it's the honest limit of what I built. The test models printf widths in awk and never sees the compiled game, and it degrades if those 120-column ternaries are ever wrapped. The right shape — hoist the literals into a table, assert with real `snprintf` — touches `score()`, which is too much for a one-space fix.
- **`ui-review` found something out of scope I did *not* file:** on a plain `quit` the game prints no score sheet, then immediately asks "Do you want your score recorded?" — a number the player was never shown. It predates everything here, and by the step 9 bar it's terse 1978 UX rather than a defect that misleads. Say the word if you'd rather it were tracked.

Remaining: **#46** is now the only issue about the game itself; the other five are the process-integrity ones this session generated.

input.prompt:
Review branch `fix/tui-resize-repaint` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek (uncommitted, diff against `main`). This closes #46 and it is squarely in your remit — it changes how the full-screen interface behaves under the player's hands.

What changed in `tui.c`:
1. `tui_getch()` (the paging pause) — on `KEY_RESIZE` it now calls `tui_refresh_panels()` and waits again, instead of silently swallowing the resize and leaving the old screen until the player pressed a key. Safe there because curses reports the resize *by returning from* `wgetch`, so nothing is reading the screen at that moment.
2. `tui_readline()` — `wgetnstr` is replaced by a hand-rolled reader that takes one keystroke at a time: printable ASCII, backspace, Enter, Ctrl-D, and `KEY_RESIZE` handled between keystrokes. This is what lets a resize be redrawn mid-prompt, and it keeps the partially typed line, which `wgetnstr` discarded. Ctrl-D on an empty line now ends the session on its own keystroke instead of needing an Enter after it.

`tests/tui.sh` gains three sections: resize during a pause, resize while an answer is half typed, and Ctrl-D.

Please be hard on this from the player's side — a hand-rolled line editor is exactly where a terminal game gets subtly worse:
- **Typing feel.** Does the prompt behave as a player expects at 80x24 and 72x24? Backspace at the start of a line, backspace past the prompt (it must not eat the prompt or the panel border), a very long answer that wraps or hits the buffer limit, fast typing, holding a key down.
- **Keys that are no longer accepted.** The reader takes printable ASCII only, so arrow keys, Home/End, Delete, Tab and pasted text with control characters are now ignored rather than inserted. Is any of that a regression a player would feel? Pasting a command is the case I am least sure about.
- **The resize behaviour itself** at both sizes, during a pause and mid-typing, including shrinking (not just growing) and a resize below the 72x24 minimum.
- **Ctrl-C, Ctrl-U, Ctrl-W** and anything else a terminal user might reflexively press at a prompt.
- Whether the paging pause still needs exactly one keystroke, and whether a resize can still page away unread text.

Report findings; do not edit files. Use tmux on your own socket per AGENTS.md.

content.text:
## Verdict

**Needs changes.** The core of the fix is real and welcome: a resize during a pause now repaints immediately, a resize mid-typing no longer eats the half-typed answer (on `main` it genuinely did — I reproduced "srsc" + resize + "an" running as `an` → UNRECOGNIZED), Ctrl-D ends the session on one keystroke with a clean sign-off, plain mode is byte-identical, and the whole suite is green. But the new reader only behaves correctly when the terminal **grows**. Shrinking the height throws away the bottom of the message window — including the `[HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]` prompt and unread help text, and including the prompt-plus-typed-line mid-answer — which fails issue #46's first acceptance criterion ("leaves a correctly drawn screen without waiting for the player"), and the three new test sections only exercise growth. Separately, backspace across a wrapped answer, which `wgetnstr` handled correctly, is now broken and lets the screen and the submitted string disagree. Both are worth fixing before this lands.

## Findings

### 1. should-fix — a terminal that gets *shorter* loses the prompt and unread text
`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c` (`tui_readline` / `tui_getch` KEY_RESIZE branches, via `make_windows`'s `wresize`)

`wresize` keeps the **top** of the window, so shrinking the message window discards its bottom rows — which is exactly where the current prompt and the newest text live.

- During a pause (100x30 → 72x24, `help move`): before the resize the page ended `There are two command modes for movement...` / `manual mode requires...` / `MOVE MANUAL <deltax> <deltay>` / `[HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]`. After the resize, with no keystroke, all four lines are gone; pressing Space resumes at `<deltax> and <deltay> are the horizontal...`. Three lines of help are paged away unread — the precise failure `tui_getch`'s KEY_RESIZE guard exists to prevent, now reachable by a different route — and in the meantime the player is looking at a screen with no prompt and no cue that the game is waiting.
- Mid-typing (100x30 → 72x24 after typing `srsc`): the ` COMMAND> srsc` line vanishes and the cursor is parked mid-way along an old intro line; the next characters echo into the middle of the briefing text. The buffer is fine (Enter still ran `srscan`), but the screen is a lie.
- Width-only shrink and any growth are both fine.

The in-code comment "The typed line is not redrawn: wresize keeps what the window holds... Nothing is lost, on screen or in buf" is only true for growth.

Suggestion: have `tui.c` keep the text written since the last newline (a "current line" buffer maintained in `tui_puts`/`tui_puts_slow`) and, after a repaint triggered by a resize, re-emit that line plus the reader's `buf` on a fresh line. That satisfies the issue's own suggestion ("would let the prompt be reprinted and the partially-typed line restored") for both the pause and the typed prompt. A cheaper stopgap: before shrinking, `wscrl(wmsg, old_msgh - new_msgh)` so the bottom of the conversation survives the truncation instead of the top.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# Super Star Trek

Super Star Trek is an old text-only game, an early example of a turn-based space strategy sim, written in BASIC. In this game, you are the captain of the starship Enterprise, and your mission is to scout the federation space and eliminate all the invading Klingon ships. You will have to manage the ship energy carefully, use phasers and torpedoes to destroy the Klingons, and find starbases to repair damages and replenish your energy. All of this, rendered with a few characters on screen and a lot of imagination.

Super Star Trek is probably the most famous early text-only game ever created and it inspired many other videogames. Since the code was public domain, during the years, it was changed and improved many times. There are literally thousands of versions out there. All of them are nice, but my preference goes to the classic 1978 version called Super Star Trek.

[Read more about Star Trek and Super Star Trek.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek_%281971_video_game%29)

### Full-screen mode

Run `sst -t` for a full-screen interface: the short-range scan and the
ship's status stay on screen in two panels while the usual game
conversation scrolls below them. It needs a terminal of at least 72x24
and can be combined with the fixed-coordinate option (`sst -f -t`).
Without `-t` the game uses its classic scrolling display.

If full-screen mode isn't possible — the terminal is too small, the
game isn't attached to one (piped input, redirected output, a job with
no tty), or `TERM` names a terminal that can't address the cursor —
`-t` prints a notice and plays in the classic display instead.

### Building

The build is CMake, and a build type is required:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   # or Release
cmake --build build
./build/sst
```

You need a C17 compiler and ncurses (`libncurses-dev` on Debian and
Ubuntu; already present on macOS). `ctest --test-dir build` runs the
test suite, which includes a full-screen session driven through a real
terminal and needs `tmux` — without it that one test reports as skipped.

### Windows

There is no working Windows build at the moment.

The old instructions here were `cl /DWINDOWS /Fesst.exe *.c` from a
Visual Studio Developer Command Prompt. That has not worked for some
time: `tui.c` includes `<curses.h>` unconditionally, and `sst.c`,
`finish.c` and `osx.c` all call into it, so the full-screen display
cannot simply be left out of the file list either.

Making it work again means stubbing the display out under `#ifdef
WINDOWS` — `tui_init()` returning false, so the game always runs in its
classic scrolling form — and then actually building it on Windows to
find out what else has drifted. Nobody has a toolchain in play to check
that, so rather than leave instructions that fail, this says so.

input.message:
All three should-fixes addressed, plus the comment nit. Please re-review — particularly the shrink case, which is the one I want you to try to break again.

**1 (shrinking loses the prompt and unread text).** You were right and this was the serious one. `wresize` keeps the top of the window, so the rows it drops are exactly where the newest text and the prompt live. `make_windows()` now scrolls the difference away *before* resizing when the message window is losing height, so the oldest rows go instead of the newest:

```c
int oldh = getmaxy(wmsg);
if (msgh < oldh)
    wscrl(wmsg, oldh - msgh);
```

Verified at 100x30 → 72x24 during a `help move` pause: before the fix all four bottom lines including `[HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]` were gone; now the prompt and the three lines of help above it survive, and one Space still advances exactly one page rather than skipping the text that used to be discarded.

**2 (backspace across a wrapped answer).** Fixed — `erase_one()` now steps to the end of the row above when the cursor is at column 0, instead of returning and letting the buffer and the screen disagree. The `len > 0` guard is what keeps it off the prompt, since it can never erase more characters than were typed.

**3 (Ctrl-U).** Restored — it erases the whole line, screen and buffer together, with a comment saying it was the one piece of line editing `wgetnstr` had that this reader would otherwise have dropped.

**7 (the stale comment).** `tui_getch`'s note no longer says "the line read below" — `tui_readline` is above it, and it is no longer something you cannot repaint under.

I also took the README suggestion: one sentence saying the display follows the terminal, including mid-answer.

**Something you should know before you re-test.** While checking the shrink fix I hit `COMMAND> sc` where `srsc` had been typed, and chased it as a possible new bug. It reproduces identically on a pre-fix binary built from `main`, and the cause is mundane: `help move` has more pages than the four Spaces I was sending, so the `s` and `r` answered the remaining pause prompts before the game reached the command prompt. Not a regression, and not timing — a three-second settle makes no difference. Flagging it so you do not spend the time I did.

**6 (sub-minimum garbling)** is filed as #78 rather than fixed here: it predates the change, and deciding between "say the terminal is too small" and "genuinely clip" is a design call that deserves its own slice. The issue records that #46 made it more visible rather than caused it.

**4 and 5** (ignored keys; the silent buffer cap) will be called out in the commit as deliberate, as you asked.

The three new test sections still pass on the fixed build and all five of their assertions still fail against a pre-fix binary. I have not yet added a shrink case to the tests — tell me whether you want it in `tui.sh` given the pause section already resizes, or whether the growth case plus the manual shrink evidence is enough.

input.message:
Your finding 1 was deeper than either of us thought, and my first two fixes for it were wrong. The state has changed enough since my last message that I would ignore that one and re-test from scratch — especially the shrink.

**What was actually happening.** Curses clips the message window when *it* processes the resize, and it does that before handing the game `KEY_RESIZE`. So the bottom rows — the newest text, the prompt — are gone before any of the game's code runs. I proved it by instrumenting a scratch build: at the moment the game is told, `getmaxy(wmsg)` already reads 24 where the window had been 27.

That killed two attempts:
- scrolling the height difference away before resizing — the content sits at the *top* until the conversation has filled the window, so this threw away everything and left a blank panel (100x30 → 72x24 looked fixed, 120x40 → 72x24 went blank);
- doing the same before `resize_term` via a `TIOCGWINSZ` ioctl — too late as well, for the reason above.

**What works.** `tui.c` now keeps `curline`, the text since the last newline, updated in `tui_puts`/`tui_puts_slow`. After a resize the repaint reads the row the cursor is on and reprints that line only if the clip took it — so the prompt comes back on a shrink and is not duplicated on a growth. `tui_readline` re-echoes its buffer after that, so the answer follows the prompt back onto the screen.

Measured across five directions, all showing the prompt exactly once and the page text intact: 80x24→120x40, 100x30→72x24, 120x40→72x24, 80x24→72x24, 72x24→100x30. The 120x40→72x24 case is the one that was blank.

**Your other findings:** backspace across a wrapped line steps to the row above now; Ctrl-U restored; the stale `tui_getch` comment fixed; README sentence added.

**Tests.** `tui.sh` has a shrink block as you asked (120x40 → 72x24, the case that failed). Seven of its eight new assertions fail against a pre-fix binary and all pass against this one. The eighth — "shrinking paged away unread text" — passes pre-fix too, because the clip took the prompt and left that text; I kept it as a property worth holding and said so in the comment rather than let it look like evidence.

Please re-run your typing-feel checks as well as the resize ones: `curline` is written on every output line now, and the reader re-echoes into the window after a repaint, so I would like both paths re-tested rather than assumed. #78 is filed for the sub-minimum garbling.

## Verdict

**Needs changes.** The shrink case I asked to break is genuinely fixed on the path that mattered: at a `help move` pause, all five directions (80x24→120x40, 100x30→72x24, 120x40→72x24, 80x24→72x24, 72x24→100x30) now show the prompt exactly once with the cursor on it, and one Space still advances exactly one page; it also survives a simulated mouse drag (eight rapid resizes ending smaller, 3/3). Backspace across a wrapped answer now matches `main` exactly, Ctrl-U is back and works on wrapped lines, Ctrl-D still ends the session cleanly, a seven-command TUI journey with no resizing is byte-identical to `main`, plain mode is identical, and the suite is green. But the `curline` restore has introduced three new visible defects, all reproducible: the typed answer is echoed **twice** on any resize that did not clip the prompt (4 of the 6 directions I measured), every setup question is **duplicated** when the terminal grows, and the restore **chops the line above the prompt mid-word** after a width shrink. The first is the serious one — it hits "type a command, resize the window", and it makes the screen disagree with the buffer.

## Findings

### 1. should-fix (close to blocker) — the half-typed answer is echoed twice unless the prompt was clipped
`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c`, `tui_readline` KEY_RESIZE branch

`sync_size()` reprints `curline` only when it decides the line was clipped, but `tui_readline` re-echoes `buf` unconditionally afterwards. When nothing was clipped, the answer lands on the screen a second time. Typed `srsc` at `COMMAND>`, then resized:

| resize | line on screen |
|---|---|
| 80x24 → 120x40 | ` COMMAND> srscsrsc` |
| 80x24 → 100x30 | ` COMMAND> srscsrsc` |
| 72x24 → 100x30 | ` COMMAND> srscsrsc` |
| 80x24 → 72x24 | ` COMMAND> srscsrsc` |
| 100x30 → 72x24 | ` COMMAND> srsc` (correct) |
| 120x40 → 72x24 | ` COMMAND> srsc` (correct) |

It is not merely cosmetic. From `COMMAND> srscsrsc` I pressed Backspace four times — what a player does to undo what looks like a doubled word — and the screen settled on ` COMMAND> srsc` while the buffer was **empty**: typing `chart` then ran CHART, not `srscchart`. The display is lying about what is pending.

Suggestion: have `sync_size()` (or a small wrapper) return whether it restored the line, and re-echo `buf` only in that case. Also tighten the test — `screen | grep -qE 'COMMAND> *srsc'` in `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/tui.sh` matches `COMMAND> srscsrsc`, which is why the suite is green; anchor it (`'COMMAND> *srsc *$'`) or count occurrences.

### 2. should-fix — growing the terminal during the setup questions duplicates the question and overwrites the line above
Same file, `sync_size()`'s clipped-or-not test

Reproduced at the first two questions of a fresh game, 4/4 attempts, on every growth (72x24→100x30, 80x24→100x30, 80x24→120x40); shrinks are fine.

```
 Type in tournament number-
 Would you like a regular, tournament, or frozen game?Type in tournament number-
```

and at the difficulty question:

```
 Are you a Novice, Fair, Good, Expert, or Emeritus player?
 Would you like a Short, Medium, or Long game? Are you a Novice, Fair, Good, Expert, or Emeritus pl
 ayer?novice
```

The player then types into the second copy while the first sits above it. The trigger is the message window not yet being full — true for the whole setup conversation and the start of any game — where curses leaves the cursor a row off the pending line, so `mvwinnstr(wmsg, y, 0, ...)` reads the wrong row, `strstr` misses, and a copy is appended. The same misfire happens in-game whenever the pending line wraps: at 80x24 with 75 characters typed, a growth produced a third `COMMAND> zzz…` line below the wrapped original.

Suggestion: don't infer from a single row. Search the last few rows (or the whole window) for `curline` and, if found, just `wmove` the cursor to the end of it; only reprint when it is genuinely absent.

### 3. should-fix — the restore chops the line above the prompt mid-word
Same code path, the `waddch(wmsg, '\n')` before `waddstr(wmsg, curline)`

After a width-shrink during a pause, the last surviving line of text is cut off in the middle of a word, 2/2 attempts each for 120x40→72x24 and 100x30→72x24:

```
 current warp factor (see "W
 [HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]
```

(the real line is `current warp factor (see "WARP FACTOR").`, and `main` shows it whole). In ncurses, adding `'\n'` to a window clears to the end of the line, so the restore erases the tail of whatever row the clip left the cursor on — 28 columns here, exactly the width of the ` [HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]` prompt the cursor had been sitting after.

Suggestion: instead of `waddch('\n')`, scroll the window by one (`wscrl(wmsg, 1)`) and print the restored line on the now-blank bottom row, or `wmove` to column 0 of the next row and clear only that row. Losing the oldest row is the game's normal behaviour; mangling the newest one is not.

### 4. nit — the README sentence promises more than a shrink can deliver
`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/README.md`: "Resizing the terminal is fine at any point: the display follows it straight away… and an answer you were halfway through typing survives." The answer does survive; the *conversation* above it does not — shrinking 120x40 → 72x24 during `help move` still leaves the reader looking at the top of the page with the twelve newest lines gone, and the next Space skips past them. That is inherent (curses clips before the game is told) and the test comment says so honestly, but the README should not imply otherwise. Suggest a clause such as "text that no longer fits scrolls away, as it would in any terminal."

### Confirmed fixed from my previous pass
- Backspace across a wrapped answer at 72x24 (`emeritus maybe` → ten backspaces → `emer`, cursor after it, submitted value matching the screen) — identical to `main` now.
- Ctrl-U clears short and wrapped lines, screen and buffer together; a no-op on an empty line.
- `tui_getch`'s stale "the line read below" comment.
- Sub-minimum garbling correctly deferred to #78; the pause prompt is at least visible at 40x14 now, and 40x14 → 80x24 comes back to a clean layout.

The trigger is the message window not yet being full — true for the whole setup conversation and the start of any game — where curses leaves the cursor a row off the pending line, so `mvwinnstr(wmsg, y, 0, ...)` reads the wrong row, `strstr` misses, and a copy is appended. The same misfire happens in-game whenever the pending line wraps: at 80x24 with 75 characters typed, a growth produced a third `COMMAND> zzz…` line below the wrapped original.

Suggestion: don't infer from a single row. Search the last few rows (or the whole window) for `curline` and, if found, just `wmove` the cursor to the end of it; only reprint when it is genuinely absent.

### 3. should-fix — the restore chops the line above the prompt mid-word
Same code path, the `waddch(wmsg, '\n')` before `waddstr(wmsg, curline)`

After a width-shrink during a pause, the last surviving line of text is cut off in the middle of a word, 2/2 attempts each for 120x40→72x24 and 100x30→72x24:

```
 current warp factor (see "W
 [HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]
```

(the real line is `current warp factor (see "WARP FACTOR").`, and `main` shows it whole). In ncurses, adding `'\n'` to a window clears to the end of the line, so the restore erases the tail of whatever row the clip left the cursor on — 28 columns here, exactly the width of the ` [HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]` prompt the cursor had been sitting after.

Suggestion: instead of `waddch('\n')`, scroll the window by one (`wscrl(wmsg, 1)`) and print the restored line on the now-blank bottom row, or `wmove` to column 0 of the next row and clear only that row. Losing the oldest row is the game's normal behaviour; mangling the newest one is not.

### 4. nit — the README sentence promises more than a shrink can deliver
`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/README.md`: "Resizing the terminal is fine at any point: the display follows it straight away… and an answer you were halfway through typing survives." The answer does survive; the *conversation* above it does not — shrinking 120x40 → 72x24 during `help move` still leaves the reader looking at the top of the page with the twelve newest lines gone, and the next Space skips past them. That is inherent (curses clips before the game is told) and the test comment says so honestly, but the README should not imply otherwise. Suggest a clause such as "text that no longer fits scrolls away, as it would in any terminal."

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# Super Star Trek

Super Star Trek is an old text-only game, an early example of a turn-based space strategy sim, written in BASIC. In this game, you are the captain of the starship Enterprise, and your mission is to scout the federation space and eliminate all the invading Klingon ships. You will have to manage the ship energy carefully, use phasers and torpedoes to destroy the Klingons, and find starbases to repair damages and replenish your energy. All of this, rendered with a few characters on screen and a lot of imagination.

Super Star Trek is probably the most famous early text-only game ever created and it inspired many other videogames. Since the code was public domain, during the years, it was changed and improved many times. There are literally thousands of versions out there. All of them are nice, but my preference goes to the classic 1978 version called Super Star Trek.

[Read more about Star Trek and Super Star Trek.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek_%281971_video_game%29)

### Full-screen mode

Run `sst -t` for a full-screen interface: the short-range scan and the
ship's status stay on screen in two panels while the usual game
conversation scrolls below them. It needs a terminal of at least 72x24
and can be combined with the fixed-coordinate option (`sst -f -t`).
Without `-t` the game uses its classic scrolling display.

Resizing the terminal is fine at any point: the display follows it
straight away, even while the game is waiting for you to answer or to
press a key, and an answer you were halfway through typing survives.

If full-screen mode isn't possible — the terminal is too small, the
game isn't attached to one (piped input, redirected output, a job with
no tty), or `TERM` names a terminal that can't address the cursor —
`-t` prints a notice and plays in the classic display instead.

### Building

The build is CMake, and a build type is required:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   # or Release
cmake --build build
./build/sst
```

You need a C17 compiler and ncurses (`libncurses-dev` on Debian and
Ubuntu; already present on macOS). `ctest --test-dir build` runs the
test suite, which includes a full-screen session driven through a real
terminal and needs `tmux` — without it that one test reports as skipped.

### Windows

There is no working Windows build at the moment.

The old instructions here were `cl /DWINDOWS /Fesst.exe *.c` from a
Visual Studio Developer Command Prompt. That has not worked for some
time: `tui.c` includes `<curses.h>` unconditionally, and `sst.c`,
`finish.c` and `osx.c` all call into it, so the full-screen display
cannot simply be left out of the file list either.

Making it work again means stubbing the display out under `#ifdef
WINDOWS` — `tui_init()` returning false, so the game always runs in its
classic scrolling form — and then actually building it on Windows to
find out what else has drifted. Nobody has a toolchain in play to check
that, so rather than leave instructions that fail, this says so.

All three reproduced defects fixed, and one of them had a cause worth telling you. Please re-test.

**1 (answer echoed twice).** `restore_curline()` now reports whether it actually wrote the line out again, and `tui_readline` re-echoes its buffer only in that case. Measured across all six of your directions with `srsc` pending — 80x24→120x40, 80x24→100x30, 72x24→100x30, 80x24→72x24, 100x30→72x24, 120x40→72x24 — every one now reads ` COMMAND> srsc` exactly once. Your point about the test pattern was right and it is now anchored (`'COMMAND> *srsc *$'`), with a comment saying an unanchored one matched `srscsrsc` happily while the bug was live.

The remembered line became "Would you like a regular, tournament, or frozen game?Type in tournament number-", which exists on no single row, so the search failed and appended a copy. The reader now tells `note_out` about that newline. I also made the search scan every row bottom-up as you suggested and move the cursor to the end of the line when it finds it, and `tui_clearmsg` forgets the line. Measured: one copy in all four directions, and a partly typed `nov` at the difficulty question survives a growth with the question shown once.

**3 (line chopped mid-word).** The newline is gone — the window scrolls by one and the line is written on the blank bottom row. `current warp factor (see "WARP FACTOR").` now comes through whole on 120x40 → 72x24.

**4 (README).** Now says the question and the answer are kept, and that text which no longer fits scrolls away as it would in any terminal.

Seven of the eight new assertions fail against a pre-fix binary and all pass against this one; the eighth is the property-only one I flagged last time. Full `ctest` is rerunning in both build types.

Given three rounds of my fixes have each introduced something new, please be as unkind as you were last time — particularly to the setup conversation and to any path where the message window is not yet full, since that is where both this round's and last round's surprises came from.

Fixed, using your framing of the invariant — that was the piece I had been missing each round.

`tui.c` now keeps `pending_answer`, set by `tui_readline` around its `tui_refresh_panels()` call and NULL at a pause. `restore_curline()` builds the line it expects to see — `curline` plus whatever the reader has echoed — and looks for *that* on the last non-blank row, requiring blanks only after the pair. A surviving prompt-plus-answer is recognised and nothing is drawn; the cursor still goes to the end of `curline`, so the unconditional re-echo writes the same characters over themselves. The comment states the invariant in your words: the bottom of the conversation is the game's unfinished line and the player's unfinished answer, and the restore compares against both.

Measured, with `srsc` pending:
- one prompt in all six directions — 80x24→120x40, 80x24→100x30, 72x24→100x30, 80x24→72x24, 100x30→72x24, 120x40→72x24, each still reading ` COMMAND> srsc`;
- the twelve-step widen drag that stood up eight copies: **one** prompt, and finishing with `an` runs `srscan`;
- six alternating resizes: **one** prompt.

Your point about the tests was right and the count assertion is in: after the resize with an answer pending, `screen | grep -c 'COMMAND>'` must be 1, with a comment saying the line-shape check cannot see a duplicate because the last copy looks perfectly correct. Nine assertions fail against a pre-fix binary, all pass here, and `ctest` is rerunning in both build types.

Two things I would like you to be unkind about, since this is the fourth round and each has moved the failure somewhere new:
1. The setup conversation with an answer pending, in both directions — that is where the pending-answer path and the not-yet-full window overlap, and both have surprised me before.
2. Anything where `curline` and the echoed answer are not adjacent on one row: an answer long enough to wrap, and a prompt long enough to wrap on its own at 72 columns.

If the README's "the display follows it straight away" clause needs re-reading now that growth with a pending answer behaves, tell me the wording you would use.

## Verdict

**One should-fix left, and it is exactly the second thing you asked me to be unkind about.** The setup conversation with an answer pending is now solid in both directions — I threw seven size pairs, a twelve-step widen drag and an eight-step shrink drag at it, plus the tournament-number and password prompts (the latter right after a `clearscreen`), and every one gave a single copy with the answer intact and the cursor after it. The pending-answer invariant holds everywhere the pair fits on one row: all six directions single-copy with `srsc` finishing as `srscan`, the twelve-step drag down from eight copies to one, history-plus-shrink still landing on a fresh prompt. What is still broken is the case where `curline` and the echoed answer are **not adjacent on one row**: the search reads a single row, so a pair that wraps can never be found and is reprinted at every non-clipping resize — and it accumulates on a drag. Everything else I re-ran is clean, and I have wording for the README below.

## Findings

### 1. should-fix — a prompt-plus-answer that wraps is never recognised, so every non-clipping resize reprints it
`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c`, `restore_curline()`: `want` is built as one string but compared against a single row (`mvwinnstr(wmsg, r, 0, …)` on the last non-blank row).

- **72x24 setup question, `emeritus maybe` typed** (the question is 57 columns and the window 70, so 14 characters is enough to wrap) → grow to 100x30: the question appears **twice**, the stranded wrapped copy above and the fresh one below.
- **80x24 `COMMAND>` with 75 characters typed** → grow to 100x30: **2** copies.
- **Twelve-step widen drag with that 75-character answer pending**: **4** copies stacked up the window, each two rows tall, the briefing pushed off the top. (Fewer than the eight from last round only because the widening eventually unwraps the line, at which point the search starts working again.)
- Width-only changes fail in **both** directions: 110x30 → 80x30 (an answer that fitted now wraps) gives 2 copies, and 80x30 → 110x30 (a wrapped answer now fits) gives 2.
- Shrinks that clip the pair are fine — the reprint is the right answer there, and the re-echo rebuilds the wrap identically (`…player?emeritus mayb` / `e`, cursor after the `e`, backspace working).

Suggested fix, in the same spirit as the invariant: the on-screen form of the expected line is `want` split every `getmaxx(wmsg)` columns, so compare against that many rows rather than one. # Super Star Trek

Super Star Trek is an old text-only game, an early example of a turn-based space strategy sim, written in BASIC. In this game, you are the captain of the starship Enterprise, and your mission is to scout the federation space and eliminate all the invading Klingon ships. You will have to manage the ship energy carefully, use phasers and torpedoes to destroy the Klingons, and find starbases to repair damages and replenish your energy. All of this, rendered with a few characters on screen and a lot of imagination.

Super Star Trek is probably the most famous early text-only game ever created and it inspired many other videogames. Since the code was public domain, during the years, it was changed and improved many times. There are literally thousands of versions out there. All of them are nice, but my preference goes to the classic 1978 version called Super Star Trek.

[Read more about Star Trek and Super Star Trek.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek_%281971_video_game%29)

### Full-screen mode

Run `sst -t` for a full-screen interface: the short-range scan and the
ship's status stay on screen in two panels while the usual game
conversation scrolls below them. It needs a terminal of at least 72x24
and can be combined with the fixed-coordinate option (`sst -f -t`).
Without `-t` the game uses its classic scrolling display.

Resizing the terminal is fine at any point: the display follows it
straight away, even while the game is waiting for you to answer or to
press a key, and an answer you were halfway through typing survives. A
terminal that gets smaller keeps the question and the answer; text that
no longer fits scrolls away, as it would in any terminal.

If full-screen mode isn't possible — the terminal is too small, the
game isn't attached to one (piped input, redirected output, a job with
no tty), or `TERM` names a terminal that can't address the cursor —
`-t` prints a notice and plays in the classic display instead.

### Building

The build is CMake, and a build type is required:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   # or Release
cmake --build build
./build/sst
```

You need a C17 compiler and ncurses (`libncurses-dev` on Debian and
Ubuntu; already present on macOS). `ctest --test-dir build` runs the
test suite, which includes a full-screen session driven through a real
terminal and needs `tmux` — without it that one test reports as skipped.

### Windows

There is no working Windows build at the moment.

The old instructions here were `cl /DWINDOWS /Fesst.exe *.c` from a
Visual Studio Developer Command Prompt. That has not worked for some
time: `tui.c` includes `<curses.h>` unconditionally, and `sst.c`,
`finish.c` and `osx.c` all call into it, so the full-screen display
cannot simply be left out of the file list either.

Making it work again means stubbing the display out under `#ifdef

## Verdict: request changes

Reviewed state: branch `fix/tui-resize-repaint` at `dbcaa63` (no commits ahead of `main`); everything is unstaged — `tui.c`, `tests/tui.sh`, `README.md`. No staged or untracked files. I built with `-DSST_WERROR=ON` (clean), ran `ctest` (11/11 pass), ran `tests/tui.sh` against this build (OK) and against a `main` build (9 of the new assertions fail, so the new tests really do catch the bug), and confirmed plain mode is byte-identical to `main` on a deterministic tournament journey.

The state machine holds up under stress: 12 interleaved keystrokes and resize steps, a mixed grow/shrink drag, backspace across a wrap, Ctrl-U on a wrapped answer, and a 100x30 → 72x24 hard shrink with an 82-character pending answer all leave exactly one prompt with the answer intact. The defect below is in `restore_curline`'s write position, not in the four static variables.

---

### Findings

**1. should-fix — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c:329`: the rewrite is anchored to the bottom of the window, but the stump is only at the bottom once the conversation has filled it.**

`r = maxy - rows;` assumes the clipped line occupies the last rows of `wmsg`. That is true only when the message window is full. Before it fills — the whole setup conversation, and after every `clearscreen()` — the live line sits in the middle, so the clear-and-rewrite lands on blank rows below it and the mangled stump survives above.

Reproduced on this build (not on a hypothetical): `sst -t` at 110x40, type an 82-character answer to the first setup question, then shrink width only to 76:

```
29: Would you like a regular, tournament, or frozen game?abcdefghijklmnopqrstuv
30: REDACTED            <- stump, plus a stale wrap remnant
   (8 blank rows)
39: Would you like a regular, tournament, or frozen game?abcdefghijklmnopqrstu
40: REDACTED
```

Same shape for a corner drag at the command prompt (120x24 → 76x34): stump at rows 13-14, live copy at rows 23-24, nine blank rows between. The comment at tui.c:312-321 says these rows get "rubbed out and [the line written] in their place", and the block comment at tui.c:246-254 separately accepts a duplicate — the two disagree, and the code does the worse of the two whenever the window is not full. By the standard the new tests themselves apply (`grep -c 'COMMAND>' -ne 1` at tests/tui.sh:626), this is a failure.

Fix: the scan at tui.c:272-274 already computes the last non-blank row; keep it (`last = r`) and use `r = last - rows + 1`, clamping `r < 0` to 0 and falling back to `maxy - 1` when `last < 0`. When the height shrank, `last == maxy - 1` and the behaviour is unchanged; when it did not, the stump is erased and there is no duplicate at all. While there, note `rows = total / oldmsgw + 1` (tui.c:328) over-counts by one when `total` is an exact multiple of `oldmsgw`, which with the anchored fix would rub out a row of live history above the stump.

**2. should-fix — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/tui.sh:601-648`: no test types an answer and then shrinks.**

"resize typing" grows (80x24 → 110x32), and "shrink history" types *after* the shrink. So the one path where a pending answer can actually be clipped — a width shrink with `pending_answer` set — has no coverage, which is why finding 1 survived five review rounds. A case that types a wrapping answer and then narrows the terminal (asserting the pair appears exactly once) would have caught it, and would also lock in the behaviour the block comment at tui.c:246-254 promises.

**3. nit — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c:190`: `note_out` treats `\r` as an ordinary character; curses treats it as a column reset.**

`pause()` (sst.c:784) writes `"\r                           \r"` through `proutn`, so after every paging pause `curline` holds 56 bytes that render as an empty row. I confirmed with an instrumented build that those CRs do land in `curline`. The search in `restore_curline` can then never match the screen, so the line is reprinted rather than recognised. It is masked at the command prompt only because `chew()` zeroes `linecount` before that prompt's `skip(1)`; any prompt printed straight after a pause with no intervening newline (e.g. `plaque()`'s `skip(2)` then `proutf("File or device name…")`) is exposed. One-line fix: reset on `\r` as well as `\n` — after the erase, `curline` then equals exactly what the row shows.

**4. nit — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c:549`: `cursor_at_prompt` is only reset inside `sync_size`'s resized branch.**

If a `KEY_RESIZE` is ever dequeued after the size was already adopted by an earlier `tui_refresh_panels()`, `sync_size` returns at tui.c:356 and `cursor_at_prompt` keeps a stale `TRUE`, so `waddstr(wmsg, buf)` doubles the answer on screen. I could not produce it — ncurses only queues `KEY_RESIZE` from `resizeterm` when the OS size differs from `LINES`/`COLS`, which `resize_term(0, 0)` has already equalised — so this is defensive only. Setting `cursor_at_prompt = FALSE;` immediately before the `tui_refresh_panels()` call in the `KEY_RESIZE` branch makes the invariant local and removes the need for that argument.

**5. nit — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c:256`: `want[sizeof curline + 160]` encodes an undocumented coupling.**

The 160 is sized against `readinput`'s callers (`line[128]` in sst.c:12, `winner[128]` in finish.c). It is safe today (255 + 126 + 1 = 382 < 416) and `snprintf` cannot overflow, but if `line[]` ever grows past 162 the string is silently truncated and the search stops matching — a silent behaviour change, not a crash. A comment naming the buffer it is sized against would keep that honest.

---

### Not blocking, for the record

- A resize below the 72x24 minimum and back permanently corrupts the layout: `make_windows` never re-sizes `wquad`, and ncurses' `resize_term` stretches it to the whole screen on the way back, hiding the message window (typing then goes nowhere visible). I reproduced this identically on the `main` build, so it is pre-existing and out of scope — but the new README paragraph at `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/README.md:17`, "Resizing the terminal is fine at any point", reads as a stronger promise than the code keeps.
- A stray glyph can be left in the message window's unowned right-hand column after a shrink (the emulator's own reflow; `msgw = COLS-2` leaves that column unpainted). It self-corrects at the next resize. A `clearok(curscr, TRUE)` in `sync_size` would remove the class.
- `room = buflen-2`, the `buf[len] = 0` / `strcat(buf, "\n")` pair, and the `strncat` bound in `restore_curline` are all correct for the buffers actually passed (`readinput` is only ever called with 128).

### What I could not review

- Behaviour on terminals wider than 511 columns (`onscreen[512]`) or under a non-ncurses curses: I only exercised ncurses under tmux on Linux.
- The macOS/`WINDOWS` builds of `osx.c`'s `getch()` path.
- Whether real terminal emulators (xterm, Kitty, Terminal.app) clip `wmsg` the same way tmux does on shrink — the whole premise of `restore_curline` is ncurses-side, so it should hold, but I verified it only through tmux.
